en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Great Chronicle (Mahāvaṃsa-pāḷi), First Chapter.
Having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One, who is perfectly pure and born of a pure lineage,
I shall proclaim the *Mahāvaṃsa*, which contains various [accounts] neither deficient nor redundant.
This [work] was composed by the ancients, though in some places it is overly prolix,
in others excessively concise, and contains many repetitions.
Avoiding those faults, this [work] is easy to grasp and retain.
It inspires serene confidence and a sense of spiritual urgency,
and it has been handed down through oral tradition.
Listen to that which generates confidence and spiritual urgency when encountered in a place that produces such states.
Having seen the Perfectly Enlightened One Dīpaṅkara,
the Conqueror made a vow for enlightenment in order to liberate the world from suffering. Then,
[he saw] that very same Perfectly Enlightened One, Koṇḍañña, and the Sage Maṅgala.
Sumana, Revata, and Buddha; Sobhita and the Great Sage (Mahāmuni);
the Sambuddha Anomadassi, Paduma, and the Victor Nārada;
the Sambuddha Padumuttara, and the Tathāgata Sumedha.
Sujāta and Piyadassin, the Leader Atthadassin;
Dhammadassin and Siddhattha, Tissa and the Victor Phussa.
Vipassī, the Sambuddha Sikhī, and the all-pervading Sambuddha Vessabhū.
The Fully Enlightened One Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana as well,
and the Sugata Kassapa— having propitiated these twenty-four Fully Enlightened Ones,
the Great Hero was prophesied for enlightenment by them.
Having purified all perfections and attained supreme enlightenment,
the supreme Buddha Gotama liberated beings from suffering.
At Rūvelā in Magadha, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Great Sage—
On the full moon of Visākha, he attained supreme enlightenment.
For seven days there, that master dwelt, experiencing the supreme bliss of liberation and manifesting its sweetness.
Then, having gone to Bārāṇasī, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma;
dwelling there for the rains retreat, he made sixty [disciples] Arahants.
Having dispatched those bhikkhus for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma,
Having then instructed the Bhaddavaggiyas, thirty in number,
the Protector, while dwelling at Uruvelā during the winter, brought to maturity the thousand jaṭilas headed by Kassapa, whom he was to instruct.
When the great sacrifice of Uruvelakassapa was underway,
Rimaddana, having understood the desire for his own arrival,
brought alms from Uttarakuru.
Having eaten at Lake Anotatta, at the time of evening,
on the ninth month from his enlightenment, on the full moon day of the month of Phussa,
the Victor arrived at the island of Laṅkā in order to purify the island of Laṅkā.
"Lanka is indeed known by the Jina as a place that illuminates the Sasana;
and because Lanka was filled with yakkhas, [he said], 'May the yakkhas attain Nibbana.
Thus it was known in the midst of Lanka, in the delightful region of Gangabhiraka."
In that delightful Mahānāgavana garden, three yojanas long and one yojana wide,
upon the battlefield of the yakkhas,
there was a great assembly of mighty yakkhas from the island of Laṅkā.
The Sugata arrived at that great assembly of yakkhas;
in the midst of that gathering, the Jina stood there in the air above their heads at the site of the Mahiyangana Thūpa.
He caused a storm of wind and darkness, creating a sense of urgency in them.
Those yakkhas, standing in fear, begged the Victor for safety;
the Victor, the giver of fearlessness, spoke to those yakkhas who were trembling with terror.
"Yakkhas, you have fear and suffering; I shall take this away from you.
Grant me, all together, a place here for me to sit.
Those yakkhas said to the Sugata, "We give it to you here, O Noble One."
"Grant us all, indeed, freedom from fear throughout the entire island.
Having dispelled their fear, cold, and darkness on that granted ground,
the Victor spread out his leather mat, sat there, and remained.
He extended his skin-hood, which was ablaze on all sides;
overcome by the heat and terrified, they stood at the edges all around.
Then the Protector brought them here to the delightful Isle of the Mountain.
When they had entered therein, the Protector established them each in their proper place.
He then condensed the Dhamma, and at that time the devas assembled;
in that assembly of theirs, the Teacher proclaimed the Dhamma.
There was a realization of the Dhamma for many millions of beings;
countless others became established in the refuges and the precepts.
Having attained the fruit of stream-entry on Mount Sumanakūṭaka, they remained there.
The great lord of gods, Mahāsumana, having made offerings,
requested an offering. Having touched his head— whose hair was dark and as pure as the *āmala* fruit—
the Jina, for the sake of that being’s life, gave him a handful of hair.
Thus, taking that excellent golden casket from the Teacher,
he placed it upon a heap of various jewels fashioned at the place where [the Buddha] had sat,
setting his hair-treasures down on all sides within a space of seven ratanas.
Thus, with a stupa of sapphire, he covered it and paid homage.
When the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained parinibbāna, the elder named Sarabhū, by means of his supernormal power,
took the collarbone of the Victor from the funeral pyre.
The disciple of the Elder Sāriputta, having brought [the relics] to that very cetiya and established them there, surrounded by monks,
that one of great psychic power had it covered with stones the color of fat.
Having caused a stupa twelve cubits high to be built, he departed.
Seeing that marvelous cetiya, Uddhacūḷābhaya by name, the younger brother of King Devānaṃpiyatissa, [was moved].
Having covered that [stūpa], King Maddanta, the subduer of the Damilas and the bringer of suffering to his enemies, erected a cetiya thirty cubits high while stationed there.
He then constructed for it an outer casing-cetiya eighty cubits high.
Thus was this Mahiyaṅgaṇa Thūpa established.
Having thus made this island worthy of men,
the Wise One, the Lord of heroic prowess, went to Uruvelā.
The arrival at Mahiyaṅgaṇa is concluded.
The Teacher of Great Compassion, who delights in the welfare of the entire world, arrived at Nāgadīpa.
In the fifth year after his enlightenment, the Victor resided at Jetavana.
For the sake of the nāgas Mahodara and Cūḷodara—
maternal uncle and nephew— he [performed a miracle] on account of a jeweled couch.
Having seen the battle arrayed before him along with his followers,
the Fully Enlightened One, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha,
took up his excellent bowl and robe at the very break of dawn.
Out of compassion for the nāgas, he went to Nāgadīpa.
At that time, even the king of the snakes was full of great reverence;
he dwelt in the ocean abode of the nāgas, which extended for one thousand yojanas.
His youngest sister was Kaṇhā; on Mount Vaḍḍhamāna she was given in marriage to a nāga king, and his son was Cūḷodara.
His mother, O Great Mother, [gave] an excellent jeweled couch.
Having given her away, the Nāga queen passed away, and thus he was reunited with his maternal uncle.
A battle had indeed arisen for his nephew;
those mountain-dwelling Nāgas were possessed of great supernatural power.
A deity named Samiddhisumana, taking the Rājāyatana tree standing in the Jeta Grove,
[created] his own beautiful mansion. With the Buddha’s very permission,
he fashioned it in the shape of a parasol over the Victor.
Bearing [the burden], he approached that place where he had previously lived.
For he was a deity in Nāgadīpa, and in his immediately following existence, he became a human being;
standing at the Rājāyatana site, he saw it.
Seeing the Paccekabuddhas eating, he gladdened his heart and gave them branches for cleaning their alms-bowls;
by that deed, he was reborn in the delightful Jeta Grove where a tree had grown.
On the side of the Dvārakoṭṭhaka gate, he was later situated outside.
Seeing the growth of that god among gods,
[the Buddha] brought that tree here to this place for the sake of its benefit.
Seated there in the sky in the midst of the battle, the Leader,
the dispeller of darkness, brought about the destruction of those elephants.
Consoling them as they were overcome by fear, he caused light to be shed.
Seeing the Sugata, they were delighted and paid homage at the feet of the Teacher.
The Jina taught them the Dhamma that brings about harmony;
both of them, being filled with joy, offered that couch to the Muni.
The Teacher, having descended to the ground and being pleased with that seat,
was gratified by those nāga kings with divine food and drink.
There were eighty million serpents dwelling both in the water and on the surface of the earth.
The Leader established him in the Refuges and the Precepts.
Maṇiakkhika, the maternal uncle of the Nāga Mahodara and king of the Nāgas in Kalyāṇī, went there to wage war.
In the first [visit] to Buddhagāma, having heard the teaching of the True Dhamma and being established in the refuges and precepts, he there entreated the Tathāgata:
"O Protector, this great compassion has been shown by you."
If you do not come, we shall all be reduced to ashes.
O Father, have compassion for the earth; let there be a separate, great realm, and let this place be my own dwelling through your return.
Having consented by remaining silent, the Blessed One established the Rājāyatana Shrine right there.
And that Rājāyatana Shrine was a most precious couch-throne.
The Lord of the World went to pay homage to those Naga kings.
"O Naga kings, you should pay homage to my Relic Shrine of Use (paribhoga-cetiya);
that will be for your protection, for your welfare, and for your happiness."
Having thus given this and other such instructions to the nāgas, the Sugata,
out of compassion for the world, went back to Jetavana.
Thus ends the account of the visit to Nāgadīpa.
Then, in the third year, that lord of nāgas,
Maṇiakkhika, arrived auspiciously.
Having approached the Fully Enlightened One,
he invited him along with the community of monks.
In the eighth year after his enlightenment, the Victor was dwelling at Jetavana.
The Lord, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus,
the Conqueror, the Chief of Sages, on the second day at the time of the meal,
during the delightful month of Vesākha on the full moon day.
Having put on his outer robe right there and taking up his bowl,
he went to that auspicious region where the jeweled eye was fixed.
At the site of the Kalyāṇī Cetiya, within the constructed pavilion of gems, he arrived.
He entered upon the great, worthy couch together with his assembly.
With divine foods, both hard and soft, the Naga king, with a joyful mind, gratified the Jina,
the King of Dhamma, along with his own retinue.
Having taught the Dhamma there, the Teacher,
compassionate and the Leader, ascended Mount Sumana and displayed his footprint.
At the foot of that mountain, the Saṅgha together with him remained as they pleased.
Having spent the day in meditation, he approached Dīghavāpī.
There, at the site of the cetiya, the Protector sat together with the Saṅgha and applied himself to concentration for the attainment of the state of an Arhat.
Then, having risen from that place, the Great Sage, skilled in what is possible and impossible, went to the site of the Mahāmeghavana Monastery.
Having sat down at the site where the Great Bodhi tree stands, together with his disciples, he—
Likewise, the Protector entered into samādhi while standing at the Mahāthūpa;
and likewise at the site of the Thūpārāma and at the very spot where the stupa stands.
Then, emerging from samādhi, he went to the site of the Silācetiyas.
When the host of gods had assembled, the Teacher instructed the assembly;
then the Buddha, the All-Knowing One, went to Jetavana.
Thus the Lord of Laṅkā, possessing immeasurable wisdom, looked toward the welfare of the future.
At that time, perceiving the welfare of the hosts of gods, nagas, and others in Laṅkā, the Lamp of the World,
possessed of exceedingly vast compassion, came three times to this most excellent island. Because of him,
this island became a source of great honor for the virtuous, shining like the Island of the Dhamma.
The Arrival of the Auspicious One,
titled "The Approach of the Tathāgata," from the Mahāvaṃsa composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The First Chapter.
The Second Chapter:
The Lineage of Mahāsammatu.
The Great Sage was born in the lineage of King Mahāsammata;
at the beginning of the eon, he was the king named Mahāsammatanāmaka.
Then there were Roja and Vararoja, as well as the two Kalyāṇakas.
Uposatha and Mandhātā, Caraka and Apacara the two,
Cetīya and Mucala as well as the one named Mahāmucala,
Mucalinda and Sāgara, and Sāgara Devavana by name.
Bharata and Bhagīratha, Ruci and Suruci;
Patāpa and Mahāpatāpa, and likewise Panādā and [Mahāpanādā], these two;
Sudassana and Neru, and likewise two by two.
And "the latter" refers to the kings, his sons and grandsons.
These twenty-eight rulers of the earth, possessing incalculable lifespans,
dwelt in Kusāvatī, Rājagaha, and Mithilā.
Then there were one hundred and fifty-six kings;
eighty-four thousand and thirty-six more after that;
thirty-two, twenty-eight, and twenty-two after those.
Eighteen, seventeen, fifteen, and fourteen;
nine, seven, and twelve; twenty-five, and then another;
twenty-five, twelve, and twelve, and nine as well.
There were eighty-four thousand [kings] beginning with Makha-deva,
and eighty-four thousand beginning with Kaḷāraja-naka.
These descendants of Okkāka down to Rāsi number sixteen thousand.
Each one ruled the kingdom individually, governing in succession:
Okkāmukha was the eldest son, followed by King Okkāka,
Nipura, Candimā, Candamukha, Sivi, and Sañjaya.
The great king Vessantara, Jālī, and Sīhavāhana,
and Sīhassara— these were his sons, his children.
There were eighty-two thousand [sons] of King Sīhassara.
Putta, Pa, and Putta were the kings, Jayasena being the last of them.
These were renowned as the Śākya kings in Kapilavatthu;
the great king Siṃhahanu was the son of Jayasena.
And the daughter of Jayasena was named Yasodharā;
Devadaha had a king named Devadaha.
Then Añjana and Kaccānā were his two sons.
Kaccānā was the chief queen of King Sīhahanu.
She was Yasodharā, the chief queen of Añjana-Sakka.
Añjana had two daughters: Māyā and Pajāpatī.
There were two sons with staffs in hand, Suppabuddha and the Śākya;
there were five sons and two daughters born to Sīhahanu.
[They were] Suddhodana, Dhotodana, Śakrodana, Sukrodana, and Amitodana.
"Amitā and Pamitā"—these five and these two [are mentioned].
Amitā was the chief queen of Suppabuddha the Sakyan;
she had two sons, Bhaddakaccānā and Devadatta.
Māyā and Mahāpajāpatī were the chief queens of King Suddhodana;
that Conqueror was the son of Māyā and the great King Suddhodana.
While the lineage of Mahāsammata remained undivided, the Great Sage appeared.
Thus born at the time of his manifestation, she stood above all the Khattiyas.
She was the chief queen Bhaddakaccānā to the young prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta; her son was Rāhula.
Bimbisāra and Prince Siddhattha were companions; their fathers, too, had been friends.
The Bodhisatta was five years older than Bimbisāra.
At the age of twenty-nine, the Bodhisatta went forth.
Having exerted himself for six years and subsequently attained enlightenment,
he approached Bimbisāra at the age of thirty-five.
Then, at the age of fifteen, the highly wise Bimbisāra was himself consecrated and attained that kingdom.
When he had reached his sixteenth year, the Teacher taught the Dhamma.
He indeed reigned for fifty-two years.
Fifteen years of his reign had passed prior to the previous meeting with the Jina;
thirty-seven years remained while the Tathāgata was still living.
The son of Bimbisāra, Ajātasattu, having killed his father through evil counsel,
ruled the kingdom for thirty-two years.
In the eighth year of Ajātasattu’s reign, the Sage attained Parinibbāna.
Afterwards, he ruled the kingdom for twenty-four years.
The Tathāgata, who had attained supremacy over the entire world, came under the power of impermanence.
"Thus, he who here contemplates impermanence, which gives rise to fear,
becomes one who has gone beyond suffering."— From the *Mahāvaṃsa*,
composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Second Chapter, titled "The Lineage of Mahāsammatā.
The Third Chapter.
The First Council on the Dhamma:
The Conqueror Pañcanetta, together with forty-five companions,
having stood firm and performed all his duties in every way for the sake of the world.
Between the twin sāla trees in Kusinārā, on the full moon day of Vesākha,
that island of the world passed into parinibbāna.
There, bhikkhus gathered in numbers beyond counting.
Khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, and likewise devas—
seven hundred thousand of these were the leading bhikkhus among them;
at that time, the Elder Mahākassapa was the senior of the Saṅgha.
Having performed the rites for the relics and bodily remains of the Teacher,
that great elder, desiring the long endurance of the Teacher’s Dhamma,
[acted] when the Lord of the World, the Ten-Powered One, had attained final Nibbāna seven days prior.
The Buddha remembered Subhadda’s ill-spoken words;
he remembered the gift of the robe and likewise his placing [Subhadda] on equal footing.
For the sake of establishing the True Dhamma, the Sage bestowed this favor.
In order to perform the rehearsal of the True Dhamma, the ascetic [Mahinda] approached the five hundred bhikkhus—
preeminent, great destroyers of the cankers— who were bearers of the ninefold Dispensation and possessed of all its branches,
in accordance with the will of the Fully Enlightened Ones.
However, because of the Elder Ānanda, he was appointed with one person short [of the required number]. Then, when the monks requested it,
the Elder Ānanda was also appointed to perform the recitation, for it was not possible to do so without him.
Having spent half a month— the seven days of the "Excellent Play" festival and the seven days for the distribution of the relics—
the Compassionate One toward all the world remained in Rājagaha for the rains retreat; we shall now perform the compilation of the Dhamma.
Having made the firm resolve that no others should dwell there,
those elders wandered on their journey throughout Jambudīpa, consoling the great masses of people who were afflicted with grief here and there.
During the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷhī,
those who desired to abide in the bright fortnight approached Rājagaha, where the four requisites were fully provided.
It was right there that Mahākassapa and the others entered the rains retreat.
The elders, endowed with steadfast virtues and skilled in the doctrine of the Fully Enlightened One,
spoke to Ajātasattu and had repairs carried out in all the monasteries during the first month of the rains.
When the restoration of the monastery was completed, the king said:
"Now we shall perform the rehearsal of the Dhamma.
When asked what should be done, they assigned him a seat and other such arrangements.
Having asked them, "Where is the king?", he had a pavilion quickly constructed by them on the side of Mount Vebhāra at the place they indicated—
a delightful spot near the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, resembling the assembly hall of the gods.
Having had it thoroughly adorned on every side,
he had priceless rugs spread there for the assembly of monks.
Relying upon the southern part, [he arranged] that supreme [seat] facing north.
A most precious and well-prepared seat for the elders was there;
in the center of that pavilion, facing eastward,
a supreme Dharma-seat worthy of the Sugata was well-prepared.
The king informed the elders, "Our work is not yet finished";
those elders spoke to the elder Ānanda, the bringer of joy:
"Ānanda, there is an assembly tomorrow; one who is still in training must go there."
"You are not engaged in the true goal; therefore, be diligent!
Thus exhorted, the Elder exerted balanced energy and attained Arhatship, which is free from the [ordinary] modes of conduct.
In the second month of the rains, on the second day,
those elders assembled in that beautiful pavilion,
except for the seat appropriate for the Elder Ānanda.
The Arahants sat down upon their seats according to their rank.
That Elder did not go among them to announce his attainment of Arahantship;
however, when some asked, "Where is the Elder Ānanda? [he appeared].
Having plunged into the earth or traveled by way of the path of light,
the Elder Ānanda sat down upon the seat prepared for himself.
The Elder Upāli [sat] regarding the Vinaya and all the remaining teachings without exception.
All the senior elders appointed the Elder Ānanda as their leader.
The Great Elder himself was appointed to inquire about the Vinaya concerning his own affairs,
while the Elder Upāli was appointed to provide the answer to that very matter.
Having sat upon the elder’s seat, he asked that matter of the Vinaya;
having sat upon the Dhamma seat, he himself answered it in that very way.
By means of the path of those who know the Vinaya, according to the sequence of the answers given, they...
All those skilled in the principles of the Vinaya engaged in recitation.
Having appointed themselves as the guardians of the treasury of the Great Sage—
the foremost among those of great learning— that Elder questioned the Dhamma.
Having thus appointed himself, he himself took his place upon the Dhamma-seat;
and Ānanda Thera expounded that Dhamma in its entirety.
By that sage Vedeha, in the order in which it was expounded, those [questions] were answered.
All those experts in the Dhamma and its meaning performed the recitation.
Thus, within seven months, the Council of the Dhamma was completed;
for the benefit of the entire world, it was accomplished by them for the welfare of the whole world.
By the Elder Mahākassapa, this teaching of the Sugata was rendered capable of enduring for five thousand years.
With extreme joy having arisen, [he became] the bearer and the sustainer.
At the conclusion of the *Saṃgīti*, the great earth shook in six ways,
and many wonders occurred in the world in manifold manners.
Because they were performed by elders (*thera*), this is called the lineage of the Elders (*Theravāda*).
Having first compiled the vast collection for the welfare of the entire world,
all those elders remained for the full span of their lives and then attained final Nibbāna. Those elders, too,
were lamps of wisdom that destroyed the darkness.
The great lamps that dispel the darkness of the world have been extinguished by the terrible great wind of death;
therefore, the wise person should abandon pride in life.
The third chapter, titled "The First Council of the Dhamma," in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and a sense of spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
In the fourth chapter,
the second council:
Having had him killed, the noble Ajātasattu’s son gave [the wealth] away.
That betrayer of friends reigned for sixteen years.
His son, Udayabhadda, had him killed;
and Anuruddhaka, the son of Anuruddha, had that one named Muṇḍa killed.
Mittadduna and Dummatin, they too exercised sovereignty;
in the reigns of both of them, eight years passed away.
Muṇḍa’s son, Nāgadāsaka, having slain his father, [ruled].
That evil one reigned for twenty-four years.
This was the lineage of the patricides;
then the citizens, filled with indignation, assembled and removed King Nāgadāsaka.
They consecrated Susunāga, the minister renowned and esteemed by the virtuous,
upon the throne, their hearts intent on the welfare of all.
He ruled the kingdom as king for eighteen years.
Kāḷāsoka was his son, who caused twenty-eight [stūpas] to be built.
In the tenth year past from the final nibbāna of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
one hundred years had thus elapsed since the passing of King Kāḷāsoka.
Then at Vesālī, many Vajjiputtaka monks [proposed] these ten points:
salt in a horn, two finger-breadths [of food], and likewise [eating] within the village boundary;
consent for a residence, customary practice, unchurned butter, and water with sediment.
"The sitting mat without a border, gold and so forth—
these ten bases the shameless ones declared to be allowable.
Having heard this while wandering on tour among the Vajjis, the Elder Yasa spoke thus.
Possessing the six supernormal powers and having attained the [ten] strengths,
the illustrious descendant of Kākaṇḍaka set out with determination to meet him and came to that Mahāvana forest.
Leaving behind his bowl for the Uposatha ceremony along with the bronze vessel containing the water, he remained there.
"Give kahāpaṇas and other wealth to the Saṅgha," said the lay followers.
"That is not allowable; do not give it," the Elder thus forbade them.
They then performed an act of reconciliation (paṭisāraṇīya-kamma) against the Elder Yasa.
Having requested an accompanying envoy, he went to the city together with him;
after making himself known as one who speaks according to the Dhamma, he returned to the ocean.
Hearing the words of the envoy, they came to seize him.
The monks stood surrounding the elder’s dwelling.
Then the elder, having ascended into the sky and traveled from there to Kosambī,
quickly went into the presence of the Pāveyyaka Vajjiputta monks.
He himself dispatched messengers, who went to Mount Gaṅga and reported everything to the Elder Saṇavāsin and to the Elder Sambhūta.
Also the sixty elders of Pāveyyaka and those of Asita-Avantika.
All those great ones whose taints were destroyed descended at the Ahogaṅgā.
Monks had gathered there from every direction;
they numbered ninety thousand, and all of them were free from blemish. Having consulted together, they all descended.
Soreyya, knowing that the Elder Revata was highly learned and free from taints—
that leader of the assembly— set out to see him.
Having heard their deliberation, the Elder departed for Vesālī.
Desiring a pleasant journey, he departed from there at that very moment.
Because of the great distance of the place he had departed from early each morning,
those arriving there every evening perceived him together with the three fires.
Therein, the Elder Yaśas was exhorted by the Elder Sambhūta;
at the conclusion of hearing the True Dharma,
he approached the most excellent Elder Revata and asked him about the ten points, but the Elder rejected them.
Having heard of that legal dispute, he said, "Stop it!
Even those who were wicked, looking for an opportunity against the most excellent Elder Revata,
prepared many inferior requisites.
Having traveled quickly by boat, they reached the vicinity of Sahajāti and,
when the time for the meal had arrived, they prepared the distribution of food.
While residing at Sahajāti, the Elder Sāḷha reflected:
"The inhabitants of Pāvā are speakers of Dhamma," thus the one free from taints perceived.
Having approached him, Mahābrahmā declared, "He has reached the culmination in the Dhamma";
and he [the Tathāgata] spoke to him of his own steadfastness in the Dhamma.
Taking those requisites, they saw the Elder Revata;
the Elder did not accept them, but sent away his disciple who had taken their side.
Then they went from there to Vesālī, and from there they went to Pupphapura.
The shameless ones spoke thus to King Kālāsoka:
"We, guarding the Teacher’s perfumed chamber there,
dwell in the Mahāvana monastery in the land of the Vajjis."
"We shall take the monastery," said the village-dwelling monks;
"O Great King, do not obstruct them as they come.
Having caused the king to hold a mistaken view, they arrived at Vesālī.
At the foot of the Revata Thera tree,
eleven hundred thousand bhikkhus together with ninety thousand more assembled there at that very moment. That was the occasion for the Saṅgha.
The Elder did not approve of the proposal to reconcile with the schismatics without the presence of the original founders;
consequently, all those monks returned to Vesālī.
That king, having misunderstood the situation, dispatched his ministers there.
By the power of the gods, those [messengers] departed for another place.
Having sent them away, that protector of the earth saw himself in a dream that very night cast into a cauldron of molten iron.
The king was terrified; he could not find a bridge across the darkness.
But the sister, the nun Nandā, free from taints, traveled through the air.
"A heavy deed has been done by you; ask forgiveness from the noble lady who lives in the Dhamma."
"Having become their partisan, you must uphold the teaching.
When this is done, there will be safety for you. Having said this, he departed;
the king set out from Pāsāṇaka to go to Vesālī.
Having gone to the great forest and assembled the community of monks,

The Sixth Chapter:
The Arrival of Vijayā.

The *yakkhas* in the city were agitated, but one daring man,

Then her uncle, the *yakkha*, having gone out from the city;
Seeing those children, he asked, "Whose sons are you?

Right there in Malaya, indeed, was the origin of these Pulindas.

"Ruling over the entire island of Laṅkā in accordance with the Dhamma,

The Consecration of Paṇḍuvāsudeva.
That great king Vijaya remained in his final year.

Those [waters] from the Mahākandara river descended into your mouth;

The eighth chapter, titled "The Consecration of Paṇḍuvāsudeva," in the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The ninth chapter:
The Consecration of Fearlessness.

When the time for childbirth arrived, I entered the birth-chamber.

"Relying on him in this task," O village headman and attendant.
When they refused to give that promise, the princes had them executed;

This concludes the section titled "The Consecration of Abhaya" in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Ninth Chapter.
The Tenth Chapter:
The Consecration of Paṇḍukābhaya.
At the command of Ummādacittā, a maidservant took the boy,

"I am going to the gateway to offer my daughter's ball of rice and cake," she replied.
"Bring it down! they said, addressing the prince.

at that very moment, they assumed the form of a great boar.

"Since you were seven years old, O uncle, having recognized this,

Submerging himself and entering through a hole,

When he had arrived among men, the prince put on his garment,

Having heard that the prince was still alive,

On that very day, the cowherds obtained a single four-footed animal.
He sent that young boy to the village to fetch fire.

"There you shall eat charcoal and meat"—
having heard those words, he did not [believe] them.

Then, when she was sixteen years old, her maternal uncles recognized her [maturity];

Having given him a thousand slaves, he sent him to the presence of Paṇḍula.
There was a brahmin named Paṇḍula, wealthy and a master of the Vedas,

The prince, having gone there, saw the brahmin Paṇḍuka;
having asked, "Are you Paṇḍukābhaya, dear one?

Learn a craft, dear son," he said, and so he had him learn a craft;

He gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for the purpose of gathering warriors;

Having addressed the Great Sage Kurucanda, my son and the chaplain,

Having gained power in the town near Kāsapabbata,

Surrounded by his followers, he went to the mountain named Girikaṇḍa.
There, Paṇḍukābhaya’s maternal uncle, named Girikaṇḍasiva,

When a hundred karīsas had been harvested, the kṣatriya then caused them to be gathered.

Having caused him to eat his father’s meal, he went to the chicken-farm.
There, seeing a young girl among the people, they informed the prince;

Seeing them, the prince recalled the words spoken by the twice-born.
In the village of Mahesibhāva, he was pleased because he had obtained a maiden.

Taking the girl, the kshatriya ascended his chariot.
Surrounded by a great force, he marched out in pursuit.
Hearing of this, her father dispatched all his men;

There was a village named Kalahanagara;

All of them, Candoyeva, the son of Paṇḍula, put to death.

then Paṇḍukābhaya, exerting his great power, [advanced].
On the further bank of the Ganges,
he went to Doḷapabbataka.
There, O Mātula, he dwelt for four years.
Having heard this and setting aside the king, they approached for the sake of battle.
Having established their camp near Dhūmarakkha,
they fought with their nephew, while the nephew fought with his maternal uncle.
Having bathed in the Oruvela Ganges and returned,
he dwelt for two years in their military camp. Then,
having gone to Upatissa’s village, they reported that matter to the king.

"Cross over to the further bank of the Ganges; do not go back this way.

For twenty years, this Abhaya, the giver of fearlessness,
ruled the kingdom there in Upatissagāma.
She dwells in the Dhūmarakkha mountain range, at the Tumbariyaṅgaṇa lake;

"O horse-stealer, such is this! he announced to the prince.
Taking the reins, the prince approached to seize him;
seeing that he was not coming from behind, she became terrified by his splendor.
Having run and vanished from sight, they ran after me in pursuit;
as I ran, that lake surrounded me seven times.
Having descended into the Great Gaṅgā and then having crossed over it;
He encircled that mountain Dhūmarakkha seven times.

Having gone to that Dhūmarakkha mountain and ascended it, that one of great strength dwelt there for four years in the Dhūmarakkha cave. Then,

Having protected the army, he entered the camp;

In that very village, he had a most excellent city built.

The Mahāsusāna execution ground, likewise the western Rājī river;

The site of the Yona assembly hall, and the Mahejja house as well.

And between King Paṇḍukābhaya and Abhaya—

The Eleventh Chapter.
After the consecration of Devānampiyatissa had passed away, his son, renowned as Muṭasiva—
the son of Suvaṇṇapālī— attained a kingdom free from turmoil.
The king had that beautiful Mahāmeghavana garden constructed, which was endowed with fruits and flowering trees and celebrated for its name and its excellent qualities.
At the time of selecting the site for the garden, an unseasonal great rain fell.
Through the rain that fell, the park became a great cloud-grove.
King Muṭasiva reigned for sixty years in the excellent city of Anurādhapura,

He had ten sons who sought each other’s welfare,
and two daughters who were well-disposed and worthy of their family.
His second son was renowned as Devānaṃpiyatissa.

After his father’s passing, that Devānampiyatissa became king;

In the entirety of Laṅkādīpa, treasures and jewels that were situated within rose up and ascended to the surface of the earth. Furthermore,

At the foot of Mount Chāta were three bamboo poles,

Among them, one is a staff of *ekālatā* creepers, and there a creeper has the luster of silver;
beautiful and golden-hued, these are seen to be delightful.
One, however, is a staff of flowers, and there indeed are flowers.
"Various and of various colors, they are seen clearly.
There, many birds and deer stand together in a single row;

Bhayā, gajjā, rathā, amalā, valayā, aṅguliveṭhakā, kakudhaphalā, and apākatikā— these are the eight species.
Emerging from the ocean like pearls, they remain on the shore like beads.
All this is the manifestation of the merit of Devānaṃpiyatissa:
these sapphires, beryl, rubies, and precious gems;
and these silver [objects], pearls, and coral beads.
Within seven days, they brought them into the presence of the king;
seeing them, the king was filled with joy and thought thus:
"These priceless jewels are indeed Dhammāsoka's."
There is no other companion for the Arahant; therefore, I shall give these two to him:
Devānampiyatissa and Dharmāśoka—these two kings who have long been his unseen companions.

Having taken these priceless treasures,

a right-spiraling conch shell, and those eight kinds of pearls.
Having boarded a ship at Jambukola,

A lower robe with excellent borders, a costly hand-towel,
collyrium brought by nāgas, and clay with the luster of dawn;

The conch shell and the Nandiyāvaṭṭa design, the *vaḍḍhamāna* and the *kumārikā*;
the section on the golden vessel, and the costly palanquin;
the *harīṭaka* and the *āmalaka*, the precious medicine that is the deathless.
Having given at the proper time to his brother-in-law sixty thousand loads of well-harvested rice,
along with the royal consecration requisites distinguished by their excellence and attendants,
the lord of men presented these gifts as tokens of honor.
O messenger, bring back this gift of the true Dhamma as well:
"I have gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
I have declared myself a lay follower in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans."
"O Supreme among Men, you yourself take these supreme jewels;
having gladdened your heart, go for refuge with faith.
'Perform the consecration for my companion once again.'"
Having spoken thus, he honored those ministers and sent them away.
Having stayed for five months, those ministers, who were highly honored,
dispatched messengers on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vesākha.
Having boarded a ship at Tāmaliptī and disembarked at Tejambukolaka,
they saw a well upon reaching here on the twelfth day.
Those messengers gave the gifts intended for the island of Laṅkā.
The Lord of Laṅkā caused great honor to be paid to them.
When the moon and sun had risen in the month of Maggasira,
the ministers, devoted to their master, consecrated the Victor as the Lord of Laṅkā.
Having spoken these words to Dhammāsoka,
those who delight in the welfare of their lord consecrated him once again as one who delights in the benefit and happiness of Laṅkā.
Thus did the king [act] on the full moon day of Vesākha.
He whose speech was dear to the gods, whose name was hidden,
he who brought joy to the festival of the purification of Laṅkā,
that giver of happiness to the people, consecrated himself.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Consecration of Devānaṃpiyatissa," in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Twelfth Chapter:
The Glorification of Various Lands.
That Elder Moggaliputta, the illuminator of the Conqueror’s Dispensation;
Having completed the Council and looking toward the future,
he surveyed the establishment of the Dispensation in the border regions;
in the month of Kattika, he dispatched those elders here and there.
He dispatched the elder Majjhantika to Kaśmīra-Gandhāra;
he dispatched the elder Mahādeva to the region of Mahiṣamaṇḍala.
He dispatched the elder named Rakkhita to dwell in the forest.
Likewise, he dispatched to Aparantaka the one named Yona Dhammarakkhita;
and to Mahāraṭṭha, he sent the Elder Mahādhammarakkhita—
that Elder Mahārakkhita he sent to the Yona world.
He dispatched the Elder Majjhima to the region of Himavanta;
the two Elders Soṇa and Uttara to Suvaṇṇabhūmi;
and that Elder Mahinda, along with the Elders Itthiya and Uttiya.
"Establish the Sambala and Bhaddasāla [monasteries] for your own co-residents;
establish the delightful teaching of the Jina in the delightful island of Laṅkā," he thus dispatched the five elders.
At that time, when the crops in Kaśmīra and Gandhāra had ripened,
the powerful Nāga king Aravāla caused a rain of hailstones to fall.
Having rained down upon the ocean, that terrible one cast everything back into it.
There, the Elder Majjhantika, having traveled swiftly through the air,
performed walking meditations and other practices upon the surface of the Aravāla Great Lake.
When the nāgas saw this, they became enraged and reported it to the king.
Then that enraged Nāga king created various kinds of illusions:
great winds blew, clouds thundered and rained,
lightning bolts struck, and flashes of light issued forth from every direction.
The great trees and the mountain peaks are falling down;
and nāgas of hideous forms terrify from all sides,
breathing smoke and blazing by themselves while reviling in many ways.
Having warded off that terrifying display with his supernormal power,
the Elder spoke to that Naga king, demonstrating his supreme strength:
"Even if the entire world, including the devas, were to come and terrify me..."
You would not be able to produce fear or terror in me,
even if you, O Great Naga, were to lift up the entire earth together with its oceans and mountains and hurl it over me.
"You would not be able to produce fear or terror in me;
on the contrary, O lord of serpents, it would be your own exhaustion.
Having heard this from him who was free from pride, the Elder taught him the Dhamma.
Then the Naga king established himself in the refuges and the precepts.
Likewise, eighty-four thousand serpents,
as well as many Gandhabbas, Yakkhas, and Kumbhaṇḍas from the Himalayas, did the same.
The yakkha named Paṇḍaka, together with his yakkhinī wife and their five hundred sons, attained the first fruit [of the path].
"Do not now give way to anger, from this point forward as before."
"Do not cause harm to one another, for living beings desire happiness.
Practice loving-kindness toward all creatures, so that human beings may dwell in peace.
Thus instructed by him, they practiced accordingly.
Then that lord of serpents, having seated the Elder upon a jeweled couch, stood nearby fanning him.
At that time, men dwelling in Kaśmīra and Gandhāra arrived.
Having consulted with the Elder of great psychic power for the sake of worshipping the Nāga King,
they saluted the Elder himself and sat down to one side.
The Elder then taught them the Dhamma using the simile of the venomous snake.
There was the realization of the Dhamma for eighty thousand;
one hundred thousand men went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Elder.
From that time onwards, they [spread] to Kaśmīra and Gandhāra, even until now.
There were once those who wore the saffron robes and took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Having gone to the region of Mahisamaṇḍala,
the Elder Mahādeva stood in the midst of the people and preached the Devadūta Sutta.
Forty thousand purified the Eye of Dhamma;
forty thousand went forth into homelessness in his presence.
Then, having gone there, the Elder Rakkhita stood in the sky above Vanavāsi.
Standing in the midst of the people, he preached the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* beginning with the *Anamatagga*.
There was a realization of the Dhamma for sixty thousand men,
and thirty-seven thousand went forth into homelessness in his presence.
Five hundred monasteries were established in that region;
thus did that Elder establish the teaching of the Conqueror right there.
Having gone to Aparantaka, the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita—
Having preached the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta in the midst of the people,
he, who was skilled in the Dhamma among all things possessing Dhamma, caused thirty-seven thousand living beings who had gathered there to drink the nectar of the Dhamma.
A thousand men and even more women,
having gone forth from the very khattiya clans, renounced the world.
Having gone to Mahāraṭṭha, that great seer Mahādhammarakkhita—
There he related the Jātaka known as the Mahānāradakassapa.
Eighty-four thousand attained the paths and fruits,
and thirteen thousand went forth into homelessness in his presence.
Having gone to the realm of Yona, that seer Mahādhammarakkhita,
standing in the midst of the people, preached the Kāḷakārāma Sutta.
There were one hundred and seventy thousand living beings.
Ten thousand attained the fruits of the Path and went forth into homelessness.
Having gone with the four elders, the Sage Majjhima taught the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma in the region of the Himalayas.
Eighty million beings attained the paths and fruits;
five hundred thousand men brought faith in each of the five elders individually.
Out of faith, they went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Together with the Elder Uttara, the Elder Soṇa of great psychic power then went to Suvaṇṇabhūmi at that very time.
Whenever a child was born in the royal palace,
the Rākṣasī Rudda would emerge from the ocean, devour him, and then depart.
At that very moment, in the royal palace—
A young boy was born;
seeing him there, men [said],
"He is a companion of the rākṣasas."
Thinking thus, she approached the young man to kill him;
having asked, "What is this?", he said to the elder,
"We are ascetics from the Himalayas, not Rākṣasas, O friend."
That rākṣasī, together with her retinue, had emerged from the ocean.
Seeing her, the great multitude raised a loud cry;
the Elder, having fashioned twice as many terrifying rākṣasas, [stood there].
Having surrounded that ogress and her retinue on all sides,
thinking, "This [place] is cleared by these [means]," she fled in fear.
Having established a guard over that region on every side, she departed.
At that assembly, the Elder preached the Brahmajāla Sutta.
Many people took refuge and established themselves in the precepts;
indeed, there was a realization of the Dhamma by sixty thousand.
Four thousand five hundred noble youths went forth into homelessness,
and one thousand five hundred noble maidens likewise went forth. From that time on,
whenever a prince was born in the royal palace, [they would go forth].
The kings gave him the names Soṇa and Uttara.
Even for the Victor, who brings relief to the great multitude,
they abandoned the bowl, the deathless, and happiness.
They performed what was beneficial for the world here and there;
may whoever is negligent regarding the welfare of the world [be inspired].
In the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Renown of Various Countries.
The thirteenth chapter:
The Arrival of Mahinda.
At that time, the great sage Mahāmahinda Thera was twelve years old;
commanded by his preceptor and by the Saṅgha,
he was sent to bring grace to the island of Laṅkā.
He reflected, observing the time:
"King Muṭasiva is old;
let his son be king."
In the meantime, having set his mind on seeing his circle of kinsmen,
he paid homage to his preceptor and the Saṅgha, and questioned the Lord of the Earth.
Taking with him four elders and the son of Saṅghamittā, [he departed].
And the novice Sumanas, possessed of the six supernormal powers and great psychic might,
went to Dakkhiṇāgiri to provide for his kinsmen;
there, as he lived, six months passed by.
Gradually reaching Vedisagiri, the city of his mother’s queen,
he saw his mother; and the queen, seeing her beloved son,
had him and his retinue fed at the meal she herself had prepared.
He caused the Elder Subha to ascend the Vihāra on Cetiyagiri. Previously,
while yet a prince, that Asoka was enjoying the kingdom of Avanti which had been given to him by his father before departing for Ujjenī.
Having gone to live in that beautiful city of Vedisa,
he obtained a maiden named Devī, the daughter of a guild-leader.
He lived in cohabitation with her, and by him she conceived a child.
In Ujjenī, she gave birth to that auspicious prince Mahinda.
After two years had passed, she also bore a daughter, Saṅghamittā;
at that time, she was dwelling there in the city of Vedisa.
The Elder, having sat down there, knowing the proper time, thought thus:
"My father has commanded the great festival of consecration.
Let that Great King Devānampiyatissa enjoy it."
And having heard of the virtues of the Triple Gem, let him know from afar:
"On the Uposatha day of the month of Jeṭṭha, let him ascend Mount Missaka;
on that very day, we shall go to the excellent island of Laṅkā."
Approaching Mahinda, the most excellent Elder Mahinda, he said:
"Go to Laṅkā to inspire faith, for you were prophesied by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
We too shall be your supporters there. Thus he spoke.
The queen’s sister’s son was named Bhaṇḍuka.
Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Elder to the queen,
he attained the fruit of non-returning and lived in the Elder’s presence.
Having dwelt there for a month, on the full-moon day of the month of Jeṭṭha,
the Elder, together with four other elders— Sumana and Bhaṇḍu, along with that layman—
was not delighted by the cause of his kinsmen.
Therefore, that one of great psychic power rose up from the monastery into the air and,
arriving here in an instant, stood upon the delightful Missaka Mountain,
on the excellent and beautiful Amba-plateau at Vilūka.
He was prophesied by the Sage while lying on his final bed for the benefit of Laṅkā, due to the virtue of his delight in Laṅkā;
he who is like a Teacher to Laṅkā for the sake of its welfare.
Honored by the inhabitants of Laṅkā, he sat down there.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Arrival of Mahinda" in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.

King Devānampiyatissa, having granted the city-dwellers the privilege of sporting in the water, went out to hunt,
surrounded by forty thousand men.
Running on foot alone, he went to Mount Missaka.
Desiring to show himself there on that mountain, the god stood upon that crag in the form of a cow-eared [mountain spirit], as if devouring the thickets.
Seeing him, the king thought, "He is negligent; it is not right to shoot him.
Even as he made the sound of his bowstring, Gokaṇṇa had gone between the mountains.
The king ran after him in pursuit and arrived in the presence of the elders.
When he was seen by the king, the Elder vanished right there. Thinking, "If many see me,
he will become excessively afraid," and having looked upon the lord of the earth, he showed himself once more.
The Elder stood there, and being afraid, he said, "Come, Tissa!
At the mere words "Tissa," the king thought, "I am a Yakkha. [The Elder replied:
"We are ascetics, O Great King, disciples of the Dhamma-King."
"Out of compassion for him alone, you have come here from Jambudīpa.
Having heard this, the Elder spoke thus, and the king became free from fear;
remembering his friend’s message, he was certain that they were indeed "equal."
Having laid aside his bow and arrows, he approached that seer;
greeting the elder with joy, he sat down near him.
Then those men of his came and surrounded him.
Then the Great Elder pointed out the remaining ones who had arrived with him.
Seeing them, the king asked, "When did they come?
When the Elder replied, "Together with me," the king asked this again:
“Are there other such ascetics in Jambudīpa? he asked.

[The other replied: “O one whose radiance is like the saffron robe, indeed there are in Jambudīpa those who possess the threefold knowledge, have attained supernormal powers, and are skilled in reading the minds of others.”
“There are many Arahants with divine ears, disciples of the Buddha.
He asked, “By what means have you come?”—“Neither by land nor by water,” they replied.
When they said, “We have come,” he understood that their arrival was through the sky.
Possessing investigative wisdom and great insight,
the lord of the earth, being questioned again and again, answered each question posed by Kaṇha.
"This tree is named 'Rāja' (King), but this other plant is called 'Taru' (Tree)."
"Excluding this mango tree, O Venerable One, there are many other mango trees.
Excluding this mango and those mangoes, there are still trees;
there are many trees, Venerable Sir, that are not mango trees."
"Other than mangoes and non-mangoes, there are trees upon the earth;
this, venerable sir, is a mango tree—you are wise, O Lord of Men.
You have kinsmen, O King; you have many people, venerable sir."
“There are others unknown to you, O King, and there are many who are your kinsmen.
Aside from those kinsmen and others, is there anyone else [you do not know]?
“Venerable sir,” he replied, “it is well that you say this; you are wise, O Lord of Men.”
Knowing him to be wise, the great-minded elder taught the Cūḷahatthipadopama Sutta to Mahīpāla.
At the conclusion of the teaching, together with those men...
Forty thousand people established themselves in the refuges.
At that time, they brought an offering of food to the king in the evening;
then the lord of the earth said to the people, "I shall not eat now."
"It is indeed proper to ask," [thought the seer].
When the meal had not been requested, the seer said, "We shall not eat now. Then he asked about the time.
When the time was stated, he spoke thus: "Let us go to the city."
"Go you, O Great King; we shall dwell here.
This being so, let this prince go with us;
for he, O King, has attained the fruit and understood the teaching."
"Desiring the going-forth, he dwells in our presence;
now we shall let him go forth—go you there, O lord of the earth.
At dawn I will send a chariot; standing upon it, you shall enter the city."
Saying "As you say," he paid homage to the Elder, led Bhaṇḍu to one side, and asked about the Elder's account. He related everything to the king;
realizing it was the Elder, he was delighted and thought, "What a gain for me!"
Because of Bhaṇḍu’s status as a householder, the Lord of Men was free from apprehension;
he recognized his human condition and thought, “Let us ordain him.
At that very moment, the Elder performed it within the boundary of that village.
Regarding the prince Bhaṇḍuka’s going forth and full ordination—
at that very moment he attained arahantship.
Then the Elder addressed the novice Sumanas.
"Proclaim the time for hearing the Dhamma," he requested.
"To what extent shall we proclaim it, venerable sir? they asked.
When the Elder replied, "The whole of Tambapaṇṇī," by means of his psychic power—
Making it resound throughout all of Laṅkā, he proclaimed the time for the Dhamma.
The King, accompanied by his four [sons], sat down on the side of the golden [throne];
while eating, hearing that sound, he sent a messenger to the Elder.
“Is there some danger? he asked. “There is no danger,” he replied;
“the time has been proclaimed for hearing the words of the Sambuddha.
Hearing the sound of the novice, the earth-dwelling deities raised a cry.
Gradually that sound ascended as far as the Brahma-world.
Because of that cry, a great assembly of deities gathered;
at that gathering, the Elder taught the Samacitta Sutta.
An incalculable number of devas attained the realization of the Dhamma;
many nāgas and supaṇṇas established themselves in the refuges.
Just as this discourse was spoken by the elder Sāriputta, so it was.
Likewise, for the Elder Mahinda, there was a gathering of the gods.
The king sent forth his radiance; the charioteer went to the chariot and said to them, "Mount the chariot, let us go to the city."
"We shall not mount the chariot; go, we will follow behind you.
Having spoken thus and dispatched the charioteer Sumanoratha, they ascended into the air and [positioned themselves] to the east of the city.
At the first appearance [of the Buddha], those of great psychic power descended.
At the place where the Theras first alighted, a shrine was built;
even today it is called by that name, thus "the First Shrine" (Paṭhamacetiya).
Having heard of the Elder’s virtues,
all the women of the harem desired to see him; therefore,
the lord of the earth had a beautiful pavilion constructed within the royal precincts.
Covered and beautifully adorned with white *vattha* flowers, [the dwelling was seen].
Because of having heard from the Elder, he who was full of doubt [thought]: "The Elder might sit upon a high seat," and so forth.
In the meantime, seeing them standing there, the charioteer,
his mind filled with great wonder at those who were putting on their robes,
went and informed the king; and the wise monarch heard everything.
“They will not sit upon stools,” he was certain. Having said,
“Very well, prepare a ground-covering,” he went out to meet the elders and paid them respectful homage.
Taking the bowl from the hand of the Elder Mahāmahinda,
he led the Elder into the city with due honors and rites of worship.
Seeing the preparation of the seat, the diviners prophesied thus:
“By us the earth has been taken; we shall be lords over the island.
The lord of men, honoring them, led those elders to the inner palace;
there they sat upon cloth-seats according to their rank.
The king himself satisfied them with gruel, hard food, and soft food;
when the meal was finished, he sat down beside his younger brother,
the crown prince Mahānāga, and [his] wife.
Like one dwelling in a royal palace, he summoned Anulā.
Having arrived with five hundred women,
Queen Anulā paid homage to the Elder, honored him, and sat down to one side.
The Elder taught the *Petavatthu*, the *Vimānavatthu*, and the *Saccasaṃyutta*; those women attained the first fruit [of the path].
Having heard many of the Elder’s virtues from people seen yesterday, [many others came].
Desiring a sight of the Elder, the citizens gathered together and raised a great clamor at the king’s gate.

the seer Sihasina, having emerged from the water at Natittha and gone from the bank to the Vaja bank, reached Paṇṇatittha and touched the boundary marker.
But when this sign was struck, gods and humans uttered cries of "Excellent!
as the Teaching became firmly established.
He proclaimed the sign regarding the gift of the furrowed land (Sītā) to the King.
Having described the thirty-two shrines and the purpose of the Thūpārāma,
the great-minded Mahāthera, having duly described the boundary markers and the boundary markers at the border of the Siyam kingdom, [proceeded].
On that very day, he bound all the boundaries;
when the binding of the boundaries was completed, the great earth trembled.
On the fifth day, the Elder, having eaten at the king’s residence, [departed].
Having sat in the Nandana Grove and taught the *Khajjanīyaka Sutta* to the great multitude,
he caused a thousand humans there to drink the drink of the Deathless, and then dwelt in the Mahāmegha Grove.
On the sixth day as well, the Elder, having eaten at the king’s residence,
sat in the Nandana Grove and prepared a lump of cow dung for a seat. Having delivered his teaching,
he who was skilled in instruction [bestowed it] upon the great multitude of humans.
Having caused [the king] to attain realization, he dwelt in Mahāmeghavana.
On the seventh day as well, the Elder, having eaten at the royal palace,
sat in the Nandana Grove and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
Having taught the Suttanta and led a thousand humans to full realization,
he dwelt in the Mahāmegha forest.
Thus, Jutindhara [taught] eight thousand nine hundred.
Having caused the realization [of the Truth] to be accomplished within just seventy days,
that forest was called Mahānandana by that Neutral One (Tādin);
and because it was a place illuminated by the Teaching, it is known as Jotivana.
At the beginning, the king quickly had a palace built for the Elder in the Tissa Monastery by means of a torch.
Having dried the clay,
that palace appeared black;
because of that, it was so there.
It became known as the Kāḷapāsāda Pariveṇa.
Thereafter, he had the Mahābodhi House, the Lohapāsāda,
the Salākagga, and the refectory (bhattasālā) constructed with great care.
He had many monastic cells built, as well as excellent lotus ponds,
and established night-quarters, day-quarters, and so forth.
On the bank of that bathing lotus pond, he constructed a bathing pavilion.
"Sunahātapariveṇa"— thus is a *pariveṇa* called.
And at the place where that virtuous elder walks back and forth,
that long walkway is called his *pariveṇa*.
Because he attained the attainment of the highest fruit (aggaphalasamāpatti) there,
it is for that reason called the Pariveṇa of the Highest Fruit (Phalagga).
Seeing no other reclining place, the Elder sat down right there.
The elders relied upon this cell, therefore it is called the Elder’s Cell (Therā-passaya-pariveṇa).
Where many hosts of gods waited upon him as he was being roasted,
for that reason it is called the Maru-Host Cell (Marugaṇa-pariveṇa).
For the Elder Dīghasandaka, who was the general of the king,
he had the Cūḷapāsāda built with eight great pillars.
That place there is known as the Dīghasanda Senāpati Pariveṇa.
This is called the Pariveṇa, the foremost and preeminent structure.
It was by the one named Aṣagula, who spoke the words of Devānampiya,
that this first Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra) was established in Laṅkā.
That king, having approached the great and wise Elder Mahinda,
caused this [work] to be composed here, free from blemish and beyond measure.
Thus ends the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Fifteenth Chapter: The Acceptance of the Mahāvihāra.
The Sixteenth Chapter.
The recipient of the Cetiyapabbata Monastery,
having wandered for alms in the city and performed service for the people,
ate at the royal palace while providing service to the king.
On the sixteenth day, the Elder dwelt in Mahāmeghavana on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷha.
Having eaten at the royal palace, he was with the high-minded Great King.
Having taught the Mahā-Appamāda Sutta, he then,
desiring the construction of a monastery there on Cetiyapabbata,
departed from the eastern gate and went to Cetiyapabbata.
Having heard that the Elder had gone there, the king mounted his chariot and,
taking two queens with him, followed in the Elder's wake.
At the Nāgacatukka, the Elders bathed in that lake.
They stood in a row to ascend the mountain.
Then the king, having mounted his chariot, paid homage to all the elders.
When they asked, "O King, why have you come? You are weary from the heat," he replied:
When he said, "I have come fearing that you might depart," the Elder,
who was skilled in the Khandhakas, replied, "We have come to spend the rains retreat right here.
He then gave him the introductory instruction for that section.
Having heard that, the king’s nephew and the great minister Mahāriṭṭha expounded it;
together with his fifty-five brothers, both elder and younger, he stood before the king.
Having made their request, on that very day they went forth in the presence of the Elder;
all those great-witted ones attained arahantship at the very point of the razor.
At the site of the Kaṇṭaka Cetiya, he [the Elder] remained there for the entire day.
Having had sixty-eight caves constructed,
the king returned to his city, while the Elders remained right there; out of compassion,
they would enter the city for alms at the proper time.
When the work on the cave was completed, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha,
the king went and gave the donation for the monastery to the elders.
And for that monastery, there were thirty-two pavilions.
The Elder Sīmaṃtigo, having bound them that very day within the Tumbaramāḷaka enclosure—
the very first of all— conferred the full ordination upon those who were seeking admission to the going-forth.
These sixty-two arahants, all on Cetiyapabbata,
having entered the rains retreat there, performed services for the king.
That [service], counted by the multitudes of gods and men—
And approaching that assembly,
whose fame was spread wide by its virtues,
they honored it as a vehicle [to liberation] and performed vast accumulations of merit.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "The Acceptance of the Cetiyapabbata Monastery," in the Mahāvaṃsa composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Seventeenth Chapter:
The Arrival of the Elements.
Having completed the rains residence and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the full moon day of the month of Kattika;
The Great Elder of great wisdom said this to the Great King:
"O Lord of Men, we have not seen the Fully Enlightened One, our Teacher, for a long time.
We have lived in a state of homelessness; there is nothing here for us to offer in worship."
“Was it not said by you, O Bhante, that ‘the Sambuddha has attained Nibbāna’?
He replied, “When the relics are seen, the Victor is seen.
“Your intention regarding the construction of the stupa is known to me.”
"I shall honor the stupa; you yourselves must know the relics," the Elder said to the king with a joyful mind through mantras.
The king said to that novice: "From where shall we obtain the relics?"
Having adorned the city and the road, O lord of men, the king,
observing the uposatha together with his retinue, mounted an auspicious elephant.
Holding a white parasol and accompanied by cymbal players, he set forth.
"Go to the Mahānāga forest grove this evening, O King.
There you will find the elements, for he knows their dissolution.
Thus spoke the novice Icchāna to you, who were so joyful and of such a happy mind."
Then the Elder, having gone from the royal palace to Cetiya Mountain,
addressed the novice Sumana, whose destination was auspicious:
"Come, noble Sumana, go to the excellent city of Pupphapura."
"Speak these words to our grandfather,
the Great King: 'O Great King, your friend, the Great King Maruppiya,
who has faith in the Buddha's teaching, wishes to have a stupa built.'"
Give me the relics of the Sage, the bowl used by the Teacher, and his remains;
for there are many bodily relics in your presence.
Taking those filled in the bowl, go to the excellent city of the gods.
Speak these words to Sakka, the lord of the devas:
"The tooth-relic of him who is worthy of offerings in the three worlds, O Lord of Devas, is in Tāvatiṃsa; and the right collar-bone relic is in Dakkhiṇāgiri."
“You yourself should worship the tooth; give the collarbone to the Teacher.
Do not neglect the affairs of the island of Laṅkā, O Lord of the Gods.
Having said, “So be it, Venerable Sir,” that novice of great psychic power—
At that very moment, he went into the presence of Dhammāsoka.
There he heard that the Great Bodhi tree had been placed at the foot of a *sāla* tree;
having honored it with offerings on the festival of the full moon of Kattika, he beheld it.
Having spoken these words to the Elder, and having received the relics from the king,
he took them in the bowlful and went to the Himalayas.
Having placed that supreme bowl containing the relics in the Himalayas, he departed.
Having gone into the presence of the Lord of Devas, he spoke the Elder’s words.
Sakka, the ruler of the gods, took the Cūḷāmaṇi jewel from the shrine and gave it to the novice at the right corner.
Taking that relic and the relic-casket, the ascetic, being well-pleased,
returned from there to Cetiya-giri and gave them to the Elder.
He then proceeded to the Mahānāga-vana garden according to the prescribed ritual.
At the time of evening, the king, preceded by his royal army,
had all the relics deposited right there on the mountain by the Elder;
therefore, they called that mountain the Cetiya Mountain (Missakapabbata).
Leaving that relic bowl behind on Cetiyapabbata, the Elder took the bone-relic and, together with his retinue, went to the appointed place.
"If this is indeed the relic of the Sage, let my parasol bow down of its own accord."
"Let the relics be placed upon my knees; this is the reliquary casket.
May it rest upon my head, having come here together with the relics"—thus the king thought, and what he thought came to pass exactly so.
The king was delighted, thinking, "He has indeed been consecrated with the nectar of sovereignty.
Taking him by the head, he placed him upon the neck of the elephant.
The joyful elephant let out a trumpeting cry, and the earth trembled.
Then the powerful elephant, accompanied by the elder, turned back,
entered the beautiful city through the eastern gate,
and then departed again through the southern gate.
To the west of the site of the Cetiya in the Thūpārāma,
he went to the place called Pamojava, turned back at the site of the Bodhi tree, and stood facing eastward;
thus was the site for the Thūpa established as beneficial at that time.
A funeral pyre was made of kadamba flowers and creepers.
That pure spot was guarded by devas and man-devas;
having had it thoroughly cleaned and adorned, they did so with great care at that very moment.
In order to lower him from his element, the king began [the task] from the elephant's back;
but the elephant did not wish for it, so the king asked the Elder about that intention.
He wished to place him in a position equal to his own back.
"By that, the placing of the relic-element is not desired," he said.
Having given the command, in that very instant,
he was bathed and anointed with fragrant oils.
Having leveled that spot with pieces of dried mud and having adorned that supreme site in many ways, the king—
Having removed [the relics] from the elephant’s shoulder where they had been placed,
and having appointed Dhātārakkha to guard them while leaving the elephant there,
the king, with a mind full of haste, set about the construction of the relic stupa.
Having quickly appointed many men to perform the task of preparing the ground,
the King, reflecting upon his duty regarding the elements, entered the city together with his ministers.
Meanwhile, the Great Elder Mahinda [proceeded to] the beautiful Mahāmeghavana grove.
Saggaṇa, having approached, established his residence there.
At night, the Nāga roamed around that place containing the relic;
by day, he remained at the Bodhi shrine within the hall, together with the relic.
After that, following the opinion of the elders, the king had a stupa built for the relic to the height of a man's leg; having had it announced there,
within a few days the lord of the earth arrived.
From every direction, the great multitude gathered together.
At that assembly, the relic— carried on the shoulder of an elephant and raised to the summit of the mountain—
was seen remaining in the sky at a height of seventy palm trees.
They amazed the people with a twin miracle;
like the Buddha at the root of the Kaṇṇamuṇḍa tree, he performed a hair-raising feat.
Then, from flames that issued forth, he sprinkled himself with streams of water.
This entire earth, adorned with every ornament,
was illuminated by the Conqueror as he lay upon the bed of final Nibbāna;
for with his five eyes, he made the five great resolutions.
When the great Bodhi branch was being grasped by Aśoka as a gift,
it broke off of its own accord and settled within the vessel.
Having settled there, that branch shone with beautiful rays of six colors.
Gladdening all the quarters with its fruits and leaves, may it be released.
Having risen up, beautiful with its golden basin,
may it remain invisible for seven days within the womb of the snow.
May my right eye-socket, as it is being established in the Thūpārāma,
rise up into the sky and perform this miracle!
Upon the Hemamālika Cetiya, which is the very ornament of Laṅkā.
The relics, measuring a *doṇa* in quantity, established themselves.
Having assumed the appearance of Buddhas, they rose up and remained in the sky;
then, having performed the twin miracle (*yamaka-pāṭihāriya*), they established their foundation.
There are five resolutions indeed; the Tathāgata resolved them.
Therefore that relic performed that miracle at that time.
Descending from the sky, it stood upon the summit of Mount Sineru.
The king, being exceedingly joyful, enshrined it in the cetiya.
And when that relic was thus enshrined in the cetiya,
there occurred a great earthquake, wonderful and hair-raising.
Thus inconceivable are the Buddhas, inconceivable are the qualities of a Buddha;
for those with faith in what is inconceivable, the result is inconceivable.
Having seen that miracle, people gained confidence in the Teacher.
Prince Mattābhaya, the youngest son of the king,
having gained faith in the Lord of Sages and having entreated the Lord of Men,
went forth into the teaching together with a thousand men.
From Cetārigāma, from Dvāramaṇḍala, from Vihīrabīja,
and likewise from Gallakapiṭṭhi; likewise from Upatissagāma—
five hundred and five [monks].
The children went forth, joyful, having conceived faith in the Tathāgata.
Thus, in former times, all those outsiders then went forth;
there were thirty thousand bhikkhus in the teaching of the Victor.
Having completed the construction of the excellent stupa in the Thūpārāma,
the lord of the earth constantly caused it to be honored with many offerings, such as jewels and other valuables.
The king’s women, the nobles, the ministers, and likewise the citizens [did the same].
All the various districts offered individual honors.
The King had a monastery built there, preceded by a stupa;
therefore, that monastery became renowned as Thūpārāma.
Even though the Lord of the World has attained final Nibbāna, by means of this very body of the Sakya realm,
he continues to bring about the welfare and happiness of the masses in a perfect manner.
"Many were the miracles performed while the Conqueror remained [in the world].
This concludes the chapter titled "The Bringing of the Relics" from the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Seventeenth Chapter.
The Eighteenth Chapter:
The Taking of the Great Bodhi Tree.
The lord of the earth, remembering the words spoken by the Elder,
commanded the Elder Mahābodhi and the nun to his own palace.
While seated in the presence of the Elder for a single day during the rainy season retreat, he [listened].
Having consulted with his ministers, he himself appointed his own nephew,
a minister named Ariṭṭha, to that task;
having deliberated and addressed him, he spoke these words.
"Will you be able... from the presence of Dhammāsoka to bring the Great Bodhi tree and the Elder Nun Saṅghamittā here?
I shall be able, O King, to bring those two from there."
"O giver of honor, if I may receive permission to go forth here, having come for that purpose," he said.
"So be it," replied the king, and sent him there.
Having received the message from both the Elder and the king, and having paid his respects, he departed.
On the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja, having departed on the second day,
he boarded a ship at the port of Jambukola and set out upon the great ocean,
remaining devoted through the power of the Elder’s resolve.
On the very day of his departure, he went to the delightful city of Pupphapura.
At that time, Queen Anulā, together with five hundred women of the harem and five hundred other ladies, [followed him].
Having undertaken the ten precepts, pure and clad in saffron robes,
those seeking ordination look toward the lineage of the Elder Nuns.
In a delightful portion of the city, at the nunnery, they wait.
Having had it constructed by the lord of men, those of excellent vows took up residence there.
At that time, he was addressed by the female lay disciples as "the Bhikkhunī-vihāra";
thus it became renowned in Laṅkā as the Upāsikā-vihāra.
The nephew Mahā-Ariṭṭha, having delivered the king’s message to King Dhammāsoka,
spoke this message for the Elder: "O elephant among kings,
[this] is from your brother's wife, the companion of your majesty."
Desiring the going forth, she dwells ever self-restrained.
Dispatch Saṅghamittā the bhikkhunī to ordain her,
along with the southern branch of the Great Bodhi tree itself.
And the Elder spoke this very matter as uttered by the Elders;
having gone into her father’s presence, that Elder nun declared the Elder’s opinion.
The King said, "O mother, how can I not see you?"
"I shall dispel the grief born of separation from my son and grandson.
Thus she spoke to me, O Great King, for her brother’s word was weighty to her;
and since many were to be sent away, she said, "I must go there with him."
“The Great Bodhi tree is not fit to be struck by a blade;
how indeed shall I take its branch?”—thus the king reflected.
By the advice of his minister named Mahādeva, he...
Having invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and fed them, the king asked:
"Venerable Sir, should the Mahābodhi be sent to Laṅkā?
The Elder Moggaliputta, having replied, "It should indeed be sent," [spoke thus].
He spoke the fivefold Great Resolve with his five eyes;
having heard that from him, the lord of the earth was satisfied.
He [prepared] a seven-yojana road leading toward the Great Bodhi tree.
Having had it thoroughly cleaned, he had it adorned in many ways.
He had gold extracted for the purpose of making the bowl;
and Vissakamma, possessing a form as beautiful as a balance-beam, arrived there.
“‘What should be the size of the cauldron? I ask you this;
‘Having ascertained the size yourself, you should make it,’ he replied.
Then, taking gold and rubbing it with his hand—”
Having instantly fashioned a cauldron— nine cubits in circumference,
five cubits in depth, three cubits in width,
and eight finger-breadths thick, beautiful to behold— he departed.
Having seized that young elephant, whose face was as large as its trunk,
the king [drank] it like a mere drop of wine.
It was seven yojanas in length and one yojana in width.
Accompanied by a fourfold army and a great multitude of bhikkhus,
he approached the Great Bodhi tree, which was adorned with various ornaments,
inlaid with diverse jewels, and garlanded with many kinds of banners.
Strewed with various flowers and resounding with the music of various instruments,
[the city] was surrounded by the army and enclosed with a curtain.
With a great multitude headed by a thousand great elders, they [proceeded].
Surrounded by more than a thousand kings who had received the consecration of sovereignty,
he respectfully gazed upon the Great Bodhi tree, raising his hands in the añjali gesture.
On its southern branch, having avoided a space of four cubits and the trunk, the branches vanished.
Having seen that miracle, the lord of the earth was filled with joy.
“I shall worship the Great Bodhi tree,” he proclaimed, “with my kingdom.
The lord of the earth consecrated the Great Bodhi tree in the great sovereignty;
having worshipped the Great Bodhi tree with flowers and other offerings, he circumambulated it.
Having performed [the rites] in eight places and having paid homage with palms joined,
he placed that golden bowl upon a high,
well-constructed throne inlaid with gold and adorned with various gems and jewels.
