Having been severed, it shall remain established here in this golden basin.
At the place where the marks are inscribed, that Great Bodhi tree itself,
having been cut, shall stand upon this basin filled with fragrant mud.
Above the original line, at intervals of three finger-breadths each,
the Lord of Men drew lines of ruby, encircling [the base].
He took the large roots first, and then the smaller ones.
Emerging ten by ten, they descended as a mass of nets.
Seeing that miracle, the king was exceedingly delighted;
right there he raised a shout of joy, as did the entire assembly around him.
The community of bhikkhus, with hearts full of joy, gave shouts of approval;
thousands of cloths were waved about on every side.
Thus, by the power of a hundred roots, that fragrance arose there from the mire.
The Great Bodhi tree took root, inspiring faith in the great multitude.
Its trunk was ten cubits high; its five branches were enchanting, each four cubits long and adorned with ten half-fruits.
There were a thousand branches, and on those branches there were [buds];
thus was the Great Bodhi tree, possessing a captivating splendor.
At the moment the Great Bodhi was established upon its basin, the earth—
Various miracles occurred and there was trembling.
Among both gods and humans, the sounds of musical instruments resounded spontaneously, along with the cries of "Excellent! from the hosts of devas and brahmas.
From the cries of clouds, beasts, birds, and yakkhas and others, and from the earth-trembling sounds,
there arose a single great clamor.
From the fruits and leaves of the Bodhi tree, beautiful rays of six colors shone forth.
Having emerged, they illuminated the entire world-system.
The Great Bodhi tree, having ascended from its chariot-stand into the sky,
remained for seven days invisible within the womb of the clouds.
The king, having descended from his throne and dwelt there for those seven days,
constantly performed manifold offerings to the Great Bodhi tree.
During that past week, all the inhabitants of Himavā—
They entered the Great Bodhi tree, and rays of light issued forth in every way.
Like a pure lotus established in a water-jar,
the delightful Great Bodhi appeared to all the great multitude.
While the Great Bodhi tree was performing various miracles,
it amazed the people as it sprouted forth upon the surface of the earth.
Delighted once more by those many miracles, he—
The Great King worshipped the Great Bodhi with a great sovereignty.
Having consecrated the Great Bodhi with the great sovereignty and worshipping it with various offerings for seven days,
he dwelt right there once more.
On the fifteenth day of the Uposatha in the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja,
he took possession of the Mahābodhi tree; seven days after that,
on the fourteenth day of the Uposatha in the dark fortnight of Assayuja.
Having placed the Great Bodhi tree upon a beautiful chariot, the preeminent of charioteers,
honoring it on that very day, brought it to his own city;
there he adorned it in many ways and had a beautiful pavilion constructed.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kattika,
there at the auspicious foot of the great sāla tree to the north, having had the Great Bodhi tree established,
he performed manifold offerings day after day.
In the seventeenth year of his reign,
nine Aṅkirasas were born to him all at once. With a joyful heart,
that lord of many men again honored the Great Bodhi tree with royal offerings.
Having been consecrated in the great kingdom,
the great lord performed various kinds of worship for the Great Bodhi tree.
Thus, in Kusumapura, he [honored] the Lord of Sages...
Vast and filled with many kinds of beautiful banners,
that most radiant and excellent worship of enlightenment caused the hearts of gods and men to blossom.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Taking of the Great Bodhi Tree," in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Nineteenth Chapter:
The Arrival of the Bodhi Tree.
For the purpose of protecting the Great Bodhi tree, he [the King] set out with eighteen chariots and his retinue.
Having given deva-shrines, eight families of ministers,
eight families of brahmins, eight families of merchants,
and the families of cowherds, hyenas, and sparrows.
Likewise, having given eight golden jars each to the weavers,
the potters, all the guilds, and the nāgas and yakṣas, Mānada bestowed them.
Having placed the Great Bodhi tree upon a boat adorned on the Ganges,
the Great Elder Saṅghamittā, together with eight bhikkhunīs,
likewise placed it [on land] along with those headed by Ariṭṭha.
Having departed from the city,
the lord of the earth quickly traversed the Vindhya forest and reached Tāmaliṭṭhi in just seven days. There,
he was honored with supreme offerings by gods, nāgas, and humans alike.
Worshipping the Mahābodhi, they arrived in seven days.
Having had the Mahābodhi established on the shore of the great ocean, the lord of the earth then worshipped it with the gift of a great kingdom.
The Wish-Fulfiller (Kāmada) consecrated the Mahābodhi in the great kingdom on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Aggasira. Then,
with those very same eight [elephants], he raised up the Mahābodhi.
Having been given [the relics] by those families who had received portions from the root of the Sāla tree,
he lifted up the Great Bodhi tree and,
having plunged it into a depth of water reaching his neck there, he firmly established it upon the ship.
Having embarked him upon the ship, he spoke these words to the Great Elder (Mahātherī) together with her attendants,
and to the great minister Mahāriṭṭha:
"Three times have I honored the Great Bodhi Tree with my sovereignty."
"In this very way, may my friend the King honor me with his sovereignty.
Having said this, the Great King stood on the bank with palms joined;
watching the Mahābodhi tree as it departed, he shed tears.
Through separation from the Great Awakening,
phenomena are sorrowful and full of grief;
having cried out and lamented, [one is overcome].
He returned to his own city.
The ship carrying the Great Bodhi tree leaped into the ocean;
its waves subsided for a league all around, and it settled peacefully upon the great sea.
Five-colored lotuses bloomed on every side,
and many musical instruments resounded in the sky.
By countless deities, manifold offerings were performed.
The nāgas attempted to employ their supernormal powers to seize the Great Bodhi tree,
but the great Therī Saṅghamittā, who had reached the further shore of the power of direct knowledge,
assumed the form of a supaṇṇa and terrified those great serpents.
Terrified by them, those great serpents entreated the Great Elder;
then, having led Mahābeṇadhi to the abode of the *bhujaṅgas*,
they honored him for seven days with various offerings and with the sovereignty over the *nāgas*.
Having honored it and brought it here, they placed the ship [on land].
On that very day, the Great Bodhi tree arrived here at Jambukola;
King Devānampiyatissa was devoted to the welfare of the world.
Sumanā had previously heard from the novice monk that there was a recitation of the scriptures;
beginning from the day of the month of Māgasira, he became diligent in his speech.
[He traveled] along the great highway from the Northern Gate as far as Jambukola.
Having adorned everything, with his heart set upon the Great Bodhi tree,
he stood at the site of the Samuddāsana hall by the great ocean and beheld the Great Bodhi approaching through the great psychic power of the Elder.
In that place, a hall was built, a wonderful stone bridge;
it became well-known here by the name "The Hall for Washing in the Ocean.
By the power of the Great Elder, together with those other elders, [it was established].
On that very day, King Sa-senaka went to Jambukola.
Overwhelmed by the surge of joy at the Great Bodhi tree, he uttered this inspired utterance:
"Having plunged into water reaching up to my neck, I am deeply agitated."
Taking the Mahābodhi tree together with its sixteen families and its crown,
the Lord of Laṅkā brought it and planted it within a beautiful pavilion on the shore.
Having established it there, he honored it with the sovereignty of Laṅkā.
Having entrusted the sovereignty over his realm to sixteen clans,
the lord of men himself stood in the position of gatekeeper for three days,
performing various acts of worship right there.
Having mounted the Great Bodhi tree onto the beautiful chariot on the tenth day,
the lord of men, bringing it along, had that king of trees placed in its position within the Pācīna monastery, he who was discerning regarding locations.
He provided a morning meal for the people together with the Saṅgha.
There, the Elder Mahāmahinda recounted to the King in its entirety that deed performed by the One Possessing Ten Powers: the taming of the Nāga.
Having heard the Elder’s words and having had markers made here and there at the places where the Teacher had used them for sitting and other activities,
the King [did so] at the gate of the brahmin Tivakka’s village.
Having had the Great Bodhi tree established in those various locations,
[he did so] upon beds of pure sand strewn with diverse flowers,
along paths where banners were raised and adorned with flower garlands.
Worshipping the Mahābodhi day and night without weariness,
he arrived at Anurādhapura on the fourteenth day.
When the shadow had increased in length, the city was beautifully adorned.
Having entered while worshipping through the northern gate,
and having exited through the southern gate and re-entered,
he reached the Great Meghavana Monastery, frequented by the four Buddhas.
Having led him with pleasant words to that delightful spot designated as the "Good Place," the site where the former Bodhisatta had stood,
the king, together with sixteen clans wearing ornaments, [honored him].
Having removed the Great Bodhi tree, they established it and released it.
As soon as it was released from their hands, the eighty-cubit tree rose into the sky and,
remaining there, emitted beautiful rays of six colors.
Spreading across the island and reaching as far as the Brahma-world,
those delightful rays remained fixed until the setting of the sun.
Ten thousand men, filled with faith at this miracle, [were established in the Dhamma].
Having contemplated the state of arahantship and having attained it here, they went forth.
Then, descending from the Great Bodhi tree at sunset,
it was established upon the earth under Rohiṇī, and the ground trembled.
Those roots, having shot up from the rim of the mouth of the bowl,
entwined that bowl and descended to the surface of the earth.
When the Great Bodhi tree was firmly established, all the people gathered together.
They worshipped from all sides with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and the like.
A great cloud rained down from all directions, filled with frost;
thick clouds, cool and dense, covered the Great Bodhi tree.
For seven days the Great Bodhi remained invisible right there;
it sat within a womb of snow, generating serene confidence in the people.
After seven days, when the clouds had passed, they all disappeared.
The Mahābodhi tree was visible, as were rays of six colors.
The Elder Mahāmahinda and the nun Saṅghamittā arrived there with their retinues,
as did the king with his retinue.
The Kshatriyas of Kajaragāma, the Kshatriyas of Candanagāma,
the Brahmin Tivakka, and the people dwelling on the island,
having great zeal for the Great Bodhi, came by the power of the gods.
In that great assembly, amazed by the miracle,
while they were watching a ripe fruit fall from a branch— ripe yet unblemished—
the Elder took it as it fell and gave it to the king to plant.
Into a golden bowl filled with soil mixed with perfumes,
the Lord of Ropaṇī placed it at the spot where the Great Seat stood.
While everyone was looking on, eight sprouts shot forth.
Bodhi saplings were born, each four cubits in height.
Seeing those Bodhi saplings, the king’s mind was filled with wonder;
he honored them with white parasols and bestowed upon them the consecration.
He established [the relics] at the port of Jambukola; then,
from the ships at Rohaṇa, the Great Bodhi tree was placed in its location,
as well as in the village of Tivakka and likewise in the Thūpārāma.
In the Issarasamaṇārāma, at the first shrine courtyard;
at Cetiyapabbata in Rāma, likewise at Kājaragāmaka,
and at Candanagāmaka— thus there was one Bodhi tree at each location.
The remaining thirty-two Bodhi trees were of fourfold origin,
established here and there in monasteries within a radius of one league,
for the benefit of the people dwelling on the island.
At the foot of the Great Bodhi tree, by the splendor of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the assembly of Anulā and her followers, having gone forth in the presence of the elder nun Saṅghamittā, attained arahantship.
That nobleman Ariṭṭha, together with his retinue of five hundred,
went forth in the presence of the Elder and attained arahantship.
He brought here the eight great Bodhi-branches from the families of the merchants.
"Bodhāharakula" is how they were called by him.
Regarding the "Upāsikāvihāra," it was known as the nunnery for bhikkhunīs;
there the Great Elder Saṅghamittā dwelt together with her community.
He had houses built there, headed by three principal ones;
among them, he established twelve in one great house.
He also placed the mast-base for the ship that was to carry the Great Bodhi tree.
In one [place] they were dear to me, and in another they were hostile toward one another.
Even when born into different sects, those twelve families always made use of the houses,
including the *hattha-āḷaka*, together with the bhikkhunīs.
That auspicious elephant of the king, wandering at his pleasure on one side of the city in a cool mountain glen,
stood within a cluster of kadamba flowers while grazing upon his food.
Knowing that the elephant delighted in that place, they constructed a trough there.
Then one day, the elephant did not take his morsels of food;
the king questioned the Elder Dīpappasādaka regarding the cause.
"In the Kadamba flower grove, he built a stupa;
'He desires this,' the Great Elder said to the Great King.
There, he established a stupa containing relics, as well as a shrine for that stupa."
The King, who was ever devoted to the welfare of his people, acted swiftly.
The Great Elder Saṅghamittā, longing for empty dwellings,
found that very monastery crowded as she lived there.
Desiring the growth of the Dispensation and for the welfare of the bhikkhunīs,
that wise woman, wishing for another bhikkhunī residence,
went to that Cetiya monastery, which possesses the great bliss of seclusion.
The stainless ones, skilled in the practice of meditation, spent the day in seclusion.
Having heard that the Elder nuns had gone there to pay their respects, the king went to the bhikkhunī quarters; having arrived there and paid his homage, he remained.
Having exchanged greetings with her, he asked the reason for her coming there;
knowing her intention, he who was wise understood her purpose.
He [pointed out] the delightful dwelling place for the bhikkhunīs all around the stupa-house.
That great king, Devānaṃpiyatissa,
had it constructed near Hatthāḷhaka. Because the nunnery was built there,
it became renowned as the Hatthāḷhaka Vihāra.
Sumittā— that Saṅghamittā, the great elder of great wisdom—
dwelt there indeed in that delightful residence for bhikkhunīs.
Thus, may there be welfare for Laṅkā and the growth of the Dispensation.
Searching for it, this Lord of the Great Bodhi Trees quickly reached his destination in the delightful Mahāmegha forest on the island of Laṅkā, accompanied by many spirits.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Bodhi Tree," in the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Twentieth Chapter:
The Parinibbāna of the Elder.
In the eighteenth year of King Dhammāsoka’s reign;
In the Mahāmeghavana grove, the Great Bodhi tree was established.
Then, in the twelfth year [of his reign], the beloved chief queen of that king, Asandhimittā, who cherished the Fully Enlightened One, passed away.
Then, in the fourth year, King Dhammāsoka placed the treacherous Tissarakkhā in the position of chief queen.
But in the third year, she, foolish and conceited of her beauty—
“I too shall cause this king not to attain Great Enlightenment.
Having thus fallen under the power of anger and acting for her own detriment,
she struck at the Great Enlightenment with you by means of the frog-thorn.
Then, in that very year, the illustrious Dhammasoka attained impermanence;
these [reigns] lasted thirty-seven years.
King Devānampiyatissa, however, delighted in the qualities of the Dhamma.
Having completed the new construction work as was appropriate at the Mahāvihāra, at Cetiyapabbata, and at the Thūpārāma,
he questioned the Elder Dīpappasādaka, who was skilled in answering questions.
"Venerable sir, I shall have many monasteries built here;
but how shall we obtain relics to enshrine in the stūpas?
Having filled the Perfectly Enlightened One’s bowl, they were brought here with great joy."
"O King, there are relics deposited on Cetiyapabbata.
Having placed those relics upon the back of an elephant, bring them here.
Thus addressed by the Elder, he brought the relics accordingly.
Having had monasteries built at intervals of one yojana each,
he deposited the relics there in stūpas as was appropriate.
As for the alms-bowl used by the Perfectly Enlightened One, [he placed it] in the beautiful royal palace.
Having established [the shrine], he honored it at all times with various offerings.
In the presence of the Great Elder, at the place where he had resided after going forth,
he was known as Issarasamaṇaka, the "Lordly Monk," for he commanded five hundred [monks].
Five hundred years after [the Parinibbāna], at the place where the Great Elder had resided after going forth,
there likewise arose Vassagiri.
Whatever cave was inhabited by the Elder Mahāmahinda, [there too it arose].
Among the mountain monasteries, that Mahinda Cave was the first; the Mahāvihāra was the second;
and the beautiful Thūpārāma, preceded by the Stūpa, was the third.
The fourth was indeed the establishment of the Great Bodhi tree;
and the fifth was the careful [establishment] of the beautiful stone stupa at the site of the Thūpaṭhānīya, in the location of the Mahācetiya.
The enshrining of the neck-bone of the Perfectly Enlightened One, and its consecration;
the sixth was Issarasamaṇa, the seventh Tissavāpiṇḍu;
the eighth was the first stūpa, and the ninth was named Vassagiri.
The delightful residence called Upāsikā, and likewise the one called Hatthāḷhaka—
these two were for the support of the nuns, for the sake of providing comfort to the bhikkhunīs.
Having entered Hatthāḷhaka, they stayed in the nuns' quarters.
Having gone with the community of monks for the purpose of receiving alms-food,
[he reached] the hand-palm hall named Mahāpāḷika,
which was provided with all requisites and attended by excellent female servants.
Likewise, for a thousand bhikkhus, he gave the most excellent gift of requisites during the Pavāraṇā ceremony, and this was done every year. Furthermore,
at the city of Tambapaṇṇi on Nāgadīpa, he established the Jambukola Vihāra.
The Tissamahāvihāra and the Pācīnārāma as well—
these works were carried out by that King Devānaṃpiyatissa,
the ruler of Laṅkā, who was possessed of merit and wisdom, seeking the welfare of the people of Laṅkā.
In his very first year, he who was fond of virtue had [the stūpa] constructed;
throughout his life, he accumulated many meritorious deeds.
This island remained under the sovereignty of that king.
That king exercised sovereignty for forty years.
After him, his younger brother, renowned as Uttiya,
ruled that kingdom— which was without a [senior] heir— skillfully as a prince.
But the Elder Mahāmahinda, having thoroughly illuminated the supreme teaching of the Conqueror— the study, the practice, and the realization—
upon the island of Laṅkā, became the great leader of the community on the island of Laṅkā.
The era of the Teacher was that of Laṅkāyaśas, who performed much for the welfare of Laṅkā.
During the eighth victorious year of King Uttiya,
this sixty-year-old dwelt within the rainy season retreat on Cetiyapabbata.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Assayuja,
this day did not bear that name while he was still alive.
But on the eighth day after Mahinda had attained final Nibbāna, [it was named after him].
Because of that, that day was honored as the "Eighth" (Aṭṭhamī).
Having heard this, King Uttiya, pierced by the arrow of grief,
went to the Elder, paid homage, and wept profusely and repeatedly.
Having poured fragrant oil into a large golden bowl,
and having had the Elder’s hair tossed into it so that the bowl was beautifully perfumed,
he had it placed within a decorated gabled chamber made of gold.
Having caused him to enter the gabled pavilion, he performed a grand celebration.
With a great multitude of people arriving from here and there,
and with a vast throng of troops, he carried out the rites of worship.
Having brought him by a decorated path through the city, which was adorned in many ways,
and having paraded him through the royal streets in the city,
he led him to the Mahāvihāra, here to the Pañhambamāḷaka.
Having had a gabled pavilion erected, that lord of the earth for seven days adorned the monastery and its surroundings for three leagues with arches,
banners, flowers, and jars filled with perfumes.
By the majesty of the King, the entire island was illuminated;
likewise, by the power of the deities, it was adorned.
Having caused various offerings to be made for seven days, that lord of the earth—
In the eastern direction, within the courtyard of the elders,
having had a fragrant funeral pyre prepared,
he led that delightful gabled chamber there while circumambulating the Great Stupa.
Having had him placed upon a funeral pyre, he performed the final honors;
and having taken up his relics, he erected a stupa there.
Having also taken up half of the relics, he erected stupas on the mountain as well.
And in all the monasteries, the kṣatriya had stūpas constructed.
For that place where the body of the Seer was deposited is called, out of great reverence, "Isibhūmaṅgaṇa" (the Seers’ Ground).
From that time forth, within a radius of three yojanas around the noble ones,
the body is brought and cremated in that very place.
The Great Elder Saṅghamittā was possessed of great direct knowledge and great wisdom.
Having performed the duties of the Dispensation and likewise much for the welfare of the world,
she— during the ninth year of King Uttiya,
while residing in peace at the Hatthāḷhaka Upassaya— lived for fifty-nine years.
Vasantī attained final Nibbāna, and the king likewise caused her to receive supreme honor and offerings for seven days, just as he had for the Elder. Indeed,
all of Laṅkā was adorned just as it had been for the Elder.
On the seventh day, having brought out the body of the Elder Nun from the gabled chamber into the city,
he displayed it near the Mahābodhi tree, close to the Cittasālā, to the east of Thūparāma.
The Elder performed the fire-offering at the site where he had stayed;
and there, King Uttiya caused a stupa to be built.
Those five great elders, as well as the elder Ariṭṭha and the others—
Likewise, there were many thousands of monks whose taints were destroyed,
and starting with Saṅghamittā, there were twelve therīs and many thousands of bhikkhunīs whose taints were destroyed.
Learned and of great wisdom, knowing the tradition beginning with the Vinaya,
they illuminated it at the proper time and then departed, subject to impermanence.
King Uttiya ruled the kingdom for ten years.
Such is this impermanence, which destroys the entire world.
A person—though knowing this impermanence—is unable to restrain it, for it is exceedingly violent and powerful;
yet, through that very [realization], one becomes disenchanted with the course of existence.
"Disenchanted, he takes no delight in either evil or merit;
for him, even this net of over-delusion, though powerful and difficult to pierce, becomes bewildered.
Thus ends the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and a sense of urgency in virtuous people.
The Twentieth Chapter: The Parinibbāna of the Elder.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Then Vañca Rājaka,
the younger brother of Uttiya, [ruled]; after his passing,
Mahāsiva reigned for ten years, a servant of the virtuous.
Having gained faith in that elder at Bhaddasāla,
he had a delightful monastery built in the city square in the eastern quarter.
After his passing, Suratisso, the younger brother of Mahāsiva, [acted likewise].
For ten years he ruled the kingdom with devotion to meritorious deeds.
In the southern direction, he [established] a monastery, a city, and a community;
in the eastern direction, an elephant’s shoulder and Mount Gokanna.
On Mount Vaṅguttara, on the mountain called Pācina,
near Raheṇaka, and likewise at Koḷambakāḷaka;
at Ariṭṭhapāda, Maṃgulaka, and Acchagallaka in the east.
In the Girinelapanāyakaṇḍa, for the prosperity of the city,
five hundred [monks] indeed descended to the earth at Mādivihāra;
they were here and there throughout the island of Laṅkā, on both banks of the Gaṅgā.
Pure in both his lineage and his kingdom, he reigned diligently for sixty years,
ruling righteously over a delightful land with reverence for the Triple Gem.
His name as king was Suvaṇṇapiṇḍatissa.
His name was Suratissa, and while he had not yet attained full sovereignty,
two sons of a ferryman— Damiḷas who were Senaguttikas—
seized that mighty king Suratissa.
For twenty years they ruled the kingdom with righteousness;
then Asela, the son of Muṭasīva, having seized it,
became the ninth brother among his uterine siblings.
He ruled the kingdom at Anurādhapura for ten years. Then,
having seized King Asela, a Tamil named Eḷāra, who was of upright birth, came here from the Coḷa country seeking the throne.
For forty-four years, he ruled the kingdom during his time of worldly affairs,
remaining impartial toward all beings, both friends and foes.
At the head of his bed, there hung a bell with a very long cord.
He caused it to be lengthened so that those desiring a legal decision might hear his voice.
That son of the protector of the earth had one son and one daughter;
while traveling in a chariot toward the Tissavāpi lake, the king’s offspring [saw] them.
A young calf was lying on the road together with its mother;
he crushed its neck with his wheel and killed it unintentionally.
Having gone on, he struck the bell of the cow, having intended to strike her.
With that very wheel, the king cut off his son’s head.
A single snake devoured a young parrot in a palmyra tree;
the mother bird went and struck the bell.
Having had him summoned, the king caused his belly to be slit open;
having had that fetus extracted, he had the serpent smeared with oil on a palm tree.
[He then proclaimed] the essential nature of the virtues of the Three Jewels, the foremost of jewels.
Though he did not know [the offense], that king, maintaining his proper conduct,
went to the Cetiya shrine and invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
As he was returning, seated in his chariot, by the tip of the chariot’s yoke, he [committed the offense].
He caused a portion of the Jina’s stupa to be broken;
the ministers said, “O King, the stupa is ruined.”
They said of him, "He has been split by her.
Even though it was done unintentionally, the king descended from his chariot and issued this command upon the road:
"Cut even my own head with the wheel!"
“Great King, our Teacher does not at all desire violence toward others;
having restored the stupa to its original state, ask for forgiveness,” they said to him.
They were about to set down fifteen stones when those fell there.
The lord gave fifteen thousand kahāpaṇas.
The elder woman prepared rice, but he threw it away in the sun;
the god rained out of season and caused her rice to rot.
Having taken rice and gone there, she struck that bell;
hearing that it was not the time for rain, she released it right then and there.
The king, conducting himself according to the Dhamma, thought, "May we receive rain in due season."
To determine its meaning, he lay down for the fast.
Overwhelmed by the majesty of the king,
the divine son Baliggāhī went to the presence of the Four Great Kings and reported it to them.
Having taken him and gone there, they informed Sakka;
Sakka summoned Pajjunna, who caused rain to fall at the proper time.
The divine son Baliggāhī reported this to the king.
From that time forth, while he was ruling the kingdom, the god did not rain during the day,
but rained at night for seven days during the middle watch.
Everywhere, even the small enclosures, became completely full.
This fault of going astray was abandoned by him through mere understanding;
unassailed, he attained supernormal power that dispels the pain of wrong views.
Being possessed of pure vision, he [overcame] the fault of going astray.
"How indeed could a wise man here not abandon [this]?
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Five Kings" in the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and a sense of spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
The Discourse on the Village Headman’s Son.
Having caused Eḷāra to be slain, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi spoke thus;
this sequential narrative is for the purpose of illustrating that matter.
He was the second brother of King Devānaṃpiyatissa.
The viceroy was a great nāga named Anu, beloved even by his brother.
The king’s queen, together with her son, was foolish and desired the kingdom;
she harbored a constant intent to have the viceroy killed.
She sent [a man] to have a pond named Taraccha constructed;

he was a donor who acted according to the king's word.
The Elder Piyaṅgu, residing on the island, directed the Elder there toward Tissa, the son of a householder;
he (Tissa) went there through the air. Taking a vessel made of kara leaves, he gave it to the king.
The king had a portion and a share for the Saṅgha cast into his bowl.
Tissa also cast a share, and Vaḷavā likewise cast a share.
But Tissa placed into his bowl a portion of what was not desired.
The king gave that full bowl of the Bhaṭṭa to the Elder;
he, having gone swiftly through the air, gave it to the Elder Gotama.
Having given portions of alms-food from the bowl to the monks as they were eating, [he returned].
Having received portions from those five hundred elders,
that elder filled his bowl and threw it into the air toward the king.
Seeing it go, King Tissa caught it and fed the monarch.
Having eaten himself, he fed the mare as well;
having used it as a head-cloth for seven days, the king sent forth the bowl.
Having gone to Mahāgāma and gathered his forces once again, he departed.
Sixty thousand went forth to battle and fought with their own brothers.
King Vaḷava, mounted upon the elephant Kaṇḍula-tisso,
and his two brothers then met together, contending in the fray.
The king, having made an end of his elephant, caused a circle of mares to be formed;
yet, seeing no flaw even there, he resolved to leap over Laṅkā.
Having leaped over the mares, [he stood] above his brother the elephant.
He hurled a javelin like a shield, so that it pierced through the back.
Many thousands of men from among those people fought against the prince in battle;
they fell, and the mighty force was indeed shattered.
“Because of the groom’s deficiency, a woman has leaped upon me”;
thus thinking, the enraged elephant, shaking him off, approached a certain tree.
The prince climbed the tree, and the elephant approached his master.
As he was fleeing after having mounted it, the prince pursued him.
Having entered the monastery, he went into the house of the great elder and lay down beneath the bed, both brother and prince.
The Great Elder spread out his robe there upon the couch;
the king, following closely behind, asked, "Where is Tissa?
"He is on that couch, O Great King," the Elder replied to him.
Having understood that it was beneath the bed,
the lord of the earth emerged from there and had protection established for that [object] all around the monastery;
having placed it upon a fivefold [cushion] and covered it with a robe.
Taking him by the legs of the bed, four young ascetics carried the prince outside along the path used for deceased bhikkhunīs.
Knowing that he was being carried away, the lord of the earth cried out here: "Do not take him!"
“Tissa, you have departed having placed yourself at the head of the family deities.
There was no forceful seizing of me by the family deities;
you should perhaps remember the virtue of those family deities at some time.”
Then the lord of the earth went to Mahāgāma;
there, out of respect for his mother, he commanded her to stay.
For sixty-eight years, with a mind fixed on the Dhamma, he remained steadfast.
And the lord of the earth caused sixty-eight monasteries to be built.
But that son of King Tissa, having been expelled by the monks,
went from there to the Dīghavāpī reservoir like someone heading elsewhere.
The prince said to the Elder Tissa of the Godha clan:
"I am at fault, venerable sir; I shall ask my brother for forgiveness.
And five hundred attendants shall perform service for Tissa."
Having taken the bhikkhus with him, that elder approached the king.
Having placed the prince aside at the top of the stairs, the elder, together with the Saṅgha, entered with faith; and the lord of the earth had them seated.
The Elder prepared the gruel and other foods in his bowl.
When asked, "What is this?", he replied, "They have come bringing it.
And when asked, "Where is the thief?", he pointed out the place where he stood.
Vihāradevī went and hid her little son.
The king said to the Elder,
"Your state as slaves is now known to us."
"You should send a novice,
one who is seven years old for me;
thus, even without the destruction of people, there will be no quarrel between us."
"This is the king's fault toward the Saṅgha; he will impose a fine upon the community.
You must perform the duties that have come to you;
take the offerings of food and so forth," he said.
Having given that to the community of monks and summoned his brother,
he sat right there in the midst of the Saṅgha together with his brother.
Having eaten right there alone, the bhikkhu dismissed the Saṅgha;
he sent Tissa back to that very place to have the harvest-work performed, while he himself,
having caused the drum to be beaten, had the harvest-work performed.
Thinking thus: "Even a very good person may agree with many things that are accumulated through various forms of abstention," what wise man would [be led astray by them]?
"One would not have a mind well-disposed toward others.
This concludes the section titled "The Battle of the Two Brothers" from the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and a sense of urgency in virtuous people.
The Twenty-fourth Chapter.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter:
The Victory of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi.
Then King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi, having performed acts of service for the people and having enshrined the relic in a spear, set out with his chariots, army, and mounts.
Having gone to the Tissa Mahārāma and paid homage to the Saṅgha, he spoke to them:
“I shall go beyond the Gaṅgā to illuminate the Dispensation.
O monks, grant me your permission to go together with you;
for the sight of monks brings both auspiciousness and protection.”
The Saṅgha gave five hundred ascetics for the purpose of penal labor;
then the lord of the earth, taking the community of monks with him, departed from there.
Having had the direct path cleared through the Malaya mountains, he arrived here.
Mounting the elephant Kaṇḍula and surrounded by warriors,
he set out for battle with a great army;
his forces were joined with those of Mahāgāma at Aguttahālaka.
Having arrived at Mahiyaṅgaṇa, he seized the Damila’s parasol;
having slain the Damilas there, he returned to Ambatitthaka.
Then, at Titthamba, he encountered the Damila who had completed the moat around the Gaṅgā.
Having shown his mother the great warrior who was fighting with the four elements and had achieved mastery in battle, he seized him by that pretext;
thereafter, he mounted and subdued the seven powerful Tamil kings.
Having seized [the cattle] in a single day and made them safe, the mighty one took wealth from Bala;
therefore it is called Khemārāma.
In a pit within a great enclosure, Doṇa seized a bull.
At Hālakola he took sovereignty; at Nāḷisobbha, a measure of grain.
At Dīghābhayagallaka, he seized even Dīghābhaya;
and at Kacchipiṭṭha, he captured Kapisīsa within four months.
In Koṭanagara he established Koṭa, and from there Hālavahāṇaka;
in Vahiṭṭha, Vahiṭṭhadamiḷa, and in Gāmaṇi, Gāmaṇi;
in Kumbhagāma, Kumbha, and in Nandigāma, Nandika.
He took Khāṇu in Khāṇugāma, but two in Tambuṇṇa.
His maternal uncle and his nephew lived in the village named Tambuṇṇa;
he seized Jambuvagga and Sosa, and that village was called by that name.
“Without knowing their own kinsmen, they cause their own people to be slain”;
having heard this, the king there performed an act of truth:
“This effort of mine has never been for the sake of the pleasures of sovereignty.”
"This is my effort for the sake of establishing the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One alone.
By this truth, may the bundle of goods carried by my army become as bright as a net!"— and so it happened exactly thus at that time.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, all the Damilas were slain until only a remnant remained;
they entered the city named Vijita for the sake of refuge.
In a comfortable open space, he established his military camp.
That military camp... became well-known by that name.
Desiring to test whether the captured city could be held, the lord of men, having seen Nandimitta, dispatched Kaṇḍula.
Nandimitta caused the elephant, who had come to seize him, to kneel;
pressing down on both its tusks, he made it sit in the *ukkuṭika* (squatting) posture.
Because Nandimitta engaged in combat with the elephant at that place, [he was victorious].
Therefore, because of that village there, it is called "Elephant's Port.
Having investigated both sides, the king went to the conquered city;
at the southern gate, a terrifying battle took place between the warriors.
At the eastern gate, however, Veḷusumana slaughtered many thousands of Damilas mounted on horses.
The Damilas closed the gate, but the king dispatched his warriors.
Kaṇṇula, Nandimitta, and Suranimila were in the south.
Mahāsoṇa, Goṭṭha,
and Thera-putta— these three elders;
At those three gates they performed their duties,
while at the others they did likewise.
That city was protected by three moats and high ramparts.
The iron gate, which was difficult for enemies to overcome,
he approached after standing on his knees, breaking the stone weapons with his tusks,
and likewise the bricks; thus that elephant reached the iron gate.
But the Damilas standing at the gate-towers hurled various weapons,
as well as red-hot iron balls, cauldrons, and molten lead.
When the molten lead was thrown upon his back, Kaṇḍula then began to smoke.
"Vedanaṭṭha, go to the place of water and plunge therein!
This is not for you to drink liquor;
it is the opening of the iron gate. Go, open the gate!"—thus spoke Goṭṭhayimbara.
Having thus aroused his pride and trumpeted like a crane,
that best of elephants rose up from the water and stood upon the dry land,
arrogant and haughty. Having separated himself from the herd of elephants, he applied medicinal ointment to his body.
The king, having mounted his elephant, touched its forehead with his hand and said,
"O dear Kaṇḍula, I grant you sovereignty over the entire island of Laṅkā.
Having thus gratified him and fed him excellent food, he dismissed him.
Having wrapped it with a cloth and made it well-fastened,
he had a sevenfold buffalo hide bound upon its back.
Having caused that inner oil-skin to be given to it, he dispatched it.
Roaring like a thunderbolt, he seized his enemies together;
he pierced the threshold with his fangs and struck down the doorpost with his feet.
That door, its crossbar shattered, fell crashing to the ground.
At the city gate, Nandimitta, having caught with his arms the timber materials falling from the back of an elephant, set them rolling away.
Seeing his deed, Kaṇḍula was delighted in heart.
That enemy, the ivory throne, which had been prepared first,
he cast aside. Then the noble elephant, Kaṇḍula,
turning back and looking toward his own rear for the purpose of entering, remained there as a warrior.
“I shall not enter by the path made for elephants,” thought Nandimitta;
having reflected thus, he struck down the wall with his arm.
That wall, eighteen cubits high and as solid as a mountain, it is said, fell to the ground.
Beholding a wild animal that did not wish to take that path,
he leaped over the wall and fell inside the city.
Breaking through each gate one by one,
that band entered like Soṇa.
The elephant took a chariot wheel, while Mitta seized a cart-fender.
The group [attacked] the coconut tree, the stainless supreme sword;
Mahāsoṇa [attacked] the palmyra tree, and the Elder’s son [attacked] the great poison;
each separately, having gone to their respective streets, they crushed the Damiḷas there.
Having broken through the city of Vijita, the Kṣatriya [reigned] for four months;
likewise, having gone to Girilaka, he slew the Damila at Giriya.
Then, having gone to the city of Mahela, which had three great moats...
Surrounded on all sides by kadamba flower creepers,
with a single entrance that was difficult to enter, the king dwelt there for four months;
then, through a battle of spells, the lord of the earth captured King Mahela.
Then, while proceeding toward the city of Anurādhapura, the lord of the earth encamped his army near Mount Paritōkāsa.
In the month of Jeṭṭhamūla, having had a reservoir constructed there, he settled down.
In that place was a village called Posona-nagara.
Hearing that King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi had come for battle,
King Eḷāra summoned his ministers and spoke.
“The king himself is a warrior,
and his warriors are very famous;
what indeed should the minister do?”
"What do these men think?
These warriors of King Eḷāra, beginning with Dīghajātu, have made this firm resolve:
'Tomorrow we shall engage in battle.'"
King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī, having consulted with his mother,
had thirty-two military encampments constructed according to her advice.
Therein, he placed effigies of kings holding royal parasols.
The king himself stood within the gateway. King Eḷāra,
fully armed, mounted his great mountain-elephant and proceeded there with his equipped and powerful army.
While the battle was raging, O Dīghajānu,
that mighty and terrifying king, taking up his sword and shield,
fought on; and that royal form, rising eighteen cubits into the air, ascended into the sky.
Having cut it with his sword, he broke the first rampart of the army.
Having likewise broken through the rest, the one of great strength reached the rampart of the army where the village headman stood.
That warrior Suranimāla, who was walking before the king,
announced his own name and, being of great strength,
reviled him. The other, enraged and thinking, "I shall kill him," rose up into the sky.
As he was descending, the other held out a plank.
Thinking, "Cut this plank for me," he struck the plank with his sword; it released him and caused the other to fall.
While fitting a pearl-plate [to his armor], Dīghajantu fell there;
Sūranimila rose up and struck him down with a spear.
Phussadeva blew the conch, and the Damila army was broken.
The Eḷaras also turned back and slaughtered many Damiḷas.
There, the water in the tank became filled with the blood of those slain;
therefore, it became famous by the name Kulatthavāpī.
Having had the drum beaten there, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī commanded:
"Let no one slay Eḷāra unless he first releases me.
Then, having armed himself and mounted his own horse Kaṇḍula, who was likewise armored, he set forth.
Pursuing Eḷāra, he arrived at the southern gate.
At the southern gate of the city, both lords of the earth fought;
Eḷāra hurled a javelin, but Gāmaṇi dodged it.
And with his tusks, he struck that elephant with his own elephant;
he hurled a lance at Eḷāra, and there he fell along with his elephant.
Then, having emerged victorious from the battle, together with his chariots, forces, and vehicles—
Having made Laṅkā a place of single canopy, he entered the city.
Having caused the drum to be beaten throughout the city for a league in every direction,
he gathered the people and had them perform an offering to King Eḷāra.
At the spot where his body fell, he had it cremated with a gabled chamber;
there he erected a cetiya and provided for its maintenance.
Even today, those dwelling near that location [belong] to the Lord of Laṅkā.
By that very same method, they did not even have musical instruments played.
Thus, having subdued thirty-two Tamil kings,
Duṭṭhagāmaṇī made Laṅkā his kingdom under a single umbrella.
When the city of Vijita was divided,
that warrior Dīghajātu reported it to his nephew,
the son of Eḷāra, [offering him] his own share of Hallaka.
Having heard that he had come for the sake of the Pesa, Halluka,
on the seventh day from the day Elāra was burnt,
descended here together with sixty thousand men.
Having heard of that king’s downfall, he was overcome with shame and thought,
"I shall fight," yet out of modesty he came here to Mahātittha.
He established his camp in the village of Koḷambahālaka.
Having heard of her arrival, the king set out for battle.
Fully equipped with his war armor, he mounted the elephant Kaṇḍula, saying:
"Place the chariot-yoke upon the elephant's neck, and let the side-pieces follow behind."
That god Ummādaphussa was the foremost archer on the island;
equipped with ten times the weapons and armored, the remaining warriors followed him.
Amidst the tumultuous battle that ensued, Bhalluka stood there fully prepared for combat.
You approach me with deceit, O King, but I am Kaṇḍula, the Naga king.
To quell that impetuous force, I have retreated step by step;
and with him, the entire army has likewise retreated step by step.
The king said, “In previous battles, this [elephant] never retreated; why is it now, Phussadeva?
He replied, “Victory is ours, O Lord; we have reached the ground of victory.”
Looking back, he retreated; he would stand at the place of victory.
Then the elephant, having retreated while Phussadeva looked on, stood firmly established within the boundary of the Great Monastery.
Standing there, the Nāga king Bhalluka, a Damila,
approached the King and mocked the Lord of the Earth.
Covering his mouth with his sword, the King then rebuked him.
“I shall let it fall upon the king’s face,” he thought, and he discharged the arrow.
Striking against the blade of his sword, the arrow fell to the ground;
yet, under the impression that [the king] had been pierced in the mouth, the jackal let out a loud cry.
"Sitting behind the king, O sir, was the mighty Phussadeva;
he struck the king’s earring with the tip of his arrow as it fell,
having placed the king beneath his foot."
Having hurled another arrow and pierced his shield,
the quick-handed one brought the king down from his head;
when that Bhalluka had fallen, a cry of victory arose.
Right there, Phussadeva, wishing to make known his own fault,
cut his own kaṇḍavalli plant and showed a handful of blood.
Seeing that, Rādhañña asked the king, "What is this?"
"The king has inflicted punishment upon me," said the lord of the earth.
"Anger is indeed called hatred," he replied,
mentioning the rubbing of his earrings.
"Having perceived what was not hatred as hatred,
what have you done here, brother?
Having said this, the Great King spoke here of gratitude.
“Great honor worthy of a king shall be yours.
Having slain all the Damilas, the king will have achieved victory;
having ascended to the terrace of the palace, he will sit there upon the lion-throne.”
In the midst of the Nāṭaka ministers, he had Phussadeva’s arrow brought and placed straight upon the ground with its shaft.
With kahāpaṇa coins, they covered that arrow one upon another.
Having had it covered, he caused it to be given at that very moment to Phussadeva.
Then, on the terrace of the king’s palace, which was adorned by the lord of men,
illuminated by fragrant lamps, and filled with various perfumes.
Adorned with dramatic performances and celestial nymphs,
upon a beautiful and soft couch spread with priceless coverlets, he lay there,
indifferent even to his great majesty and prosperity.
Remembering the unshakeable destruction [of his kin], he found no peace.
When the Arahants on the island of Yuga knew of this thought that had arisen in him,
they sent eight Arahants to comfort the Lord.
Having approached them at midday, O King, they descended through the gate;
announcing their arrival, they ascended to the palace floor.
Having paid homage, O Great King, they had them seated upon thrones.
Having performed various honors, he asked the reason for their arrival.
"O lord of men, we have been sent by the Saṅgha on the island of Piyaṅgu;
we have come to see the King," they replied. Then the king spoke again: "We wish to lie down with you."
“How, venerable sir, can there be relief for me,
by whom the slaughter of Akkhobhiṇīmahāsena was caused?
“There is no obstacle to the path of heaven for you because of that deed.”
"O Lord of Men, among these one and a half humans have been slain.
One is established in the Refuges, and another in the five precepts;
the one with wrong view and immoral conduct, and the rest, are considered equal to cattle."
"You shall indeed cause the Buddha’s teaching to shine forth in many ways;
therefore, O Lord of Men, dispel this mental distress.
Thus addressed, the Great King received consolation from them.
Having paid homage to them and dismissed them, he lay down and reflected again:
"May you never eat food without the Saṅgha.
Thus did the mother and father instill the forest-dwelling life in their young children regarding food.
Thinking, "Has anything been eaten by the community of monks without first being offered?
he saw, during the morning meal, a single circle of black pepper that had been consumed by the Sangha without being set aside for them, due to a lapse of mindfulness.
"I must perform a punitive act for that purpose"— thinking thus,
he alone slaughtered ten million people here among the human masses. Having reflected on this,
one should properly consider the danger of sensual pleasures in the mind.
"One should attend to that which destroys all [suffering]—impermanence; it is good, it is good!
Thus one shall attain liberation from suffering and reach great fortune before long.
In the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter: The Victory of Duṭṭhagāmaṇi.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter.
Having made the great festival of the Maricavaṭṭika Monastery his "single umbrella" (sole sovereignty),
the one of great glory established the kingdom of Laṅkā and assigned the warriors their respective positions according to their merit.
The warrior Abhaya, son of the Elder, did not desire what was being offered to him.
When asked, "What is your purpose? he replied, "There is war. When asked, "What is the name of this war that has been waged for a single kingdom? he replied:
"I shall wage war against the thieves of the defilements, which are so very difficult to conquer.
When he spoke thus, the king repeatedly tried to dissuade him;
yet, having entreated him again and again, he obtained the king's permission and went forth.
Having gone forth in due time, he attained Arahantship;
he was surrounded by five hundred monks whose taints were destroyed.
When seven days had passed since the auspicious event of his ordination, Abhaya became free from fear.
As soon as he had been consecrated, that king, with great magnificence,
went to the Tissavāpī pond which was beautifully adorned, according to the custom for sport,
both to enjoy himself and to protect the conduct of those who had been consecrated.
They placed all the king’s regalia and hundreds of offerings in the location of the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery.
Right there, at the site of the stupa, they established the supreme spear together with its relic.
The spear-bearers, the king’s men, set it upright.
Having played in the water during the day with his harem, the Great King said in the evening:
“We shall go home; hoist the spear up, sirs!”
The king’s officials were unable to move that spear;
having assembled with the royal army, they honored it with perfumes and garlands.
Seeing this great marvel, the king was delighted in heart.
Having established a guard there and entered the city from that point,
he had a palisade constructed around the Kunta [mound] and had a cetiya built there;
having had a thūpa constructed, he also had a monastery (vihāra) built.
In three years, that lord of men completed the monastery;
for the sake of the great construction of the monastery, he convened the Saṅgha together with its assemblies.
At that time, there were one hundred thousand bhikkhus, and as for the bhikkhunīs—
Ninety thousand people had gathered together.
At that assembly, the lord of the earth said this to the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, having forgotten the Saṅgha, I ate a dish of pepper."
"May this act of penance for me be accepted," he said,
and had built the beautiful Maricavaṭṭi Monastery together with its shrine.
"May the Saṅgha accept it," he said, and offered the water of dedication.
Having brought it down, he joyfully gave the monastery to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having had a large, beautiful pavilion constructed all around that monastery,
he there offered a great almsgiving to the Saṅgha.
Even though he had set his foot upon the water of the Abhayavāpī pond,
that pavilion was constructed for him.
In Seso Kāsa, the lords of men provided an opportunity for discourse; having given food, drink, and other necessities for seven days,
they bestowed all manner of costly requisites suitable for a novice.
The first set of requisites was worth a hundred thousand;
at the end, it was worth a thousand. And the entire Saṅgha received that [relic].
By the hero in battle and by the hero in giving toward the Triple Gem—
With a serene and stainless mind, a lamp illuminating the Dispensation,
that grateful king— beginning with the construction of the stupa—
built vast monasteries in order to worship the Triple Gem.
Having relinquished here those treasures of priceless value,
the remaining nineteen crores minus one were left behind.
Though the ocean is ten-fold in its wealth, it is nevertheless defiled by the fault of impurity.
"By people endowed with a distinction of wisdom, the fivefold qualities have been attained;
having grasped the essence, they truly exist.
Thus, one who possesses intelligence should apply their mind to grasping this essence."
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery," in the Mahāvaṃsa composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Twenty-seventh Chapter:
The Great Festival of the Lohapāsāda.
Then the king reflected upon what was well-known, well-heard, and traditionally taught:
“Of great wisdom and ever meritorious, having reached his decision through wisdom:
‘The Elder who brought light to the island, to my royal grandfather—
thus indeed did King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi speak of you.’”
Possessing great merit, he will in the future cause to be built a magnificent Great Thūpa adorned with golden garlands, twenty hundred cubits high. Furthermore,
he will build an Uposatha hall embellished with various gems and jewels.
"Having constructed nine stories as well as a golden palace," thinking thus,
the Lord of the Earth had it written down and established;
he had it placed within a casket, kept right there in the royal palace for all to behold.
Having obtained a golden plate, he read the inscription upon it:
"In the future, after four thousand one hundred years have passed,
the son of Kākavaṇṇa, the wicked Gāmaṇi, will become a lord of men."
"‘This and that, and in this way, he will cause [it] to be done’—
having heard this read, the lord of the earth, joyful and uttering a cry of exultation,
clapped his hands; then, having gone early in the morning to the beautiful Mahāmeghavana grove,"
Having convened an assembly, he spoke to the community of monks:
“I shall have a palace built for you, equal to a celestial mansion.
Send a divine mansion [as a model] and then give me a description.”
The community of bhikkhus dismissed them there, for eight of them were already free from the outflows (khīṇāsava).
In the time of the Sage Kassapa, there was a brahmin named Asoka,
who dedicated eight tickets for alms-food to the Saṅgha.
He said to a female slave named Bharaṇī, "Give [it] constantly.
Having given those [offerings] with great care for as long as she lived,
she passed away from there and was reborn in a celestial mansion established in the sky, beautiful and pure.
She was always surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs (accharā).
Her jeweled palace rose twelve yojanas high,
with a circumference of forty-eight yojanas.
Adorned with a thousand gabled chambers, it has nine stories;
it is endowed with a thousand inner apartments, majestic, and facing four directions.
It functions with a thousand conch shells and possesses windows with lion-frames.
Adorned with networks of tinkling bells and surrounded by a railing,
the Ambalaṭṭhika Palace stood in its center,
appearing peaceful yet crowded with hoisted banners.
While traveling toward the Heaven of the Thirty-three, they saw that very Elder there;
having then had a painting made upon a cloth with vermilion,
they returned and presented the cloth to the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha, having taken the cloth, sent it to the presence of the king.
Upon seeing it, King Sumana came to that most excellent monastery and had a supreme Loha-pāsāda (Copper Palace) constructed, which was like a painting.
At the very time he began his work,
the wealthy man had eight hundred thousand pieces of gold deposited at each of the four gates.
He also had a thousand bundles of cloth placed at each gate.
There were many kinds of sweetmeats made of sugar, oil, sugar-candy, honey,
and flour. Having declared, "This legal action here is groundless and must not be carried out," he had the value of the legal action assessed and made them pay that amount as a fine.
One hundred cubits, one hundred cubits was each side as one looked upon it;
indeed, the four-faced palace was just that much in height.
In that most excellent palace, there were nine stories.
And for each level, hundreds of gabled chambers were provided;
all those gabled chambers were inlaid with pure gold,
and their railings were adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Their floors were made of various jewels, and their lotuses likewise;
they were encircled by rows of tinkling bells.
Therein was a palace of a thousand chambers, well-constructed.

The miracle at the foot of the mango tree, the teaching in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,

the Mahāsamaya Sutta and likewise the Rāhulovāda.
The Mahāmaṅgalasutta and the meeting with Dhanapāla;

the assembly at the Pārāyaṇa, and likewise the relinquishing of his life-span.
The taking of the boar’s delicacy, the pair of golden-colored robes,

The cremation, the extinguishing of the fire, and the honors there;
the distribution of the relics in a vessel, and those things that inspire faith—

He had the Vessantara Jātaka performed in full detail,
from the city of Kusināra up to the Bodhi tree.
Those four Great Kings stood there in the four directions.
The thirty-three sons of the gods and the thirty-two maidens;
the eight generals of the yakkhas and twenty more besides;
the devas with hands joined in reverence, and then those with jars full of flowers.
Deities who are dancers, deities who play musical instruments;
deities who carry mirrors, as well as those who hold flower branches;
deities who grasp lotuses and other such beings—various other deities in manifold ways.
A row of precious gems, and likewise wheels of Dhamma;
a row of deities bearing swords, and similarly deities bearing parasols;
upon their heads were five-handled [lamps] filled with scented oil.
A row of dukūla-cloth bundles stood with hands forever joined in reverence;
in each of the four corners of the crystal fire-altar was a great jewel.
There were heaps of gold, gems, pearls, and diamonds.
In the four corners, four radiant discourses appeared;
bright upon the very walls of stone colored like fat,
they were manifested through science, fashioned as ornaments within the relic chamber.
The Lord of the Earth had all the architectural features constructed within the delightful relic chamber of this great temple;
he appointed a supervisor of works here who oversaw everything.
The great elder Indagutta, possessed of the six supernormal powers and great wisdom—
this entire [display] was established through the sovereign power of the king, the power of the deities, and the unimpeded power of the noble ones.
Having worshipped the Sugata, who has reached the goal, the most worthy of worship, the supreme being in the world, free from all defilement—
and having worshipped his relics, which were ground into powder for the sake of desiring the welfare of mankind—
the wise man, adorned with the virtue of faith, should consider that merit to be equal.
And he worshipped the relics of the Sage, which remained as if the Sugata were still present.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Construction of the Relic Chamber" in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Thirtieth Chapter.
The Thirty-First Chapter:
The Enshrinement of the Relics.
Having completed the works on the relic chamber,
the Subduer of Enemies convened an assembly and spoke thus to the Saṅgha:
"Indeed, those works upon the relic chamber have been completed by me."
"Tomorrow I shall enshrine the relic, O Bhante; please recognize the relics.
Having said this, the Great King then entered the city;
meanwhile, the Saṅgha of monks reflected upon a monk who could fetch the relic.
He appointed the one named Soṇuttara, a dweller in the monastery courtyard who was devoted to making offerings,
to perform the task of bringing the relics. While the Protector,
wandering on his journey for the welfare of the world, was away, he [appointed him].
A young brahmin named Nanduttara on the bank of the Ganges invited the Fully Enlightened One together with the Saṅgha and fed them. Then the Teacher, along with the Saṅgha,
boarded a boat for the purpose of departing.
There, the Elder Bhaddaji, possessed of the six supernormal knowledges and great psychic power,
seeing the place where the water had washed away, spoke thus to the bhikkhus:
"A golden [image] was indeed spoken of by me as being very large."
A palace twenty-five yojanas high fell here;
having reached the waters of the Ganges, it made them turbid.
The bhikkhus, not believing this, reported it to the Teacher.
The Teacher said, "Dispel the doubt of the bhikkhus.
To make this known even in the Brahma-world, he, who was capable of exercising mastery [over the mind],
rose into the sky by means of supernormal power and stood at a height of seven palm trees.
Having placed the Dussa Stupa in the Brahma-world while extending his arm,

Having seized the upper story of the palace with his big toe and raised it up,
he showed it to the people and then hurled it back to its place.
When the young brahmin Nanduttara saw that miracle, he—
"I might be able to lead this realm that is dependent on others.
Thinking thus, he made this aspiration, and so he appointed the monk Soṇuttara—
even though he was only sixteen years old— to that task.
“From where shall I bring the relic?”—thus he asked the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha explained those relics to the Elder:
“The Leader of the World was lying upon his parinibbāna bed;”
"O Lord of Devas, you must divide those relics of mine among the various realms of the world," he said.
"O Lord of Devas, of my bodily relics, eight measures were distributed:
one measure was honored by the Koliyans at Rāmagāma."
Then it was led to the world of the Nāgas, and there it was honored by the Nāgas;
it will serve as a treasure for the Great Thūpa on the island of Laṅkā.
The Elder Mahākassapa too, the great seer of long vision—
By King Dhammāsoka, the ruler of men, the expansion of the relics was carried out.
Near Rājagaha, the great relic was caused to be built by King Ajātasattu as a well-constructed treasury.
Having brought seven *doṇa* measures of relics, he had them enshrined in Rāmagāma;

King Dhammāsoka likewise established that great relic treasury.
"Having passed over the eighth *doṇa*, he made no effort to have it brought.

Having entered the ocean, it remained there where the waters were split in two.
Upon the surface of eighteen various jewels, crowded together,
the nāgas saw that casket belonging to the black nāga king;
having approached the Mañjerika nāga abode, they announced it.
Having gone there with ten thousand koṭis of nāgas,
he paid homage to those relics and, having brought them to his own abode,
constructed a stūpa made of every kind of jewel, as well as a pavilion above it.
Having had it constructed together with the Nāgas, he always worshipped it with great reverence.
A vast guard was stationed there, for on the following day the protector of the earth would go to deposit the relics in their shrine.
Having thus heard the words of the Saṅgha, he replied, "So be it.
Then, observing that the time had come to receive [the relics], the lord of the earth thought:
"Tomorrow there will be a depositing of the relic. He went to his own private quarters.
Having arranged for all necessary duties, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city.
He had the entire city as well as the path leading here carefully decorated and beautified.
Sakka, the lord of the devas, having summoned Vissakamma,
had him decorate the entire island of Laṅkā in manifold ways.
At the four gates of the city, various kinds of food and alms were provided.
For the sake of the enjoyment of the great multitude, the lord of men had it established.
On the fifteenth day of the observance,
in the afternoon, the wise man, well-disposed and adorned with all ornaments, [attended] to his royal duties.
Surrounded on all sides by all kinds of dancers, by warriors with their weapons,
and by a great multitude of troops consisting of elephants,
horses, and chariots, and adorned with various ornaments.
He mounted a magnificent chariot drawn by well-trained, beautiful horses.
Having placed an adorned, itching elephant in front as a splendid guard,
he stood beneath a parasol with its handle made of gold.
Eight thousand beautiful city women,
adorned with full water-jars, surrounded that kingdom.
Likewise, they carried baskets of various flowers and staff-lamps.
An equal number of women, having taken up those very same [garments],
surrounded him with eight thousand one hundred well-adorned children,
bearing beautiful banners of various colors.
With the sounds of various musical instruments here and there,
and with the noise of elephants and chariots, the earth seemed as if it were splitting apart.
That highly renowned one entered the great forest of clouds in all its splendor.
Just as the king of the gods shines in the Nandana Grove,
so did he shine at the start of the King’s departure. Hearing the sound of the great musical instruments in the city,
the ascetic Soṇuttara heard it even while sitting in his own cell.
Having plunged into the earth and gone to the abode of the nāgas,
they appeared there before the nāga king.
Rising and paying homage, he seated him upon a couch.
The Lord of Nagas, having paid him honor, questioned the messenger who had arrived.
When that was said, he then asked the reason for the Elder’s coming;

"The relics deposited here by the Buddha for the purpose of being enshrined in the Mahāthūpa have come into your hands; indeed, you must give them back to me.
Hearing this, the Nāga king became exceedingly distressed.
"This ascetic is indeed powerful; it would be difficult to seize him by force.
Therefore, the relics must be taken elsewhere," he thought, and signaled this intention to his nephew who was standing there by his manner of expression.
Knowing his intention, he who was named Vāsuladatta went to that shrine-house, swallowed the casket,
and having gone to the foot of Mount Sineru, hid it in the Kuṇḍalāvatta cave.
Three hundred yojanas long and one yojana in girth,
that being of great psychic power, having spread out many thousands of hoods,
emits smoke and blazes while lying down.
Having had many thousands of snakes, similar to himself,
constructed, he had them laid down, surrounded on all sides.
Then many gods and nāgas descended there.
“We shall witness the battle between these two elephants,” so [thought] the maternal uncle, thinking, “The relics have been seized by my nephew.
Knowing this, the Elder said to him: “There are no relics here in my presence.”
The Elder Āditoppabhuti, having recounted the history of those relics,
said to that Nāga king, "Give me the relics.
To convince the Elder otherwise, that lord of serpents—
Taking him to the shrine-house, he described it to him:
"Behold, O monk, this well-constructed shrine and shrine-house, beautifully fashioned with many kinds of various jewels."
In the entirety of Laṅkā Island, all manner of jewels—even a mere brick at the foot of a staircase—are not worth even a fraction [of it]; what need is there to mention other things?
From a place of great honor, what is a place of little honor?
“O monks, this ‘guiding of the elements’ is not appropriate for you.
The ‘realization of the truths’ exists within you;
indeed, it is appropriate to lead the elements toward that state of realizing the truths.”
“Tathāgatas arise for the sake of liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra;
this is the intention of the Buddha, and therefore we shall take his relics.
Today itself that king will perform the enshrinement of the relics.”
"Therefore, without making a fuss, give me the relics quickly.
The Naga said, "If you see the relics, Venerable Sir, take them and go.
The Elder, having made him say this three times, departed.
Having measured out a small space, the elder, remaining there, O friend,
immediately thrust his hand into the mouth of his nephew.
Taking the casket of relics, he said, "Stay, O Naga!"
"Having submerged himself in the earth, the bhikkhu has emerged in the monastery enclosure.
The nāga king has gone; we have been deceived.
Thinking thus, he dispatched [the messenger] for the sake of bringing back the relics to his nephew.
Then the nephew, not seeing the basket within his womb,
came out lamenting and informed his maternal uncle.
At that time, the Naga king also thought, "We have been deceived."
All the nāgas lamented, oppressed by grief.
But the devas, having gathered together, were joyful at the nāga’s victory over the bhikkhu;
honoring the relics, they departed along with him.
Coming while lamenting into the presence of the Saṅgha, the nāgas,
afflicted by the loss of the relics, wailed in many ways.
Out of compassion for them, the Saṅgha caused a small portion of the relics to be given to them.
Delighted by that, they went and brought offerings and ritual implements.
Sakka, taking a jeweled couch and a golden footstool,
arrived at that place together with the devas.
Having had a palanquin prepared by Vissakamma at a prominent location for the Elder,
and having set it down within a beautiful jeweled pavilion,
[the king] took the Mother’s Casket from the hand of that Elder.
Having placed [the Buddha] upon a couch in the Caṅkoṭaka hall, they seated him upon an excellent throne.
Brahmā held the parasol, while Santussita held a yak-tail fan;

The four Great Kings stood there with swords in hand,

Thirty-two maidens stood holding staffs and lamps.
Having driven away the wicked yakkhas,
twenty-eight yakkha generals stood there, providing protection.
Like one playing the lute, Pañcasikha stood there,
having prepared the stage with the sounding of musical instruments like the *timbaru*.
And many sons of the gods were engaged in singing excellent songs.
The Naga king Mahākāla was praised in many ways.
Celestial musical instruments resounded, divine songs were performed,
and deities rained down showers of celestial perfumes and other offerings.
Thus, the Elder Indagutta, having fashioned an iron parasol as large as a world-system, had it erected as a defense against Māra.

While the monks who were stubborn as barren soil were performing group recitation at various places,
the great king Duṭṭhagāmaṇi arrived there exultant,
having brought [the enemy] on his head upon a golden palanquin.
Having set aside the relic casket and established it upon a seat,
Pañcalīka stood there after worshipping and paying homage to the relic. Herein,

Having passed by and heard the sounds of celestial musical instruments and the like,
the Kṣatriya Brahmadeva, seeing nothing yet filled with wonder and joy,
honored [the relics] with a parasol of the elements and consecrated him in the sovereignty of Laṅkā.
“The divine umbrella, the human one, and the very umbrella of liberation—
thus, to the Teacher, the Lord of the World,
who bears these three umbrellas, I give my kingdom three times,” he said with a joyful mind.
Three times indeed did the Kṣatriya, the giver of sovereignty over Laṅkā,
carry the relics upon his head together with the caskets, while both gods and humans paid homage to the radiance of the relics.
Surrounded by the community of bhikkhus, having circumambulated the stupa clockwise,
