Ninety-six koṭis of arahants [honored] the supreme stupa.
Surrounding him on all sides, they stood with palms joined in reverence.
As the lord of men, filled with joy, descended into the relic chamber and thought,
"I shall place [the relics] upon this costly and beautiful couch," [the earth shook].
The casket of relics, together with its contents, rose up from his head and remained suspended in the sky at a height of seventy palm trees.
Then the casket opened of its own accord, and the relics emerged from it.
Having assumed the guise of a Buddha, resplendent with the primary and secondary marks,
they performed the twin miracle at the foot of the Gaṇḍamba tree—
just as the Buddha had done while the Sugata was still living— under his empowered authority.
Having seen that miracle, with minds serene and one-pointed,
twelve koṭis of gods and humans attained arahantship;
the rest attained the three lower fruits, while those of the past exceed the path of calculation.
Then, casting off their Buddha-attire, they alighted upon the casket.
Thereupon Caṅkoṭa descended and stood upon the head of the king,
together with the Elder Indagutta and the dancers.
Having reached the beautiful bed surrounding the Relic Chamber,
the Radiant One placed the casket upon the jeweled couch. Then,
having washed his hands again with water scented with perfumes, he—
Having rubbed [the relics] with a fourfold mixture of perfumes, the Lord of the Earth, full of reverence, opened the casket, took up those relics,
and reflected thus, seeking the welfare of the great multitude.
If the relics remain undisturbed by anyone,
and if the relics shall endure as a refuge for people,
then [I shall rest] upon the couch of final Nibbāna in the manner of the Teacher’s passing away.
"Let them lie upon a well-prepared, most costly bed.
Thinking thus, he placed the relics upon that supreme couch;
then the makers and the relics alike rejoiced upon that supreme couch.
On the fifteenth uposatha day of the bright fortnight of Āsāḷhī,
under the constellation Uttarāsaḷha, the relics were thus established.
With the establishment of the relics, the great earth trembled.
Many miracles occurred in manifold ways.
The king, filled with faith, honored [the relics] with a white parasol and offered the entire kingdom of Laṅkā for seven days.
The king offered all manner of ornaments upon his body as worship within the relic chamber;
likewise did the dancers, the fish-eaters, the assembly, and the deities.
Having given garments, balls of rice, ghee, and other offerings to the Saṅgha, the lord of the earth—
Having had the bhikkhus perform group recitation throughout the entire night,
on the following day he caused the city drum to be sounded, for the benefit of the people,
saying: "May all the people behold these relics during the seven days of their manifestation."
The great elder Indagutta, possessed of great psychic power,
saw that humans on the island of Laṅkā desired to worship the relics.
At that very moment, he arrived here, paid homage to the relics, and—
"Let them go to their own homes"— thus it was as he had resolved.
That great king of vast renown, having bestowed a great gift upon the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus continuously for those seven days, [departed].
In the Relic Chamber, the work has been brought to completion by me;
the Saṅgha ought to know that the covering of the Relic Chamber [is now done].
The Saṅgha appointed those two novices to that task.
They enclosed the relic chamber with stone that had been brought from afar:
"May the garlands here not wither; may these fragrances not fade;
may the lamps not go out; and may no misfortune whatsoever befall it."
"Let six stones, the color of honey, be joined together without any gaps.
Thus those whose taints were destroyed resolved all of this here.
The Great King commanded: "Let the great multitude act according to their ability."
"Let him build here a shrine for the depositing of the relics," said he who desired their welfare.
And upon the back of the Great Relic Shrine,
the great multitude constructed thousands of relic shrines according to their ability.
Having closed up everything, the king completed the stupa;
and he also completed the square sacrificial altar there at the cetiya.
Thus did he perform these stainless meritorious deeds himself while living.
They perform every supreme attainment for the sake of the cause;
and those with pure minds, free from all harshness,
act as well for the sake of their retinue, knowing various distinctions.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Enshrining of the Relics," in the Mahāvaṃsa, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Thirty-second Chapter:
The Departure for the Tusita Heaven.
While the work on the parasol and the plastering of the stupa were not yet finished;
Afflicted by a terminal illness, the king became ill.
Having summoned Tissa, his younger brother from Dīghavāpi, he said to him:
"Complete the work on the stupa that remains unfinished."
Because of his brother’s weakness,
he had tailors fashion a tunic from pure cloth and cover the stupa with it.
He then had skilled painters construct a railing there with great care.
He had a row of five-fingered marks made on water-pots filled with scented powder,
and likewise he had umbrellas fashioned from bamboo in the shape of parasols,
as well as moon and sun symbols made of coarse leaves for the head-ornaments.
Having had it painted with lac and saffron, beautifully adorned, he reported to the king at the stupa: "What was to be done is finished.
Then the lord of the earth, having reclined upon a palanquin, arrived here.
Having performed a circumambulation of the shrine by means of a palanquin,
and having paid homage at the southern gate,
he lay down on his right side upon a bed spread out on the ground beside the most excellent Great Thūpa.
Having lain down on his left side in the supreme Lohapāsāda,
he remained joyful, looking out with the community of bhikkhus before him.
Then, those who had come from here and there for the purpose of inquiring after his health—
In that assembly there were ninety-nine crores of bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus performed communal recitation in organized groups;
and there, the lord of the earth saw the Elder Thera-puttābhaya.
He who fought twenty-eight great battles without defeat,
that great warrior who never turned back— my master is he.
When the battle with Death arrived, seeing it as my own defeat, I thought thus.
"Now he does not wish me to be his preceptor, for fear of the Elder’s son"—
thus did that elder reflect. Having understood what he was thinking,
the elder dwelt on Mount Pañjalika at the headwaters of the Karinda River.
Accompanied by a retinue of five hundred arahants who had destroyed the taints, he approached through the air by means of psychic power and stood surrounding the king.
Having seen him, the king was filled with faith and sat down before him.
"Having previously fought while taking you ten great warriors as my support, I now fight all alone; I have begun a battle with Death.
I am unable to defeat the enemy that is Death," he said.
The Elder said: “Do not fear, O Great King, lord of men!
For one who has not conquered the enemy of the defilements (*kilesasattu*), the adversary Death is unconquerable.
Indeed, every conditioned thing (*saṅkhāragata*) must inevitably perish.”
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent”—thus it was said by the Teacher.
Even for the Buddha, there is no lack of fear regarding impermanence;
therefore, contemplate that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and non-self.
Even in your second existence, when a great desire for the Dhamma had arisen for the sake of supreme benefit,
and the world of the gods was present before you, you abandoned celestial bliss.
Having come here, you performed manifold acts of merit in many ways.
This work, which illuminates the teaching of the Karanampēkara King,
is a merit performed by one of great merit. As long as today’s day lasts,
may you remember it all in this way, and happiness shall be yours immediately.
Having heard the Elder’s words, the king was delighted and spoke thus:
“You are my refuge even in the battle against death.
Then, being overjoyed, he had the book of merit brought forth.
He spoke to a scribe to read it, and he read that book aloud:
"Ninety-nine monasteries were caused to be built by the Great King;
nineteen crores [were spent] on the monastery and the pepper roll."
The supreme Lohapāsāda was built at a cost of three hundred million;
[and] priceless [relics] were placed within the Mahāthūpa.
“Twenty-four [relics] were enshrined in the Mahāthūpa; the remaining ones were enshrined by Subuddhi.

“In the Malaya country, at the place called Koṭṭha, during a time of drought,
he took two very costly earrings and gave them away.

With a mind full of faith, he gave a handful of sour millet to Cūḷaṅganiya as he was fleeing after being defeated in battle.
Having caused the proclamation of the time, [the Elder] arrived through the air.
When it was said, "This is alms-food given to one who has destroyed the taints, a self-restrained ascetic, regardless of his own self," the lord of the earth replied:
"For seven days let there be a festival for the monastery, and likewise a festival for the palace."

I bestowed a magnificent and great gift, without distinction, upon both sections of the Saṅgha from the four quarters.
I had the Mahāvesākha festival performed twenty-four times;
on the island, I had the Saṅgha provided with the three robes three times.
For exactly seven times seven days, I held this royal festival on the island.
Five times within the dispensation, with a joyful mind,
I gave. Constantly, in twelve places, with ghee and pure wicks,
I lit a thousand lamps, worshipping the Sugata.
Constantly, in eighteen places, I provided for the monks according to the rules;
I gave food and medicine to those who were ill.
In forty-four places, I prepared honeyed milk-rice.
In those very same places, and at the oil-pressing site, at the potter’s kiln,

there, together with the meals, I constantly caused this very [offering] to be given.
On the uposatha days, and on the eighth days of every month,
I caused lamps and oil to be provided for the monasteries throughout the island of Laṅkā.
Having heard that the gift of the Dhamma is greater than the gift of material things, I gave this offering.
Beneath the iron palace, in the midst of the Saṅgha, upon my seat, I thought:
"I shall recite the Maṅgala Sutta for the Saṅgha.

I had [her] given a *nāḷi* measure, and I had her given four finger-breadths.

All this was a gift from my sovereignty; it humbled and gladdened my mind.
"Disregarding my own life, while I was in a state of misfortune, I gave two gifts; that alone makes my heart rejoice.
Having heard this, the Elder Abhaya [replied] regarding those very two gifts:
For the sake of inspiring confidence in the king’s mind, he praised them in many ways.
Among those five elders, the elder Kaṅguambilagāhaka and the great elder Maliya were on Sumanakūṭa mountain.
Having given that to nine hundred bhikkhus, he consumed it himself;

Having shared it with the bhikkhus at the Kalyāṇika Monastery, [he gave it to them].

The Thirty-third Chapter:
The Ten Kings.
There were people established in the kingdom of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi.

When Lajjikatissa had died, his younger brother,

In the vicinity of the Lohapāsāda, he had thirty-two delightful palaces built to enhance the beauty of the Lohapāsāda.

The lord of the earth had a boundary wall for the Vālikāṅgaṇa and a rampart constructed;

The general Mahāratta, the lord of the earth,
seized the Nāga king Khalḷata right there in the city.
Now, that king’s younger brother was named Vaṭṭagāmaṇi.
Having slain that wicked general, he ruled the kingdom. That king,

He made his maternal uncle Nuḷādevī and the Great Sage his ministers.
Because he remained in a state of joy, they called him Pītirāja.
Thus, in the fifth month after his consecration to the kingship—
In the city of Nakula in Rohaṇa, there was a certain foolish brahmin servant named Tiya. Having heard the words of that brahmin,

The seven Damila chieftains, together with their retinues, descended at Mahātittha.

King Paṇḍukābhaya had monasteries for non-Buddhist sectarians constructed,

At the time of his passing, that elder—

The Thirty-fourth Chapter:

Upon his death, Mahācūḷi-Mahātissa caused [a stupa] to be built;

Having heard that a gift given with one's own hand bears great fruit, he [bestowed it].

Having caused a well-established monastery to be built,

he had the path prepared with carpets spread out so that they might travel with washed feet.
There, at the four gates of the city, they held festivals with songs and instrumental music, and he caused great alms-giving to be distributed.
Throughout the entire island, he established a continuous garland of lamps.
Even within a league all around the ocean,
that beautiful worship was performed for the Cetiya by Mahatena;
here, the great worship at Giribhaṇḍa is called "exalted."
When the monks had assembled for that gathering of worship,
the lord of the earth, having caused eight golden drums to be struck there by those standing nearby, established offerings in eight places.
He offered a great almsgiving for twenty-four thousand [monks].
He gave six robes and caused their release from bondage;
he constantly employed laborers at the four gates that had been established.
Without neglecting any meritorious deed established by former kings as well as by his own brother,
the lord of men caused everything to be performed.
He [offered] himself, two sons of queens, an elephant, and an auspicious horse.
Although he was being restrained by the Saṅgha, that lord of the earth gave to the Saṅgha.
He gave to the community of monks what was worth six hundred thousand,
but to the assembly of nuns, what was worth one hundred thousand.
Having given various allowable goods,
he who was skilled in diverse methods extracted himself and the rest from the Saṅgha at Kālāyana Kaṇṇika, on the mountain named Maṇināga.
The lord of men caused the Kaḷavhaya monastery to be built,
as well as the Kubu monastery on the bank of the Bandhana river, the Samudda monastery,
the Cūḷa-Huvā monastery at Kaṇṇika, and the one known as Nagapabbata.
When a monastery named Pāsāṇadīpaka had been built by himself,
the Kṣatriya [King] was pleased with a novice who had brought drinking water for him.
Having gained confidence in that service, [he granted land] extending eight yojanas all around.
To the novice who had not given the monastery’s property to the Saṅgha, the king, the lord of the earth,
being pleased, caused a maṇḍapa and a reservoir to be built at Vihāra, and likewise he granted that property to the Saṅgha.
Thus, having obtained abundant wealth through her excellent wisdom,
free from intoxication and negligence, and with her heart detached from sensual indulgence, she— delighting in meritorious deeds— ceased to cause distress to those unworthy of her service.
"Accumulating abundant and manifold merit.
Thus ends the chapter titled "The Illumination of the Eleven Kings," composed in the *Mahāvaṃsa* for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Thirty-fourth Chapter.
The Thirty-fifth Chapter:
The Twelve Kings.
Āmaṇḍagāmaṇyabhaya, the son of that [king], reigned for nine years and eight months after the passing of Mahādāṭhika.
He had a parasol made for the beautiful Mahāthūpa.
In the same way, he had a foot-bench and a head-bench constructed.
Likewise, he built the Loha-pāsāda (the Copper Palace), the one called Thūpa, and the one called Posatha;
he also constructed the courtyard of the inner chamber and the veranda of the inner chamber.
In both places he constructed a beautiful pavilion of jewels,
and the lord of men had a silver cave-monastery built. Furthermore,
he caused the Mahāgāmeṇḍa reservoir to be made on the right side of that [monastery].
The lord of men, who was rich in merit, gave to the Dakkhiṇa monastery;
he caused a general amnesty throughout the entire island,
having had all varieties of vine-fruits planted here and there.
The lord of the earth, having prepared a vessel called *sakubhaṇḍaka* filled with mango juice and having fashioned a cloth cushion,
caused it to be offered to the entire Saṅgha with a mind of complete serenity.
Having filled his bowl with mangoes, Āmaṇḍa,
the wise village headman, killed his own father, King Kaṇiṭṭhokaṇi,
and that kṣatriya reigned in the city for three years.
This is the grinding stone for the Uposatha hall that she chose at the place called Cetiya;
sixty sons of the king, having committed an offense against the king, were seized along with their weapons on Cetiyapabbata, O monks.
He caused Kaṇira, who was devoid of virtue, to be expelled from the mountain cave.
Following the passing of King Kaṇira, his son Āmaṇḍagāmaṇi,
the nobleman Cūḷābhaya, reigned for one year.
Thus, on the bank of the Goṇaka River, on the southern side of the city,
the protector of the earth had the Cūḷagallaka monastery built.
And by whom Sīvalī was the younger sister of Cūḷābhaya— by him [it was caused to be built].
The daughter of Āmaṇḍa ruled the kingdom for four months.
But when Sīvali was removed by Āmaṇḍa’s nephew,
he who was named Iḷanāga raised the royal parasol in the city.
When that lord of men had gone to Tissavāpī in his first year of reign,
many Lambakaṇṇakas abandoned the city and arrived there.
Not seeing them there, the king became angry and caused [them] to be made [slaves] by those [very people].
On the bank of the Maddaya pond, near the Mahāthūpa,
he appointed those who were suspicious as investigators and stationed outcasts there.
Consequently, all the Ālambakaṇṇas became enraged and gathered together as one.
Having seized that king and confined him in their own house,
they themselves administered the kingdom,
while the queen then adorned her own son, the prince Candamukhasiva.
Having placed [the elephant] in the hands of the nurses,
he sent word to the vicinity of Maṅgala the elephant; having led him there,
the nurses delivered the Queen’s entire message to Maṅgala the elephant.
“This is your son Sādhu;
your husband stands in prison;
you remain only because he who was to be slain by the enemy has been spared.”
"But his slaughter must be done by her.
'Kill him yourself,' they say—this is the Queen's command.
Having said this, they laid him down at the foot of the elephant.
Distressed, that nāga wept; having broken through the enclosure and entered the great compound, he firmly barred the gate.
Having opened the door-panel in the courtyard where the king was seated, he stood there.
Having seated him upon his back, the elephant approached Mahātīrtha.
Having caused the king to board the boat there,
the elephant himself went to the Malaya region on the opposite bank of the Dadhī river.
Having lived on the opposite shore for three years, that kṣatriya,
taking his army with him, came by boat to Rohaṇa.
Having disembarked at the rocky ford, the lord of the earth—
There in Rohaṇa, he assembled a great force.
Then, from the southern Malaya, the king’s auspicious elephant went to Rohaṇa itself to perform its duties for him.
There, in the presence of the great elder named Tulādhāra, who was a reciter of Jātakas concerning the Buddha named Mahāpaduma,
he heard the Kapi-jātaka and felt deep faith toward the Bodhisatta.
Having built the Nāgamahāvihāra, one hundred bow-lengths in extent,
he caused a stūpa to be made and had it enlarged as it stood;
he also constructed the Tissavāpī and likewise the Duravha reservoir.
Having gathered his forces, the king set out for battle;
hearing of this, the Lambakaṇṇas also prepared themselves for war.
At the gate of the Papallaka trunk-road, in the field of Hiṅkaravāpika—
A battle took place between the two, a mutual inflicting of harm.
Because their bodies were exhausted by the boat, the men sank down, O King;
therefore, having made his name known, the king himself entered it.
Terrified, they lay upon their bellies with their ears pressed back;
having cut off their heads, he adorned them like a heap of jewels.
When this had been done three times, the lord of the earth, out of compassion—
“Seize them alive, do not kill! he commanded.
Then the king, having emerged victorious in battle, returned to the city;
having raised the royal parasol, he entered the festival grounds at the Tissavāpi reservoir.
Having emerged for a water-sport, well-adorned and elegantly attired,
he beheld his own splendor and prosperity being obstructed.
Remembering the long-eared ones (the Nāgas), he became enraged and yoked them to his chariot.
The succession of their generations entered the city ahead of them.
Standing at the threshold of Mahāvatthu, the king gave this command:
"O men, cut off the heads of these people right here upon this threshold!"
"O bull among charioteers, these oxen are yoked to your chariot;
have their horns and hooves trimmed, my lord.
Then, being thus entreated by his mother, he desisted from the execution of her son.
The king had the nose and the big toe of those two cut off.
The Kṣatriya gave the elephant the province where he lived;
because it was the elephant’s province, it became known by that name.
Thus, in Anurādhapura, the kṣatriya King Iḷānāga reigned for six years less than six.
Upon the passing of that Iḷānāga, his son Candamukhasīva [ascended].
For eight years and seven months, the king exercised his sovereignty.
Having had a reservoir constructed in the village of Maṇikāra,
that lord of the earth gave it to the monastery named Issarasamaṇa.
The chief queen of that king, known as the Damila princess,
gave her own prize from the battle to that very monastery.
Having killed Candamukha Siva while sporting at Tissavāpi, she [offered it].
Known as Yasaḷālakatisso, his youngest brother reigned over the delightful city of Anurādhapura,
the auspicious birthplace of Laṅkā, for seven years and eight months.
To Dovatika who had been given [as a slave], the gatekeeper himself, when questioned, replied with a form identical to that of the king: "I am Subha.
Having adorned him with royal ornaments for the sake of strength, the king [employed] that Subha.
Having seated himself cross-legged upon a couch for the sake of laughter,
Yasaḷālaka fastened a turban upon his head for the sake of strength; then,
taking a staff in his hand, he himself stood at the threshold of the door.
While his ministers were paying homage, as he sat upon his throne,
the king would smile at him from time to time in this manner.
One day, the soldier asked the king who was laughing.
"Why did this Balattha laugh at me in my presence? Thinking thus,
that handsome Balattha had the king killed here and reigned for six years, renowned as Subharāja.
In two great monasteries, King Subha had a delightful row of cells built,
named "Subha" itself; likewise, near Uruvelā, he had the Vellivihāraka constructed.
In the east, at the mouth of the Ganges,
was the village of Nandi; there lived one son of Lambakaṇṇa,
a resident of the northern region named Vasabha, who attended upon his maternal uncle, the general.
Upon hearing the report, "The king named Vasabha is laughing," he had all those named Vasabha executed throughout the kingdom of Dīpa.
Then, to his wife, he said: "We shall give these to the king as a tribute."
Having consulted with the commander-in-chief, he went to the royal palace early in the morning.
As he was walking along, he suddenly placed a betel leaf,
free of lime powder, into the hand of the elephant to ensure it was well-guarded.
At the gate of Rājagaha, the commander-in-chief, seeing that there was no betel powder with the betel leaves, sent someone for the sake of that powder.
When the commander’s wife saw that Vasabha had gone for the sake of the powder, [she spoke].
Having spoken thus and given the secret, he caused that thousand [pieces] to be carried away.
Then Vasabha, having gone to the site of the Mahāvihāra,
was received there by the elders with garments soaked in milk.
After that, having heard the words of the leper who was determined to attain kingship,
he was delighted and became certain that "I shall be the thief. Then,
having obtained capable men, he proceeded to plunder the village.
Having gone to Rohaṇa while performing his duties, according to the instructions of Kapallapuva,
King Kaṇṭha, having gradually reached the kingdom with his army and vehicles,
approached the vicinity of the city within two years.
Having slain Subharāja in battle, that mighty bull [Vasabha] had his maternal uncle also raised up before the meal, for he too had fallen in the fight.
That body of his maternal uncle was one who had previously rendered him assistance.
King Vasabha acted with loving-kindness toward his chief queen, named Mettā.
He questioned a reciter of the Sotthiya-reading regarding the measure of his own lifespan;
he too said to him in private, "Twelve years."
Having given her a thousand [pieces of gold] for the sake of guarding the secret,
the king convened the Saṅgha, paid homage, and asked:
"Venerable sir, might there be a cause for the increase of the life-span?"
“It exists,” so the Saṅgha has declared, regarding the liberation from obstacles.
O Lord of Men, the gift of a water-strainer, the gift of a dwelling place,
and the gift of the protocol for the sick should be given.
“Likewise, the repair of dilapidated dwellings should be done;
having undertaken the five precepts, they should be well-guarded. And the observance of the Uposatha should be performed on the Uposatha day.”
Saying "Very well," the king departed and did everything exactly as instructed.
At the end of each three-year period,
the lord of the earth had the entire Saṅgha on the island provided with the three robes.
Having dispatched messengers, he caused it to be given to the elders who were yet to arrive;
at thirty-two locations, he had honeyed milk-rice offered.
And at sixty-four locations, he gave a great mixed almsgiving.
He caused [the lamps] to burn by the thousands at four places:
at Cetiya-pabbata, at the Thūpārāma Cetiya,
at the Mahāthūpa, and at the Mahābodhi-house— indeed, at these very sites.
At Cittalakūṭa, he had ten delightful stūpas built;
throughout the entire island and at all monasteries, he restored those that were dilapidated.
And at the Valliyera monastery, having gained faith in the Elder, he [acted likewise].
He had a monastery built named Mahāvalligotta,
and he constructed the Anurārāma near the village of Mahāgāma;
he established the estate of Heḷigāma and granted a thousand [pieces of land] to it.
Having had the Mucela Monastery constructed at Tissavaḍḍhamānaka,
he caused the portion of water from the Āḷisāra river to be given to the monastery.
At the Kalamba ford, near the Thūpa, he had a jeweled cloak fashioned.
He had a Uposatha hall built, and he had it plastered with oil-soaked clay.
Having caused a thousand *karīsa* of land to be plowed, he gave it away;
he also had an Uposatha hall built at Kumbhigallaka in the monastery.
The lord of the earth had a rest-house for the Uposatha built here at Issarasamaṇaka, as well as a stūpa and an ārāma hall.
He also constructed a row of cells in the Mahāvihāra looking toward the western side.
He built a four-sided hall and renovated what was dilapidated.
Furthermore, that same king had a shrine-hall constructed featuring images of the four Buddhas within the delightful courtyard of the Great Bodhi tree.
The chief queen of that king, who bore that same name,
likewise caused to be built a delightful stupa and a beautiful stupa-house.
Having completed the stupa-house in the Thūpārāma, the lord of the earth—
When his festival was completed, he gave a great almsgiving.
He also provided the requisites for those monks who were devoted to the Buddha’s word,
as well as ghee and molasses for the monks who were preachers of the Dhamma.
At the four gates of the city, he caused alms to be distributed to the poor,
as well as provisions for the sick monks and medicine for the ill.
He built the Rājūppalavāpī tank, the Vahakola bridge, and the village of Gāmaka.
Mahānīka, Vittavāpī, and likewise Mahārāma;
Kehāla, Kāḷivāpī, Cambuṭṭhi, Vātamaṅgana,
and Abhivaḍḍhamānaka— these are the eleven reservoirs.
He had twelve storehouses built for the sake of abundant food,
a city wall for the sake of protection, and a moat.
He also had a gate-tower at each of the four gates and a great foundation hall constructed.
He had a lake constructed in the park and dispatched a swan there.
Having had many lotus ponds made here and there in the city,
the lord of the earth caused water to be brought into them by means of underground channels.
Having thus performed various kinds of merit,
King Vasabha, having become one whose obstacles were destroyed and being ever devoted to meritorious deeds,
reigned over the city for eighty-four years.
In the forty-fourth year of the Vāsava era,
King Subharāja, fearing danger from Vasabha,
sent his own daughter to the carpenter Iṭṭhiya to perform a festival offering.
The king gave away his own woolen blanket as well as his goods;
when that [king] was killed by Vasabha, the carpenter took them.
Having established him in a position of honor, he raised him up in his own house.
While he was performing his work, a young girl brought him food.
On the seventh day, seeing that he had attained the attainment of cessation beneath a cluster of *ambapuppha* trees, the wise girl gave him the meal.
Having cooked the meal again, she brought food for her father.
When questioned about the reason for her delay, she explained the matter to him.
Delighted, he repeatedly had the Elder provided with food.
Seeing the future, the Elder spoke with confidence to the young girl:
"O girl, when you have attained sovereignty, remember this place.
And at that moment, the Elder passed into final Nibbāna.
When his son Vaṅkanāsikatissa had reached maturity,
King Sakevasabha sought out a maiden suitable for him;
having seen that young girl, he dispatched men to find her.
In the village of Iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī, those skilled in the characteristics of women informed the king.
The king then began to issue orders regarding her;
at that time, Iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī [declared] her status as the king’s daughter.
But Subharañña made his daughterhood known by means of blankets and other gifts;
the king, pleased with what he had heard, gave her that auspicious gift of "well done.
Upon the death of Vasabha, his son Tissaka, who had a crooked nose, [ascended the throne].
He reigned in Anurādhapura for three years.
On the bank of the Goṇanadī river,
King Vaṅkanāsikatissa caused the monastery named Mahāmaṅgala to be built.
But that queen Mahāmattā, remembering the words spoken by the Elder,
made a collection of wealth for the purpose of building a monastery.
After the passing of Vaṅkanāsikatissa, his son had it constructed.
Having reigned for twenty-two years, Gajjabāhuka, the village headman,
hearing his mother’s words, had a royal mother’s monastery built at the site of the Kadamba flower for the sake of his mother.
That wise mother, for the sake of the earth, gave one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] to the Mahāvihāra and had a monastery constructed.
She herself also built a stone stupa there.
He provided for the enjoyment of the Saṅgha by purchasing [articles] from here and there.
Having caused the Abhayuttara Mahāthūpa to be enlarged, he had it plastered;
and right there at its four gates, he had the entrance archways constructed.
Having had the Gāmaṇitissa Tank constructed, that lord of the earth gave it for the enclosure wall of the Abhayagiri Monastery;
and he also caused a casing to be made for the Maricavaṭṭi Thūpa.
Having purchased it for one hundred thousand [pieces of gold], he gave it as property for the Saṅgha.
In his final year, he had a monastery called Rāmaka constructed;
he also caused a great hall with seats to be built within the city.
After the death of Gajabāhu, his father-in-law,
the aged Mahallaka Nāga, ruled the kingdom for six years.
[He reigned] over Pejalaka in the east and Koṭipabbata in the south.
At the western Dakapāsāṇa, at Sālipabbata in Nāgadīpa;
at Tanaveḷi in Bījagāma, and at Tobbalanāgapabbata in the province of Rohaṇa;
and at Girihālika within Antoṭṭha.
The highly wise King Mahallanāga had these seven monasteries constructed in a very short time with wealth that was essentially worthless;
thus, from that which is insubstantial, he produced what is substantial.
"Having performed many meritorious deeds through wisdom,
fools nevertheless take [the results] for the sake of sensual pleasures,
committing many evils out of delusion."
The thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Twelve Kings," in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Thirty-sixth Chapter:
The Thirteen Kings.
Following the passing of Mahallanāga, his son Bhātikatissa [reigned].
For twenty-four years he ruled the kingdom of Laṅkā.
That lord of the earth, having caused the Gavaratissa Monastery to be built, had a rampart constructed all around the Mahāvihāra.
He gave the Mahāgāmaṇi tank to that monastery and constructed a monastery named Bhātiyatisa.
He also had an uposatha hall built in the delightful Thūpārāma.
The lord of the earth also had the Randhakaṇḍakavāpi constructed.
With a gentle heart toward living beings and intense reverence for the Saṅgha,
the protector of the earth bestowed a great almsgiving upon both divisions of the Saṅgha.
After the passing of Bhātikatissa,
his younger brother Tissa reigned over the island of Laṅkā for twenty-eight years.
Having gained faith in the Elder Mahānāga of Bhūtārāma, he—
He carefully constructed the Ratanapāsāda at Abhayagiri;
he also built a rampart at Abhayagiri and a great monastic courtyard (mahāpariveṇa).
Furthermore, he who was called Maṇisoma likewise constructed a great monastic courtyard.
Right there he had the shrine-house renovated,
as well as that at Ambatthala, and also the house at Nāgadīpa.
Having measured out the boundary of the Mahāvihāra, he had it constructed there.
The lord of men, the king, carefully constructed a row of cells at the Kukkuṭagiri monastery,
and in the Mahāvihāra he built twelve great four-sided palaces,
beautiful and delightful to behold.
At the Dakkhiṇavihāra stupa, he had a casing constructed;
he had the Mahāmegha refectory and the Vanāsima built.
Having removed [the obstruction] from the view of the Mahāvihāra wall, he caused it to be taken away.
He had the Magga and Dakkhiṇavihāra constructed,
as well as Gāmi. He also had the Bhūtārāma Vihāra and Rāmagoṇaka built,
and likewise he had the Nandatissa Ārāma constructed.
To the east of Anulātissa, on the mountain by the Ganges river,
the lord of men caused to be built the Niyelatissārāma and the Piḷapiṭṭhi Vihāra, as well as the Rājamahāvihāra.
He likewise had an uposatha hall constructed in three places:
in the Kalyāṇīka monastery, in Maṇḍalagiri,
and in the monastery called Dubbalavāpi Tissa— indeed, in these monasteries.
After the passing of Kaniṭṭhatissa, his son,
known as Cūḷanāga, reigned for only two years. Then,
King Cūḷanāga’s younger brother killed his elder brother.
For one year, Kuḍḍanāga reigned over Laṅkā.
The lord of the earth increased the Mahāpeḷa and provided an uninterrupted supply of food from a single stalk for five hundred bhikkhus.
At that time, Sirināga, the commander-in-chief and brother of Queen Devī, became a bandit against King Kuḍḍanāga.
Accompanied by a powerful army, he approached the vicinity of the city.
Fighting with royal power against the earth-lord Kuḍḍanāga,
he drove him away and, having achieved victory, ruled over the excellent city of Anurādhapura and the kingdom of Laṅkā for nineteen years less one.
Having had a parasol made for the excellent Mahāthūpa,
the lord of the earth commissioned a gold-worked ornament, beautiful to behold and delightful to the mind.
He also constructed a bronze palace, five stories high and compact.
At the four gates of Mahābodhi, he had staircases rebuilt.
Having constructed the Chatrapāsāda, he performed a great offering ceremony;
and being full of compassion, he bestowed the Kulambaṇa upon the island of Dīpa.
When Sirināga had passed away, his son Tissa,
who was skilled in righteous administration, reigned for twenty-two years.
For he established an administration here that was free from violence.
From that time on, he was known by the name King Vohāraka Tissa.
Having heard the Dhamma from the elder Deva, who resided at Kambugāma, he established the Paṭikamma practice in the five monasteries.
The devout Anurārāma, a resident of Mucelapaṭṭana, caused a continuous stream of alms-giving to be established for the Elder Mahātissa;
he also constructed a pavilion for King Tissa at both Mahāvihāras.
He had the eastern wing of the Mahābodhi temple and a pair of bronze statues made.
Having constructed the Sattapaṇṇika palace as a comfortable residence,
he caused a thousand pieces of gold to be given to the Mahāvihāra month after month.
In the Abhayagiri Monastery, known as Dakkhiṇamūla;
in the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery, known as Kulālitissa;
and in the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Monastery, known as Mahāgāmaka.
In the Mahānāgatissa stūpa, and likewise in the one called Kalyāṇīka—
thus in these eight stūpas, as well as in the southern monastery, the general Mūkanāgasena had the offering of parasols performed.
In the Marica-vatti monastery, likewise in the one called Puttabhāga,
in the one named Issarasamaṇa, in the one called Tissa, and in Nāgadīpaka—
in these six monasteries, he thus had ramparts constructed.
He had a Poṣatha hall constructed in the place called Anurārāma,
and throughout the entire island of Laṅkā, at the sites where the Ariyavaṃsa discourses were recited,
he established a cycle of almsgiving out of reverence for the True Dhamma.
Having given three hundred thousand [pieces of gold], the lord of men,
who was fond of the Sāsana, liberated the bhikkhus from their debt.
Having caused the Great Vesākha festival to be celebrated for the inhabitants of the Island, he—
He caused all the monks to be provided with the three robes.
Having crushed the Vetullavāda and carried out the suppression of evil,
he caused the Dispensation to shine forth through the minister Kapila.
The youngest of that king was known as Abhayanaṅga;
he was well-acquainted with the queen and was feared by his brother.
Having fled and gone to Halla-tittha along with his attendants, he—
As if angry with his maternal uncle, he cut off [the uncle's] hands and feet.
Having established him right here for the sake of the king’s kingdom and wealth,
and having shown him to be like a dog, he seized him by the neck.
Having boarded a ship right there, he went to the opposite shore;
then his maternal uncle, Subhava, approached the lord of the earth and,
acting like a well-wisher, bestowed that kingdom upon him.
Abhaya, knowing this, dispatched a messenger here.
Seeing that banyan tree, he went around it on all sides with a bamboo spear,
crushing it and making its base weak.
Having struck him down with his very arm and threatened him, he caused him to flee;
the messenger went and reported that occurrence to Abhaya.
Having learned of it, Abhaya then took those Damilas and Basukas.
He went to the city-dweller to fight with his brother.
Knowing this, the king fled and mounted a horse;
he went to Mount Malaya with the queen, while his younger brother pursued him.
Having slain the king in Malaya, he returned taking the queen with him;
the lord of the earth ruled the kingdom in the city for eight years.
He had a stone terrace constructed all around the Mahābodhi tree.
In the courtyard of the Lohapāsāda, the king likewise prepared a pavilion;
having distributed many garments by means of two hundred thousand [measures],
he gave a gift of cloth to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on the Island.
Upon the death of Abhaya, his nephew Sirināga ruled over the kingdom of Laṅkā for two years,
having had the rampart rebuilt all around the Mahābodhi tree.
On that very sandy ground, to the west of the Mahābodhi temple,
the lord of the earth had a delightful Haṃsavaṭṭa pond and a great pavilion constructed beyond the Mūcela tree.
The son of Sirināga, named Vijayakumāra,
reigned for one year after his father's passing.
There were three Lambakaṇṇas who were brothers at Mahiyaṅgaṇa.
Saṅghatisso, Saṅghabodhi, and thirdly Goṭṭhakābhaya— these three,
who had gone to the Tissavāpi reservoir, were blind yet possessed of vision.
As they were approaching to attend upon the king, he spoke to them by the sound of their footsteps.
“These three carry the earth-rulers,” he said.
Having heard that, Abhaya later asked again as he was traveling:
“Will his lineage endure?”
He was asked once again:
"Of the last one," he replied.
Having heard that, the two of them went away.
Having entered that city, those three favorites of the king,
dwelling near the monarch and performing royal duties,
together slew King Vijaya within the royal palace.
They consecrated Saṅghatissa as commander-in-chief and then anointed him to the two royal powers.
Thus, having been consecrated in the most excellent city of Anurādhapura,
Saṅghatissa ruled the kingdom for four years.
At the Mahāthūpa, the lord of the earth had a parasol and goldwork fashioned;
separately, he had four great gems worth a hundred thousand [pieces] set in the center of the four suns.
Upon the summit of the stupa, he likewise offered a priceless diamond cushion for the Great Parasol Pūjā;
and that lord of men caused forty thousand robes to be bestowed upon the Saṅgha.
Having heard that discourse from the Elder Mahādeva, a resident of Dāmagallaka,
which was taught in the Khandhaka and illustrates the benefits of offering rice-gruel,
he became confident in the Saṅgha and caused a gift of rice-gruel to be bestowed.
At the four gates of the city, with due care and diligence,
that king, together with his queens and his ministers,
went from place to place to eat jambu fruits, traveling toward the eastern island.
As he was traveling, the people dwelling in Pācīna were distressed;
they had placed poison in the fruits of the rose-apple trees for the king's meal.
Having eaten those ripe rose-apples, he died right there.
The general Saṅghatthabhaya consecrated him in the kingdom.
Known as King Sirisaṅghabodhi, he was renowned for observing the five precepts;
he ruled over the kingdom at Anurādhapura for two years.
He had the delightful Salākagga built at the Mahāvihāra; then,
perceiving that the people in the island were afflicted by a severe drought,
his mind was shaken with compassion, and he himself [performed rites] in the courtyard of the Great Thūpa.
Having made this resolution, the king lay down upon the ground:
"Once the god has sent down rain and I am washed away by the water,
I shall not rise up again from here, even if I am dying right now."
While the lord of the earth was thus lying down, the god sent down rain for that long,
drenching the great earth throughout the entire island of Laṅkā;
yet he did not rise up, because he was not carried away by the water.
Then the ministers opened channels for the water to flow out.
Thereupon, the righteous King emerged from the waters, floating upon them;
thus did he dispel the fear of drought on the island through his compassion.
Having heard that they were being born here and there as thieves,
the king had the thieves summoned and caused them to be executed in secret.
Having ordered their secret execution, he [ordered] the corpses of those who had died...
Having terrified them with fires, the calamity of the thieves was destroyed.
Then a single *yakkha*, known as Rattakkha,
came here and made people's eyes red here and there.
Looking at one another, trembling with fear,
those humans and devas cried out, "A yakkha has seized our splendor!
Hearing of their calamity, the king’s heart was filled with agitation.
Having observed the eightfold Uposatha fast while still in the womb,
he lay there thinking, "I shall not rise until I have seen that Yakkha.
By the power of his righteousness, the Yakkha went into his presence.
When asked by him, "Who?", he replied, "I am.
He said, "Why do you wish to devour my offspring? Do not eat them!
He replied, "Give me a man from one of your provinces."
When told, "It is not possible," he replied, "One by one.
He said, "I cannot give anything else; eat me.
To this he replied, "That is not possible," and requested that he be given the tax from every village.
Saying "So be it," the lord of the earth established him in the entire island and in excellent villages,
and caused him to receive tribute.
By that Great Being, who was compassionate toward all living beings—
A great fear of disease arose, but it was dispelled by the lamp of the island.
He was the king’s treasurer,
the minister Goṭṭhabhāya.
Having crossed over at Cero,
he arrived at the city from the north.
Taking his water-strainer, the king [entered] from the southern gate.
Disliking violence toward others, he fled all alone.
Taking a meal in a basket and traveling along the road ahead,
he repeatedly detained the king who was seeking to enjoy his meal.
Having strained the water and eaten, the compassionate king, wishing to show him favor, spoke these words:
"I am King Saṅghabodhi; come, take my plow."
"Show [this] to Goṭṭhābhaya; he will give you much wealth.
Though the lord of the earth did not wish to do so, for his sake, while still seated, he took off his own head and gave it to him. He then passed away.
He showed [the elephant] to Goṭṭhābhaya, whose mind was filled with wonder at hearing it;
having given wealth to that king, he caused him to perform a great honor.
Thus, this Goṭṭhābhaya is also known as Meghavaṇṇābhaya.
Renowned for thirteen years, he ruled over the kingdom of Laṅkā.
Having had the Great Site constructed and having had a pavilion built at the site’s entrance,
he adorned it there for the Saṅgha of monks.
Seating eight thousand [monks] day after day,
he provided them with various kinds of delicious rice gruel, hard foods, and soft foods,
as well as robes, and thus established a great gift of alms.
For twenty-one days he had this [image] fashioned in a continuous sequence.
He constructed the most excellent stone pavilion in the Mahāvihāra,
and having turned the pillars of the Lohapāsāda, he set them back in place.
He established the Mahābodhi stone altar, the gateway arch at the northern gate,
and the pillars at Cakukaṇṇa together with the wheels.
He had three stone images made and installed at the three gates.
And he had a stone couch installed on the southern side.
He caused a place of striving to be built behind the Great Monastery,
and he renovated everything that was dilapidated throughout the island.
In the Thūpārāma he renovated the Thūpaghara, and likewise in Therambatthala;
in the monastery called Maṇisoma, he also carried out repairs.
In the Thūpārāma, in the Maṇisoma-ārāma, and in Maricavaṭṭaka;
In the Dakkhiṇāvha monastery and the Uposatha halls, he had a new monastery built called Meghavaṇṇābhaya,
after collecting funds from the inhabitants of the island for the great festival of the monastery.
He gave six robes to thirty thousand bhikkhus and likewise performed the Great Vesākha Festival at that very time.
And year after year, he presented six robes to the Saṅgha.
Purifying the Teaching by means of suppressing the wicked,
he caused approximately sixty monks who were proponents of the Vetulla doctrine—
thorns to the Conqueror’s dispensation— to undergo ordination while residing at Abhayagiri.
Having rebuked them, he had them cast onto the opposite bank;
there, as the Elder was being thrown, a monk clad in rags took refuge [with him].
Known by the name Saṅghamitta, he was skilled in the science of prosperity and other such arts.
Having become angry with the bhikkhus in the Mahāvihāra,
he came here. Entering the assembly at the Thūpārāma,
that unrestrained man went to the dwelling of the Elder Vāsī at the Saṅghapāla pariveṇa.
Addressing the Elder Goṭṭhāsaya by the king’s name,
he interrupted the speech of the king’s maternal uncle.
He had been a frequent visitor to the royal family, and the king placed his trust in him.
He entrusted his eldest son, Jeṭṭhatissa, and his youngest son,
Mahāsena, to that bhikkhu; the latter took charge of the second one,
and Prince Jeṭṭhatissa became devoted to that bhikkhu.
Upon the passing of his father, the eldest disciple became king;
though he was reluctant to depart while the funeral honors for his father’s body were being performed,
the lord of the earth himself went forth to restrain the wicked ministers.
Placing his younger brother in front, immediately behind his father’s body,
and then having appointed his ministers, he himself followed behind;
once the younger brother and the father’s body had departed, he followed immediately after them.
Having secured the gates and struck down his wicked ministers,
he impaled his father on a stake all around the funeral pyre.
Because of that deed, his name became "Kakkhala" (the Hard).
But that bhikkhu, Saṅghamitta, was afraid of that lord of men.
At the very moment of his consecration, after consulting with Mahāsena,
he departed from here for the opposite shore, watching for the king’s consecration.
He had his father construct a supreme iron palace,
seven stories high, worth ten million pieces of gold.
Having honored a gem there that was worth six million, he [placed it within].
He caused the Jeyyatissa-taṭa to be made,
as well as that named the Maṇi-pāsāda. He offered two highly precious jewels at the Mahāthūpa and had three archways (toraṇas) constructed for the Mahābodhi temple.
Having had a monastery built on the Pācinatissa mountain,
the lord of the earth gave it to the Saṅgha during his five-year reign.
It was formerly established by Devānampiyatissa.
King Jeṭṭhatissa, having brought the large stone and the beautiful image from the place called Thūpārāma,
established them in the monastery on Pācinatissa Mountain.
At the Kāḷamattikavāpi pond, on the mountain of the shrine,
he built a great monastery and a palace, as well as a Mahāvesākha festival.
Having done so, he gave six robes to the Saṅgha consisting of thirty thousand monks.
Jeṭṭhatissa had the Āḷambagāmavāpi reservoir constructed.
Thus, performing various meritorious deeds such as the building of palaces,
the king ruled for ten years.
Thus, sovereignty over men arises from many kinds of merit as its cause,
yet it is also caused by much evil;
it is like food mixed with poison that appears sweet.
The mind of a good person never resorts to that [evil].
This concludes the thirteenth chapter on kings in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in good people.
The Thirty-sixth Chapter.
The Thirty-seventh Chapter:
The Five Kings.
Upon the passing away of Jeṭṭhatissa,
his younger brother Mahāsena reigned as king for twenty-seven years.
Regarding that consecration of his reign:
To have it brought from the other side;
that Elder Saṅghamitta,
knowing the time had come, has come here.
Having had his consecration performed and having engaged in various other activities,
that unrestrained man, desiring to bring about the destruction of the Mahāvihāra,
said: "These Mahāvihāravāsins are speakers of what is not the Vinaya."
"O King, we are followers of the Vinaya," saying this, they seized the lord of the earth.
"He who gives food to a monk dwelling in the Mahāvihāra is one who deserves punishment from the virtuous"— thus they caused the king to impose a penalty.
Harassed by them, those monks residing at the Great Monastery abandoned the Mahāvihāra and went to the Malaya and Rohaṇa regions.
Consequently, this Mahāvihāra remained deserted for nine years.
The Mahāvihāravāsī monks had been absent;
[thinking], "This property is ownerless, like the inheritance of one who has no sons," that elder,
having persuaded the king, [dealt with] the fool, the very foolish one.
Having obtained the king’s permission to destroy the Mahāvihāra,
he, with a wicked mind, employed men to carry it out.
A servant of the Elder Saṅghamitta who was a favorite of the king—
The minister Soṇa and Dāruṇa, along with shameless monks,
having broken down the seven-storied,
most excellent Lohapāsāda and various kinds of dwellings, led them from here to Abhayagiri.
By means of many palaces brought from the Mahāvihāra,
this Abhayagirivihāra became possessed of many palaces.
[He established] Saṅghamitta, Pāpamitta, the Elder Soṇa, and the attendant.
Relying upon much evil, that lord of the earth committed [this act].
Having brought a great stone image from Pācinatissapabbata,
the king established it at Abhayagiri.
He had a temple for images, a temple for the Bodhi tree, a delightful hall for the relics, and a four-sided hall built; he was the builder known as Kukkuṭa.
Because of that terrible deed committed by the Elder Saṅghamitta—
At that time, the Abhayagiri Monastery was a sight to behold.
There was a royal counselor named Meghavaṇṇābhaya, who was everywhere influential;
yet, having become angry with his friend, he [destroyed] the great monastery’s dwelling place.
Having offered the oblation and gone to Malaya, he returned with great strength gained;
he established his camp at Duratissakavāpiya.
Hearing that his friend had arrived there, the lord of the earth—
Having gone out to meet him who was ready for battle, he established his camp.
Having obtained excellent food and drink brought from the Malaya region, he thought:
"I will not enjoy this without my companion, the King."
Taking that himself, having gone out alone at night,
he approached the presence of the king and reported the matter.
Having eaten it with confidence along with what was brought by him, [he said:]
"Why have you become a thief to me? the king asked him.
"Because you caused the Great Monastery to be destroyed," he replied.
"I shall cause the monastery to be inhabited; it shall be safe for me after my passing."
The king spoke thus to me, and he asked the king for forgiveness;
being thus persuaded by him, the king returned to the city.
Having thus convinced the king, Meghavaṇṇābhaya—
She did not come with the king because of her need for building materials.
The king’s wife, Valabhā, was the only daughter of a scribe;
she was distressed by the destruction of the Mahāvihāra, which brought ruin upon her.
Enraged, she had the Elder killed after having the carpenter arrested—
the one with a wicked mind who had come to destroy the Thūpārāma.
Having caused the death of the Elder Saṅghamittā, that perpetrator of cruel deeds;
And they had the minister Soṇa executed without due consideration.
Having brought together the necessary materials, he, who was radiant like a cloud,
caused many monastic cells to be built within the Mahāvihāra.
When that [danger] had been stilled, O monks, those who were fearless dwelt in fearlessness there;
having come from here and there, they resided in the Mahāvihāra.
As for the King, he [resided] in the Great Bodhi House in the western direction.
Having had two bronze images cast,
he had them installed for the sake of the fraudulent and crooked-minded monk dwelling at Dakkhiṇārāma,
a wicked friend and unrestrained elder named Tissa, in whom he had placed his confidence.
At the boundary of the Mahāvihāra, in a garden named Joti,
he had the Jetavana Vihāra constructed even while obstructing [the territory].
Thereafter, he requested the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to abolish that boundary.
Unwilling to give it, those monks departed from the monastery.
Here, some monks hid themselves here and there in order to provoke the other monks who were performing the formal act of abolishing the boundary.
For nine months, the Mahāvihāra was thus abandoned by the monks;
other monks thought, "We have effected its complete eradication.
Then, when the undertaking for the formal eradication of the boundary (sīmā-samugghāta) was completed,
The bhikkhus, having come here, resided at the Mahāvihāra.
There was an exhortation by the Elder Tissa, the assigner of that monastery,
concerning the final matter, which was based on the truth in the midst of the Saṅgha.
The Great Minister, having investigated the matter and being thus authorized by the Dhamma,
caused him to be expelled according to the law, even against the king's will.
That very same king then had a monastery built, adorned with jewels and gems.
Having demolished a temple of the gods, he constructed three monasteries:
at Gokaṇṇa, Erakāpilla, and Kalandaka in the Brāhmaṇa village;
as well as the Migagāma monastery and Gaṅgasenaka on the mountain.
In the western direction, King [Mahāsena] caused the Dhātusena mountain, the Mahāvihāra, and Kokavāta to be built;
he also caused the Rūpāramma-vihāra and Cūḷaviṭṭha to be built.
He established two monasteries for the monks at Uttarābhaya and Savhe,
and he had a stupa built at the site of the Kālaveḷaka Yakkha;
furthermore, he renovated many dilapidated monasteries throughout the island.
He gave a thousand pieces worth a thousand [coins] to a thousand senior elders of the Sangha,
as well as a gift for all the elders and robes every year.
There was no limit to his giving of food, drink, and other requisites.
For the sake of abundant food, he constructed sixteen large reservoirs:
the Maṇihīra Great Reservoir, the Jallura, the one named Khāṇu,
the Mahāmaṇi, the Kokavāta, and the Morakaparakavāpika.
Kubbāhaka and Vāhaka, Ratta and Mālakaṇḍaka;
Tissa and Vaḍḍhamānaka, Veḷaṅga and Viṭṭhika.
Mahāgalla, Cīravāpi, and Mahādāragallaka.
And the Kāḷapāsāṇa reservoir—these are the sixteen reservoirs.
He caused the Mahāmātī to be built, which is known as the source of the Gaṅgā.
In this way, he accumulated a great deal of both merit and demerit.
Thus, having performed both good and evil deeds throughout his life through association with the unwholesome,
King Mahāsena departed according to his karma.
Therefore, one should avoid the company of the unwholesome from afar.
Or like a snake, a wise man should quickly cast poison upon one who acts for his own harm.
Thereafter, there was a king named Sirimeghavaṇṇa, his son;
he was like a benefactor to the world, bestowing all forms of prosperity.
When Mahāsena, having fallen under the power of evil,
had caused [the monks] to be driven away, he summoned all the bhikkhus to the Mahāvihāra.
Approaching and paying homage, he sat down respectfully and questioned them.
“By his father, who was a companion of Saṅghamitta, it has been destroyed.
What, what indeed? thus the monks said to that lord of men.
“Although your father strove to effect the abolition of the boundary,” they said.
Because monks were present within the boundary, they were unable [to perform the formal act];
the beings there remained hidden in the hollows of the earth.
Among them were the minister named Soṇa and the more wicked Saṅghamitta.
Having persuaded the king, they caused him to perform demeritorious deeds.
Having demolished the supreme seven-storied Lohapāsāda and various other types of dwellings,
they led [the materials] from here to Abhayagiri.
“On the courtyard of the shrine where four Buddhas had resided for a month, those of poor wisdom caused it to be ploughed. Behold the assembly of fools!
Having heard that account of his father’s deed, he became disillusioned with the company of fools.
He restored everything there that had been destroyed by his father to its original state.
Just as if displaying it upon the surface of the earth,
he built a supreme palace for King Mahāpanāda, like the stairway to the Lohapāsāda.
He had all the cells that had been demolished rebuilt;
he restored the property of the monastery attendants to their proper places.
Because his father, who was lacking in wisdom, had cut off the supplies, [he restored them].
The wise one had a monastery built— a dwelling with open spaces and a dense interior.
When his father had the forest-monastery begun, Joti,
the lord of men, brought all the unfinished work to completion.
Then, having heard from the beginning the entire account concerning Mahinda,
the son of that lord of ascetics, the lord of men— King Tissa—
became filled with serene confidence in his qualities, which radiated such pure faith.
Thinking, "The Elder is indeed the lord of this island," he fashioned a golden image based on his own proportions,
on the seventh day of the waning moon in the month of Pubbakattika.
Having led [them] to the site of the Cetiya-tree known as Theramba,
he put on his robes there at the eighth watch; then, at the ninth,
he took up Mahāsena, who was like an army of gods.
In the city of Orodha itself, even without a house-guardian,
all the bhikkhus throughout the entire island of Laṅkā took [the goods] and,
having dismissed the men stationed as guards within the city, departed.
Having established a great almsgiving for all living beings without exception,
and performing incomparable worship with every kind of offering,
he went out to meet this Teacher of the Island, the Teacher himself.
Having performed honors for his excellent son, as the king of the gods does for the Teacher,
he had the city prepared with great care from Cetiyambathala as far as the city of Sāvatthī,
just as [the road] was from Vesālī to the city of Sāvatthī.
Having bestowed all his wealth there upon the Elder,
that father of the king acted just as he had when the Elder Moggaliputta arrived.
Having given great alms there to the poor, the destitute, and the needy, he—
Having satisfied even the bhikkhus with all four requisites,
and having taken him with great honor amidst the great multitude so that they might see the Elder’s arrival, the one of great renown [departed].
Descending from there, that great being became his personal attendant,
and having surrounded himself on all sides with a retinue of monks,
he fashioned a golden image of the Elder in the midst of the Ocean of Milk.
Enveloped by the dense twilight, he shone like Mount Meru of gold.
Thus did the Leader of the World come to the sleeping city of Vesālī to teach the Dhamma;
and so he showed it to the great multitude.
Thus performing acts of honor and respect, that bull among men personally constructed [a shrine] on the eastern side of the city gate.
Approaching the monastery in the evening, he provided protection for the physicians.
The Son of the Conqueror caused that image to dwell there for three days. Then,
after the city had been beautifully adorned, on the twelfth day,
at the Teacher’s first entry into the city, it was just like [the entry] into Rājagaha.
Having brought forth that image and made the monastery safe,
while a great festival was being held in the city shaped like an ocean,
he led it to the Mahāvihāra and kept it for three months in the courtyard of the Bodhi tree.
Having dressed and entered the city by that same method,
he had a fine residence built for the image near the royal palace, in the southeast corner.
Having had statues of the [Buddha’s] supernormal powers and so forth fashioned,
the confident Great Lord had them installed right there along with the Elder.
He established a guard and provided for their maintenance through offerings.
He enjoined them to perform it in this very manner every year.
Those who protect his command— the king and his ministers here—
preserve that ritual as long as they exist, without destroying it.
Then, having led [the Sangha] from the city to the monastery on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony,
he established an annual practice of making offerings on the thirteenth day.
At the Abhayagiri monastery, at the Bodhi tree of Tissa-vasabha;
He had a stone altar constructed and a beautiful wall built.
In his ninth year, a certain brahmin woman took the tooth relic of the Great Sage from Kalinga and brought it here.
Having taken up with great reverence the description of the lineage of the Tooth Relic as it was told, and having properly composed this supreme work,
I have placed it within a casket called the Visuddhaphalikumbha.
When King Devānaṃpiyatissa had the royal residence built,
the lord of the earth expanded it into the house named Dhammacakka;
from that time forth, that house became known as the Dāṭhādhātughara (the Tooth Relic Temple).
The king, with a mind full of merit, bestowed nine hundred thousand [pieces of gold] and then held a great festival for the Tooth Relic.
Having brought it every year to the Abhayuttara Monastery, he performed the rites.
To perform the ritual of worship for him, he employed my very form.
And out of compassion for living beings, the lord of the earth had eighteen monasteries constructed,
as well as reservoirs and irrigation channels.
Having performed immeasurable merits such as the Bodhi-pūjā, in his twenty-eighth year, he entered the womb; such was his destiny.
Then the prince was the eldest, and this [other] was his younger brother.
The lord of the earth, skilled in the art of tooth-work, leaped over the crowd of people with his parasol.
Having performed various difficult tasks,
he caused many people to sharpen this craft of his.
Commanded by his father, he created, as if by supernatural power,
the Bodhisatta’s own form— a beautiful and captivating appearance—
along with a couch, a throne, a parasol, and a jeweled pavilion.
Having performed various deeds here and there, including one involving Citradanta,
and having governed the island of Laṅkā for nine years and accumulated manifold merits, he passed away according to his karma.
Then his son was Buddhadāsa, a lord of the earth,
a mine of virtues like the ocean of all jewels.
Bringing happiness to the inhabitants of the island through every means, he—
Like a wealthy man in the rainy season guarding his lotus pond,
he was endowed with wisdom and the virtues of merit, an abode of pure compassion,
and likewise fully possessed of the ten qualities of a king.
Having abandoned the four wrong courses and administering justice,
he gathered the people by means of all four bases of sympathy.
Demonstrating to living beings the conduct of Bodhisattvas, he acted as their witness.
Like a father toward his sons, that lord of the earth felt compassion for living beings.
By the gift of wealth to the poor, he fulfilled their virtuous aspirations;
and for those already happy, he ensured the protection of all their enjoyments and their very lives.
Then, by means of kindness he gathered the virtuous, and by means of discipline the wicked;
the Great Lord gathered [the sick] through medical treatment.
Then one day, the King, having mounted the back of a noble elephant—
While traveling on the great highway to bathe in the Tissavāpi reservoir,
he saw a certain great nāga afflicted with a disease of the belly,
lying on a termite mound beside the Vihāra of Puttabhāga.
Then, seeing him lying down with a swelling known as a goitre that revealed his illness within his open belly,
he concluded that he was indeed a sick man. Thereafter,
mounting the great elephant, he approached the vicinity of the Great Naga.
Thus spoke the Great Naga, who dwells among the great nagas:
“The reason for your arrival, O Great Naga, has been understood by me.
Indeed, those of great majesty are prone to sudden anger when provoked.”
"Therefore, having touched that karma, it is not possible for me to do it for you;
nor is it possible for me even without touching it. What, then, is there to be done here?
Thus did the Lord of Serpents speak to his sons regarding his own hood alone.
Having caused him to enter inside his own belly, he lay down there, composed in mind. Then, approaching him,
he took the sword that was in his own lap and cut open the belly of that wealthy man.
Having removed that malady from him and prepared an excellent medicine, he then made that snake happy at that very moment.
Thus did he praise himself: "My great compassion—”
Even the animals understood: "Well done! We have been well-treated by him.
Seeing themselves made happy, the lord of the earth, whose voice was like a peacock's cry, gave his own precious jewel to honor him.
The king had a stone image of the Perfectly Enlightened One made,
and he placed that eye-gem upon it in the Abhayuttara Monastery.
Even a single bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village where grain was abundant, [attained his goal].
Having received dry alms-food, he went about seeking milk-alms.
Having obtained milk containing living creatures, he consumed it in his belly;
when those creatures grew strong, they devoured his stomach.
Then, having approached, he reported this to the king:
"Rāhula has been born, O King! When did you carry him away, and of what sort was he?
He replied: "In the village of Thusavitti, when my food was milk."
"The King realized, 'He has eaten milk containing living beings.
Then, even though the horse was but one, he required treatment by venesection;
the King, having performed the venesection on him, took the blood."
Having made the ascetic drink, he said, "Wait for a moment.
Hearing that it was "the jewel of Assalāyana's heart," the ascetic likewise vomited it out.
Like insects [emerging] with blood, they came forth, and he became well.
The king reported the matter to the bhikkhu, explaining his own condition thus:
“With a single stroke of the surgeon’s blade, the worms have been slain and the ascetic has been struck down;
the medical treatment was performed perfectly, and I am now free from disease.”
For one was drinking water,
not recognizing it as a deḍḍubha-snake;
he swallowed it whole.
"Born from there," thus he became a *deḍḍubha* (water-snake).
But because his snout was seen inside [the mud], he was tormented by that suffering.
The King of Magadha, having questioned him regarding the origin of that [suffering], [learned the truth].
But when the king saw that [snake] with its fangs bared,
he was oppressed by that suffering and went to the king. Having asked the king about its origin,
and having learned that it was a snake, he fasted for seven days.
Then, having bathed and anointed himself, he had him laid upon a well-spread bed.
Having opened his own mouth for sleep, he then lay down beside his face while asleep.
He caused a piece of meat to be placed there, and a cord emerged from it.
Having bitten it with its scent, the snake began to enter inside.
Then, seizing it by the cord, he pulled it out into the water.
