he caused the village named Mahānāma to be granted. Having honored the Lord of the Vaḍḍhamāna Tree according to his ability,
he also had a new dwelling built in place of the old one.
For the sake of that tree, he gave the village of Koṭṭhāgāma, which possessed great wealth;
he bestowed the village named Kāḷussa upon the Nīla monastery.
He also gave a village to the Loharūpa monastery and [another] village to the monastery.
He reflected upon his own old age and commissioned images;
the Greatly Compassionate One built palaces, shrines, and no small number of monasteries,
as well as a medical hall in the city of Puḷatthina.
Likewise, having had the wise, as well as wealth,
villages, and endowments, along with halls for cripples and the blind,
inscribed here and there in books, when the legal case was rightly adjudicated;
Out of fear of reopening old wounds, he had [the edicts] established in Rājagaha;
in the village of Bhogagāma, belonging to the one named Nāgavaḍḍhana, he gave many [gifts],
not obstructing the records of the past, but preserving the ancient tradition.
He constantly and respectfully protected his father’s great gifts and whatever other merit he had performed,
ensuring that none of it was lost.
And the chief queen of the great king caused many meritorious deeds to be done.
The queen had the Kaṇṭaka Cetiya built on Cetiyapabbata;
having caused Jayasena to construct the mountain,
she gave it to the village headman, and she gave the village of Mahummāra to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Having constructed a dwelling for the bhikkhunīs called Silāmegha, she gave female slaves named Silāmegha as well as provisions for the bhikkhunīs.
Previously, villages had been purchased there; that monastery was the means of support.
Having given those and having had them piled up, he caused them to be offered to the monastery itself.
Having covered all the great trees on Cetiyapabbata,
he honored them with banners and flags of various colors.
He renovated the Pubbārāma monastery and the palace;
he had the dilapidated watchtowers restored so that they were well-maintained for him.
He rebuilt the ruined Giribhaṇḍa monastery to its original state.
And he had the village of Bhogagāma bestowed upon the monks residing there.
Having constructed a monastery at Ambuyyāna on Mount Dappuḷa,
he gave it to three hundred monks, complete with the four requisites.
Having had a delightful monastery built with blue-walled galleries,
he caused a water gate with abundant produce to be constructed for it. Furthermore,
he renovated the dilapidated parts of the Ariyāri Monastery.
He had a new assembly hall built at Salākagga,
and he caused Senaggabodhi Mountain to be established on Vāhadīpa;
he had the Dhamma of the three Nikāyas recited by those of great learning.
And he caused knots to be tied on iron vessels for the monks, saying that everything was done as a meritorious act; he did not avoid anything.
He even gave ornaments to women of noble birth who were without protectors.
To those who desired food, he gave much at night.
He provided fodder for the cattle and meals for the crows and other birds;
and for the princes, he provided rice mixed with honey and molasses.
Having thus performed meritorious deeds, that lord of men,
together with his retinue, enjoyed the earth for five years and then relinquished it.
After that, there was a son born to him, the charioteer of the Sihaḷas.
Endowed with every form of virtue, there was a nobleman named Mahinda.
On the surface of the earth, he was like a cloud of righteous conduct,
an island of the Dhamma, a banner of the Dhamma, and one whose ultimate refuge was the pure Dhamma.
He performed everything exactly as it had been done by the lords of men in former times,
following the path of Dhamma, and he avoided all that was contrary to Dhamma.
He began the new construction work on the Royal Jewel Palace.
At all times he caused a water-strainer with a handle to be provided.
He repaired what was worn out and performed meritorious deeds;
having ruled for four years, he passed away.
Then King Aggabodhi raised the royal parasol in the city,
while bringing about the welfare and happiness of all beings without exception.
He performed a relic worship for the Teacher, who is worthy of all virtues.
The lord of men also caused a great festival for the Perfectly Enlightened One,
the Grandfather (Brahmā), and had a monastery cell and a Bodhi tree named after his father and himself erected.
Having constructed a refectory and a courtyard named Bhūta,
he gave them to his own teacher and to three hundred bhikkhus.
He also caused the village of Cūḷavāpiya to be granted for the royal hall.
He caused two villages to be granted to Kāḷūla Mallavātaka.
On Uposatha days, he prohibited the entry of fish,
meat, liquor, and other such items into his own city.
Having paid homage at the cetiya, he departed from there, saying:
"May the sands be destroyed! and thus he washed his feet.
Whatever action is conducive to the welfare of others, whatever action leads to liberation—
Having placed his faith in the Three Refuges, he performed all those deeds.
Delighting in the service of his mother, the king, it is said,
would go to attend upon her every morning, shining throughout the day and night.
Having anointed his head with oil and rubbed away the sweat,
having cleaned his nails and bathed him with due respect,
he clothed him in a new garment that was pleasant to the touch.
Having taken a discarded cloth and having wrapped it around himself,
he sprinkled his own head, which was adorned with a crown, with that water; then,
having properly worshipped that cetiya with perfumes and garlands, he departed.
Having paid homage three times and performed a circumambulation of him,
he had robes and other gifts distributed to that assembly according to their desire.
Then, with his own hands, he personally fed them that most costly meal.
Having eaten the remainder of the meal, he scattered [the food] upon the surface.
Having fed that assembly with the most excellent royal food,
he prepared a dwelling house perfumed with fragrant scents.
Having personally prepared a bed there with great care,
having washed his feet and anointed them smoothly with fragrant oil,
he sat down massaging him until he had fallen asleep.
Having circumambulated the couch three times, keeping it to his right, and having paid respectful homage,
he assigned the task to the guards as well as the slaves and laborers;
then, placing the couch upon his back, he departed from behind it.
Standing where he could not see him, and having bowed three times again,
he returned home still alive, satisfied with that deed and remembering it over and over; even so did he attend upon him.
On one occasion, having addressed him with the word "servant" and prostrated before him as his own servant,
he caused himself to be spoken to by that very person in order to obtain his own forgiveness;
he did so after having had himself given away as a slave to the Saṅgha of monks by his mother.
Knowing that wealth is the most precious thing, the wise man became his own master;
thus, being devoted to merit, he provided for the island.
After eleven years, he departed for the world of the gods.
Then, after his passing, his younger brother Dappula became king.
He practiced the entire conduct of his predecessors;
at that time, there was a son of Mahinda named Arohaṇasāmi.
They went forth, led by their father, to see the king, their maternal uncle.
Upon seeing them and hearing their account, he— being a kinsman devoted to their welfare—
gave them great forces and dispatched them to wage war against their father.
Mahinda, the lord of Rohaṇa, perceiving their state to be thus,
though possessed of great power, did not engage them in battle on that very first day.
Both of them fled, leaving behind the commander of their army.
Returning once more, they lived here serving the protector of the earth;
their father too was satisfied with him, as was his other kinsman.
Fighting, he met his death; it is said that even his own relative died.
Then King Kittaggabodhi gave his daughter named Devī, endowed with every form and virtue, to his nephew,
the king of Dappuḷa, for the sake of service to that monarch.
Taking his own army with him, he went to Rohaṇa;
becoming the lord of Rohaṇa, he was endowed with every excellence.
Increasing his sons and daughters, he made his dwelling right there.
The king had the old house of the Lord of Trees made new and firm;
he commissioned the work to be inlaid with gold for the sake of his own royal status and for the perfection of the Teacher.
Having performed what was most fitting, he carried out a great festival of offerings;
he had the dilapidated palace renovated at Hatthikucchi-vihāra.
He established the Vāhadīpa monastery and the Lāvarāva mountain.
Having fashioned a golden image of the Sage in the monastery named Jetavana and having enlarged the Bodhi-house, he performed inconceivable worship;
year after year, he established the distribution of cloth-gifts throughout the island.
He increased the Great Monastery and oversaw the refectory;
he had weights and measures standardized and renovated what was dilapidated.
He preserved the blameless conduct of former kings.
He had a general named Vajira, a great commander,
who renovated the Kacchavāla monastery for the paṃsukūlinas;
he also carefully roofed the dwelling of the stupa at the Thūpārāma.
He had gates made of gold with bricks of refined gold;
thus did that lord of men exercise sovereignty for sixteen years.
Then he went to the very region where all beings must go.
When that king had passed away, the world of the gods then came into being.
Then the one named Aggabodhi caused the royal drum of command to be sounded for his father’s brother’s son, the one named Mahinda.
For the sake of the kingdom, he did not allow his own sons to set foot first;
he showed due respect even to his younger brothers and their kin.
Unable to endure it, he fled in agitation to the opposite shore.
Having heard of their arrival, he dispatched a great force;
having waged war with them, he took their heads.
Having investigated the various schools, he performed everything that was to be done.
Throughout the entire island, he put a stop to evil conduct;
monks in the small monasteries received rice-gruel at all times.
Hearing of this at the Great Monastery (Mahāvihāra), the king’s mind became filled with disenchantment.
Having dispatched messengers to the great village of Kaṇṭhapiṭṭhi, as well as to Yābālagāma, Telagāma, Bahudañca, and Dakavāra,
he directed the bhikkhus in the monasteries to go and receive rice gruel.
From that time forth, everyone respectfully took that rice-gruel;
and having caused the drum to be beaten throughout the island, they assembled all the supplicants.
For three days, he bestowed gold according to their desires.
Having performed such deeds as these for three years, that meritorious king,
desiring to see for himself the fruit of his faith in the Triple Gem,
passed away as if traveling by a celestial chariot.
Thus, alas, all embodied beings are impermanent;
even the Omniscient One must succumb to death.
Therefore, having abandoned the passion for existence, [one should strive for liberation].
May one possess the splendor of perfect wisdom regarding the Buddha.
This concludes the chapter titled "The Five Kings" in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Forty-Seventh Chapter.
The Forty-Eighth Chapter:
Ekarājaka.
Then his younger brother Sena raised the royal parasol over the city;
like a man of great wealth beholding a beloved son, he looked upon all beings.
He practiced the conduct of former kings exactly as it had been handed down to him.
And he practiced even unprecedented conduct consistent with the Dhamma:
he performed those duties that ought to be done for the monks and nuns, for his kinsmen dwelling on the island,
and for the fish, wild animals, and birds.
Having sent Mahinda to the further shore, he engaged him in battle;
thus he completely purified all his enemies to the throne.
He bestowed great gifts upon beggars seeking wealth.
The food of the king was pleasing to both the bhikkhus and the brahmins.
Among those born after [the Buddha], there were three—Mahinda, Kassapa, and likewise Udaya; of these, Mahinda was the crown prince.
Having sacrificed himself, he followed her and attended upon her with great care;
he was known as Saṅghānāma, the king’s consort, that queen of the monarch.
When the queen had gone to the port for the sake of sporting in the ocean—
At that time, Udaya, having been defeated in the city,
took the daughter of Māṇilānī named Nālā—
who was protected by royal guards— and went to the city of Puḷatthi.
The king, not being angry with him, made an unshakeable alliance;
having sent a great embassy and satisfied him, he brought him here.
From that time forth, those kshatriyas remained thus united.
Protecting the teaching and the world, they dwelt there,
perfectly composed. Then, after some time,
the powerful King Paṇḍu came here from Jambudīpa and began to seize the island.
Having heard this, the king dispatched Mahāsena to his presence;
for the lord of men was stubborn due to the dispute with his ministers.
King Paṇḍu, destroying that entire northern region, [advanced].
He established his headquarters at Mahātālitagāmaka.
The many Damilas dwelling there, wherever they might be, all became his partisans;
consequently, he became powerful.
There, the great army of the invader began to engage the King;
King Paṇḍu also took his place, mounted upon the back of an elephant.
The Damila forces were filled with fear as they beheld the face of their lord.
Possessing great strength and courage, they were ready to sacrifice their lives for that purpose.
But the army of Dīpa, lacking a leader, was dispirited;
having broken ranks, they fought aimlessly and fled in every direction.
At that moment, the great army of King Paṇḍu descended;
like the host of Māra, they went forth, crushing the great multitude.
Seeing the army’s defeat, the king took up everything white.
Having abandoned the city of Hatthasāra, he went toward the Malaya region.
Then the crown prince Mahinda, having mounted his elephant and fighting with his own army, observed that they were fleeing.
"It is truly not possible for me alone to kill them all;
nor is death at the hands of such lowly men a happy one.
Therefore, it is better that I die by my own hand"—having thought thus, he [acted].
While still mounted upon the neck of the elephant, he cut off his own head.
Seeing that, many of his servants there also cut off their heads;
seeing this, the Damila army was delighted, thrilled, and filled with joy.
Having considered all this from beginning to end, Sakka-Sakassapa,
well-armored and bearing great weapons, mounted his excellent steed and,
alone and fearless, approached the monastery.
Having plunged into such a great army, he tore through it;
like a supaṇṇa seizing a serpent from the depths of the water,
he turned back that entire force and well protected himself.
Only a single horse was seen, appearing like a line of steeds;
he saw no person at all following him.
"What is the use of fulfilling the desire of one who is my enemy? he thought.
"Living on in another time, I shall fulfill my heart's desire.
Therefore, it is right for me to go.
Having thus resolved with great strength, the fearless great warrior approached Koṇḍivāta.
King Paṇḍu, with his great army, then seized the city;
they presented that head of the crown prince to King Paṇḍu.
Having seen it and having cremated those kings who had sought the land of Paṇḍu, he [proceeded].
He directed that all the necessary tasks for the cremation be performed.
He had all the valuable timber taken from the king’s treasury,
as well as whatever was to be gathered from the monasteries and the city.
In all the jeweled palaces, there was a golden image of the Teacher;
for the Lord of Sages, a pair of eye-like gems made of stone;
likewise, upon a golden plate at the Cetiya in Thūpārāma.
And golden images here and there in the monasteries—
he took all that was worthless and made it for the island of Laṅkā;
he abandoned the delightful city, its figures devoured by yakkhas.
The King, too, having provided protection here and there along the great highway,
took up residence at the mouth of the two Ganges rivers,
full of apprehension. Then King Paṇḍu, together with the Lord of Siṃhala, sought to act...
The Lord of Sihaḷa dispatched ministers there;
having seen them and heard their message, he accepted it all and,
having shown the messengers hospitality according to their desires, [sent them back].
Having given two elephants and all his ornaments as well,
that messenger sent them to him for his own benefit. King Paṇḍu,
seeing everything white, was delighted in his heart.
Having delivered [the message] to the messengers, he departed from the great city on that very day.
Having left the city and traveled for no long time, he reached the port;
there, having boarded a ship, he arrived at his own country.
Then, having returned to the city, the lord of the earth, Sīlāmegha,
established the island in its proper place and dwelt there in meditative composure.
Having made his second brother, the kṣatriya named Udaya, [his co-ruler],...
He gave that great lamp as an offering to the southern direction for the sake of his welfare.
Yet, before long, having performed merit according to his capacity,
he was afflicted by a single disease and entered the mouth of Death.
Kassapa, though he was the first king, lived in the city of Pulatthi;
having allied himself with King Paṇḍu, it is said that he was eventually put to death.
At that time, there were sons of the one named Kassapa who were very wealthy.
The first-born had four [sons], endowed with the marks of prosperity.
The eldest was the prince named Sena;
he was brave, heroic, of great prowess, capable of bearing the king’s burden, and steadfast.
The king, having bestowed upon him the Mahādīpa grant according to the prescribed rites,
assigned the southern region along with its mounts for his maintenance.
The sons of Kittaggabodhi were the lords of Rohaṇa.
He had four daughters, three of whom were beautiful and charming to behold.
At that time, his eldest son, the kshatriya named Mahinda,
having caused his paternal aunt to be killed, seized the country along with its forces.
His three brothers,
enraged at the slaying of their brother,
took his sister Tissa with them.
They came into the presence of the king.
Seeing them, the compassionate king, regarding them as his own children,
increased their happiness with affection, just like all the young gods.
Then the Lord of Men gave that country to the eldest of them,
named Kassapa, saying, "Take this land and go," and having granted it,
he dispatched an army. He too, having gone and slain him, took the entirety of Rohaṇa.
Having brought that place under his control, he lived there free from distress.
Then, having summoned both his brothers as well as Sena and Udaya,
and having divided the territory among them, he lived together with them.
The king, having raised them well, when those three royal maidens had reached maturity—
fortunate, like celestial nymphs in beauty— he appointed one to the position of queen and bestowed another upon the viceroy.
Having bestowed upon the Sangha a great wealth comparable to a kingdom,
there was a younger brother of the king named Mahinda,
endowed with every virtue and proficient in all the scriptures.
The king gave him two royal daughters,
Manoharā and Tissavhākittī by name, and bestowed upon them wealth according to their desire.
Acting in this way, he provided for his kinsmen with appropriate hospitality.
And winning over the great multitude through the social services of giving and the rest,
the king, endowed with righteous qualities,
showed his authority over other rulers; performing meritorious deeds, he enjoyed the earth.
Having constructed for the paṃsukūla-dwelling bhikkhus on Mount Ariṭṭha a great dwelling-place and a monastery,
as if created by supernatural power (iddhi),
the king provided them with every requisite worthy of royalty without exception.
The lord of the earth, whose heart was set upon the stage of Buddhahood,
caused a palace to be built for himself as well as many monasteries in the monastery named Jeta,
employing numerous park-keepers, slaves, and laborers, and constructing it with many stories.
Having expanded that place and having had a Jina made entirely of gold,
he established it with great wealth and caused the bhikkhus to dwell there.
In the Mahādi pariveṇa, he constructed a most beautiful dwelling.
In that very monastery, he had a palace built with a courtyard and pillars;
having created a grove of heroic sprouts in the Abhayuttara Monastery,
he caused it to be given to the Mahāsaṅghika monks and the Theriyas.
The lord of the earth also had the Pubbārāma constructed, complete with the four requisites,
together with the queen named Saṅghā and for himself as well;
he had it built right there at the Mahāvihāra.
Having constructed a monastery named Saṅghasena, which was of great wealth and grandeur,
and having fashioned a hair-relic casket entirely of gold,
that supreme man performed a great festival of worship and relinquished his sovereignty.
Gīrissādā gave the Kāṇavāpi reservoir with great generosity,
and he also caused the triple-robe to be bestowed upon the monks dwelling on the island.
In the city of Pulatthipura, he constructed reservoirs at Thusavāpi.
He established the Senaggabodhi monastery, which was closely associated with the village monastery.
And in that very place, he constructed the Mahāpāḷi and the Subhojana;
as well as the Mahāpāḷi for all [the monks] and the Mahānetta on the mountain.
He also had the Vejjasāla hall constructed at the western edge of the city,
where he provided a gift of rice gruel with solid food for the destitute. Furthermore,
he established a separate kitchen for each of the monks who wore rag-robes.
Having done so, the supreme one caused excellent food to be regularly provided with great care.
Having become Mahādipāda, he had [monasteries] built in Kappūra Pariveṇaka and in the district named Uttarāḷha.
And that great treasurer, three times, performed the tulābhāra offering;
the king also performed various other kinds of meritorious deeds.
That queen, named Saṅghā, [performed them] at the northern monastery.
Having established his residence at the place called Mahindasena, he caused the bhikkhus to dwell there.
During the reign of the wise King Dappula,
that delightful Mount Dappula was presided over by Mahādeva.
One named Dāruka-ssapa, and likewise Kassapa-rājika—
both of them having failed, the king brought them under his power.
His general was Bhadda, known by the name Bhaddasena.
He also had a courtyard built, provided with servants and wealth.
And the minister Uttara constructed in the Abhayuttara monastery a dwelling called Uttarasena,
delightful and well-supplied with requisites.
In that very place, he lived for twenty years in the city named Vajira, which was called Vajirasenaka;
and he lived for twenty years in the city named Pulatthi, which was called Rakkhasa.
Then, for twenty years, he resided in the city of Pulatthi.
Remembering the deed committed by King Paṇḍu, Saradassana,
like one giving way to Sena and granting an opportunity to the hero,
abandoned his island like an island struck by a great wind and departed.
Enjoyments, along with life itself, are impermanent;
how much more so those kinsmen and companions?
O ruler of men, behold that one alone.
The most terrible mouth of Death has arrived.
This concludes the chapter titled "Ekarājaka" in the *Mahāvaṃsa*, composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Forty-Eighth Chapter. The Forty-Ninth Chapter:
The Exposition of the Two Kings.
Thus, when he had passed away, his son Senavha, taking a great army and vehicles from Mahādīpa and other places,
arrived at the city and became king upon the earth.
O dear one, showing the conduct of kings in the first aeon:
he was faithful, possessed of great wealth, heroic, free in his generosity, and without attachment; devoted to giving when asked, of vast fortune, and endowed with a powerful army and transport.
By means of his stainless fame and likewise by the quality of his splendor,
he displayed a conjunction as it were of the moon and the sun.
He was strewn with unblemished virtues, and his qualities and non-qualities were well-discerned.
Having transcended evil, weary of the cycle of existence, and seeing the essence,
he had his wife— who was his queen— consecrated as a nun;
having granted her the status of a great lady, he provided her with maintenance as was fitting.
Having given the southern portion [of the kingdom] to his own younger brother named Mahinda, who was possessed of wisdom,
he consecrated him as the viceroy. After he had been installed as viceroy in the inner palace,
he was confirmed in that position by the king.
Having risen with his wife and son, he went incognito to the Malaya region.
At that time, a son was born to the king’s consort for the sake of the Saṅgha;
indeed, even as he appeared, the prince displayed his own form.
Seeing him as if he were newly born, the human being was deeply satisfied,
just as King Suddhodana was upon seeing Siddhattha born in Lumbini.
Endowed with the virtues of merit and prosperity, he stood alone like a solitary island.
I have heard that even in Jambudīpa, he was considered worthy of being anointed as king over the entire realm.
On the very day his name was given, through a complete renunciation,
he had him consecrated as viceroy and gave him the southern region.
The Crown Prince also, while residing in Malaya,
having propitiated the Lord of the Earth through skillful means, was granted permission by his brother.
He then arrived together with the monks who were like lions to the three Pitakas.
Seeing the king right there, he formed an unshakeable alliance with him.
The wife of that crown prince was named Rājinī;
she gave birth to a daughter named Saṅghā.
And his other wife, named Kittī, likewise gave birth to four sons and one daughter.
Then the king, having reflected, thought: "If this is so, [he is] the youngest."
"Being free from suspicion toward me," he said,
"after consulting with his wise counselors, the wise king had his daughter—
beautiful in form and named Rūpā— married to Kassapa, the son of Atta."
He caused the southern region to be given to his youngest brother, the prince;
he even gave each of his own feet as a portion of wealth.
He caused the entire kingdom to be given for his enjoyment alone.
But he alone reflected, a lamp bringing benefit to the world.
Following from their cohabitation, those two who had performed meritorious deeds,
sons and daughters were born, endowed with wealth, merit, and virtue.
Having performed a great festival for the tooth-relic with every kind of offering,
the lord of the earth ascended the excellent palace named Ratana.
At that time, he also [honored] the golden image of the Perfectly Enlightened One which had stood there previously.
Seeing the empty back seat for himself, he asked, "Why is it so?
Then the ministers said, "O Lord of the Earth,
you do not know that during the time of your great uncle Narinda, you were the ruler of men."
King Paṇḍu came here and, having destroyed this island,
departed taking away all the heartwood that was on the island.
Hearing that, the king was ashamed, as if he himself had been defeated.
On that very day, he appointed his ministers to the command of the army.
At that same time, it is said, the young prince Paṇḍu arrived;
though despised by the king, he had resolved to seize the kingdom for himself.
Having seen this, the king was satisfied and performed what was to be done for him.
Having arrived at Mahātittha, he proceeded to the port without fear,
along with a great army and the necessary provisions for it.
Having prepared his army like a divine host arrayed for battle,
the general went together with Prince Paṇḍu and,
having slain King Paṇḍu, returned from there to his own city.
"Taking all the treasures and giving this kingdom to him,
you shall return before long"— thus the one of great renown dismissed him.
And he, having promised the lord of the earth, "I shall do so," [departed].
Having found his strength and taken it up, he mounted that [vehicle] at that very moment.
Then, having gone to the opposite shore with his powerful army fully assembled,
destroying the borderlands, he besieged the city of Madhura.
Having closed the gates, he cut off all coming and going;
then he caused fire to be hurled upon the gate-towers, the watchtowers, and the city walls.
Thus did the Siṃhala army enter their own city.
While she was plundering everything and slaughtering the divisions of the army,
King Paṇḍu, having assembled his own forces,
approached her with speed and began to wage war against her.
Because his strength was not yet complete, that king,
pierced by the arrow while still mounted on the neck of his elephant, fled, leaving his own city behind.
Having escaped, he sought to save his life at the place where he went.
Because of that, his wife met her death.
Then the Sinhalese army, entering the city without fear,
plundered everything there, just as the gods plundered the city of Asura.
Then the general, having observed the food in the royal palace—
both that brought from this island and the highly precious items located there—
took all the essence situated in both the country and the city.
Having exercised sovereignty there according to his own will,
King Paṇḍu anointed the prince as king over that realm;
having granted him exemptions and privileges, he handed over the country to him.
Having taken elephants, horses, and men according to his pleasure,
dwelling here and there as he desires, he is free from fear.
Having reached the shore of the ocean, he stands there at his ease.
As if playing, that confident one boarded the ship;
having arrived at Mahātittha and paid homage to the Lord of the Earth,
he announced his mission and presented the essence of what he had brought.
The king, having said "Well done," and having bestowed favor upon him,
returned with his army to his own city after it had been well-prepared.
Having drunk the drink of victory and performed the auspicious rites of triumph, he [re-entered].
Having issued a great proclamation, he restored everything to its original state according to the wishes of the supplicants;
being without attachment even to the essence of the island,
he had the golden images reinstalled in their respective places.
He filled the empty jeweled palace of the Teacher with plaster;
by means of protective coverings, he made the surface of the earth free from fear.
From that time forth, the Island-Lord was invincible to his enemies.
Having done so, he increased his wealth until it surpassed even that of Uttarakuru, dear to him.
At that time, the living beings on the island who had been distressed by the former king were extinguished upon encountering him, like clouds in the heat.
In his twentieth year, at the monastery Abhayuttara,
the Paṃsukūlika bhikkhus departed and went forth.
That Mahinda was the crown prince of the Teacher Dhumarāja.
He had a beautiful house built, one that was lovely to behold and delightful.
While he was having that Bodhi-tree house constructed,
the carpenters saw a branch of the noble Bodhi tree being broken as they struck it with a bamboo pole.
But they informed the crown prince, "This is what must be done here.
He approached each of them in turn and honored them with great worship, [saying]:
"If the Teacher has appeared for the welfare of all living beings,"
"Having obtained this priceless merit for the building of a house here,
just as one is able to construct a house by climbing up the branches, so too,
having propitiated [the Buddha] and paid homage, he went to the Saṅgha."
Then, at night, a branch of the lord of trees rose upward;
thereupon all the laborers reported it to their master.
Having informed his father, the king, he was satisfied, thinking, "It is a crown prince."
He performed the Great Worship, distributing vast amounts of wealth.
Likewise, having caused a monastery cell to be built for one named Mahindasena, he gave it to the Saṅgha along with its appurtenances; thus did he perform merit upon merit.
He gave a meal for himself and his retinue, as well as robes, a parasol, and sandals;
likewise, he provided meals for travelers and baths with their accompanying food.
Having thus performed these various meritorious deeds, great and small, that illustrious man—
In the thirty-third year of his reign, he departed according to his karma.
Then, upon that [brother's] death, the king installed his own younger brother,
Udaya, in his place and gave everything to him alone.
By the gift of a tulābhāra, he satisfied the poor and the helpless;
by his righteous deeds, he unified the three Nikāyas into one. Having filled ten thousand golden bowls with pearls, he—
Setting aside one jewel each, most precious,
he fed a thousand brahmins from pure jeweled vessels with milk-rice porridge,
and caused golden threads to be given as gifts.
Likewise, having clothed them in new garments according to their desire,
the meritorious one gratified them with great hospitality.
And he gave the triple robe to the bhikkhus dwelling on the island.
He gave beautiful garments to all the women.
Having constructed the Loha-pāsāda, which was like the Vejayanta palace,
he had a statue made there with a pedestal fashioned from gold.
Having heard that all the chief queens were making it an Uposatha hall,
he made it his residence for the Saṅgha so that it would not remain empty;
and he gave the village of Bhoga to it and appointed guards.
He assigned thirty-two bhikkhus to reside there,
establishing the boundary of the Ganges with a jeweled girdle and creating an outlet for the waters through a reservoir of gems and diamonds.
He built the city of Kaṭṭhantara and constructed the Kāṇavāpī reservoir;
he also established the Vejjasāla monastery on Cetiyagiri.
Furthermore, he founded the Buddhagāma monastery and the Mahiyaṅgaṇa monastery.
He did not expand the Kūṭatissa Vihāra at Bhogagāma; instead,
he gave the village of Maṇḍalagiri to the monastery and had a palace and a cloister built at Uttarāḷha.
Having given a village as a protection for the Buddha Mahāsena,
she had a maṇimekhala palace built for the Bodhisatta at the Sobhava monastery, and she constructed a shrine for images.
She also raised up a palace for the Bodhisatta.
Out of devotion to the Lord of Munis, she had a house built even for one who was like an old dwelling. O King, you provided that Bodhisatta with a residence there;
having perfumed a water-basin for the Lord of Trees, she held a great festival.
Having had it written upon a golden plate with threads of every kind of jewel,
he performed a great offering for it and had the Abhidhamma recited.
Having brought a statue of Ānanda and circumambulated it keeping it to his right, he placed it at the front.
Having had the protective chant (paritta) recited by the community of monks according to the prescribed rite,
and having rendered the people free from affliction by sprinkling them with protective water,
the king thus drove the fear of disease out from his own country.
Having received the consecration at the Hemavāluka Cetiya,
he caused that conduct to be inscribed in order to perform it annually;
he gave [it] on the four Uposatha days of the month.
He gave four thousand garments along with food,
and he took part in the Vesākha festival together with the poor;
having given them food, drink, and clothing according to their desire.
On the island of Dīpa, he established a perpetual endowment for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
and with that gift, he satisfied the poor, the destitute, and the wayfarers.
And the chief queen of that king, named Saṅghā, likewise caused [an endowment] to be made.
To the mountain named Saṅghasena, which was endowed with all enjoyments and supreme security,
and to the Great Sage made of stone, who wore a blue crest-jewel,
he constantly performed worship for the Teacher with every kind of offering.
His commander-in-chief was named Sena;
his pariveṇa was called Mahābhoga; and his hero was known by the name Tuṭṭhaka.
Thus, having performed meritorious deeds together with his retinue, he became one of great renown.
In his thirty-fifth year, he passed away to the world of the gods.
After him, there was a kshatriya named Udaya,
a king who, through every means, sought the welfare of the island's inhabitants.
Having himself become king, he installed his younger brother,
named Kassapa, at the site of Mahādīpa. The king,
reflecting that he must provide for his kinsmen, [acted accordingly].
In this way, he gave his daughter— the daughter of his brother’s son named Kassapa—
to that crown prince as his wife, Senā by name;
and the king himself took another, named Tissa.
To King Mahinda Supārāja and Queen Kittī,
there was a son named Kittaggabodhi, who possessed the first step toward awakening.
Having become a thief, he escaped from the great king during the night.
One [of them], assuming a disguise, arrived at Rohaṇa.
Having brought the people into his power and having destroyed the entire country,
he had his own maternal uncle killed while he was staying there.
Having heard that, Dharaṇīpāla became exceedingly agitated;
seeking various means to bring him back,
he summoned his nephew Sakasakapa as the crown prince.
"O one of great merit," he addressed him, "be my companion.
"What should I do for you? the lord of the earth replied.
"That son of yours, Mahinda, has reached maturity and is possessed of great strength."
Born of noble lineage on both his mother’s and father’s side,
he was a hero, all-conquering and valiant, skilled and well-trained.
Wise, fit for battle, subtle, and expert in strategy.
"Having sent him, we shall lead away that wicked murderer of his maternal uncle.
Having heard these words of the king, Kassapa spoke with respect:
"O Lord, I have been addressed by Your Majesty; however, I must go only if my son accompanies me."
"The lineage has been preserved by me, and you have inspired confidence in me, O Lord;
therefore, having waited for the proper time, do as you wish.
Having heard those words of his, the lord of men was exceedingly pleased.
Having fully prepared a vast army and having appointed the prince Mahinda along with the leader Vajiragga to protect him with great honor, he set them forth.
Having made the city appear as if empty,
and having given away his entire army, vehicles, and all provisions without exception,
the lord of men himself followed after him on foot.
"Go to the earth, O tree," he commanded, O one of great merit.
That Mahinda, like Indra himself, preceded by a host of deities,
shone brilliantly as he went toward the great battle between the gods and the asuras.
Then, after traveling not long thereafter, he arrived at Gutta’s mango grove.
Thereupon all the provincial officials and the district governors,
distressed by that evil murder of their maternal uncle, approached him.
Having gone there, they surrounded him, thinking, "Our master has been found!
Even as he was falling, that thief remained standing upon the mountain ridge,
having secured all the king's highly valuable property in his hands.
Taking elephants and horses, they went and ascended Mount Malaya;
there Mahindasena slaughtered his army here and there.
Following right upon the tracks of that horse, they proceeded with their elephants and horses.
Having seen it at the foot of the Malaya mountain, he took hold of it there.
Thereupon I entered the entire Malaya forest,
where rivers and even the marshes made paths as if they were level.
Seeing the people and all his own wealth,
Bālaka, overcome by anger, cast them away in rivers, ravines, on riverbanks,
and so forth. He remained all alone, hidden in a forest cave in the mountains.
A person searching for him, having seen that lowest of men, seized him.
Delighted, thinking "I have found him," that person came straightway and pointed out Mahinda as he sat in the Gutta-sālaka grove.
"Having seen him and laughed, why did Rohaṇa eat?"— having thus addressed the Leader,
he offered [the food] to him.
King Vajiragga,
having personally taken his army with him, arrived at Mahāgāma;
acting as the lord of Rohaṇa, he provided for the welfare of the world.
Having restored the people to their natural state and having placed the Teaching back in its proper place, he caused it to be removed by that [foolish one].
Having established flower-groves and fruit-groves here and there, [he departed].
Having taken up the irrigation ponds and having had them connected to the great river,
he made the four requisites easily available everywhere for the Saṅgha;
and having warded off wicked people, both local officials and provincial rulers.
Having purified his inner core and cleared away all thorns,
he delights the entire world, endowed with the enjoyment of generosity.
He is to be approached by the wise and sought after by those seeking wealth.
Like a wish-fulfilling tree, he brought benefit to all supplicants.
Having abandoned the difficult-to-tame regions established by those of old,
he practiced the Dharma and made his dwelling right there.
Taking hold of the first foot, the leader Vajiragga approached Anurādha and pointed him out to the king.
Having seen him, the king was enraged and quickly cast him into prison.
He provided protection and defense, and he eliminated all forms of harassment.
That man of great renown gave three times the weight of a balance as an offering;
at the Thūpārāma, he covered the stupa with a band of gold.
Having constructed a palace right there and settled the community of monks,
he renovated what was dilapidated in both the monastery and the city.
At the Kadamba River, he built a cascade with firm foundations.
He caused the embankment of his irrigation pond to increase, saying, "This is mine.
Therein, the lord of the earth provided an outlet every year;
and for the sake of robes, he had fine and very soft garments given away.
During a famine, having constructed alms-halls for all living beings,
he distributed a great gift and increased the Great Commentary.
He also caused curd-rice to be given to those dwelling in the three Nikāyas.
Having performed such meritorious deeds conducive to heaven as constantly providing food for the destitute, as well as rice-gruel and snacks,
he attained companionship with the gods within eleven years.
In those eleven years, however, he gave away only gold;
it amounted to three hundred and ten thousand [pieces].
O King, the most difficult to conquer, the wise lord of men!
Even after bringing Mekapara, Rohana,
Muggadugga, and others under their control, these lords of men themselves fell into the power of death.
The forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Two Kings," in the *Mahāvaṃsa*,
composed for the purpose of inspiring faith and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Fiftieth Chapter:
The Two Kings.
Then, having been established in his kingdom, Kassapa [ruled] the southern region.
He bestowed the supreme consecration upon his wise crown prince named Kassapa;
he likewise caused the supreme consecration to be given for his daughter,
the royal maiden Tissā, as if she were his own wife.
To beggars and artisans who came from here and there,
the king always caused alms to be given under the name "Daṇḍissara.
That Mahinda was the first king.
Then, during the spring season for growth,
he arrived with an army to seize the kingdom of the two kings.
Hearing this, the king became enraged and dispatched his own army;
that great warrior Mahinda defeated them in battle.
Thereupon, the king sent his father to bring him back.
Having gone to his son, the crown prince Kassapa,
and having spoken many reasoned discourses on various doctrines in manifold ways,
he turned his son back from the fear of the Saṅgha and returned once more.
But he, having previously been the first-born, later saw the ruler of the circle executed and the countryside enraged;
seeing this, he went to the presence of the king.
The community of monks brought him there and presented him to the lord of the earth.
Having given his daughter to her, he sent her back again to Rohaṇa.
Having expelled those of immoral conduct from among the residents of the three Nikāyas,
he established new monks in various monasteries throughout that region.
With his first son, Sunu, born of the double consecration (dvayābhiṣeka),
he increased the amount of earth at the Bodhi tree in the Mahāvihāra as an act of worship.
Furthermore, he had stone images made within the three Nikāyas.
Having fashioned a golden net of rays, as well as a parasol and a crest-jewel,
and having constructed a palace there in the Abhayagiri Monastery named after himself and resided within it,
the monk caused the village to be granted.
At the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Monastery, he gave a village to the Cetiya;
he caused provisions, images, and alms-food to be given to all the bhikkhus.
Then, he granted safety from fear to all beings, both on land and in water.
He always protected the conduct of the former kings.
His general, Sena, born of the royal lineage of Ilanaga,
built a dwelling for the Theriyas behind the Thūpārāma.
He caused the Dhammārāma monastery to be built for the monks who delight in the Dhamma,
and likewise the one named Kassapasena for those from Sāgalika.
Having established the monastery called Hadayunuha on Cetiyapabbata, he—
The commander-in-chief had a pariveṇa built for the monks who delighted in the non-Dhamma, and in various monasteries,
he had individual huts constructed and granted to the resident monks.
In the Rattamāla mountain, having constructed a delightful and beautiful retreat,
he gave it as a dwelling for the teachers of the Dispensation who were devoted to asceticism.
Having built the Mahāvihāra, he bestowed upon them excellent seclusion.
Having caused dwellings named after the ocean and mountains to be built for the paṃsukūla monks in the forest,
he gave them to the monks residing in the grove at the Mahāvihāra, naming them after his own lineage.
When the monasteries were dilapidated, he had new construction work carried out;
he provided bolts for all the monks when their robes became worn.
Having established the Tissa Monastery as a residence for the bhikkhunīs, he made it their dwelling place.
He established the Maricavaṭṭi Great Bodhi tree in its protected enclosure.
Furthermore, in both Anurādhapura and Pulatthipura,
he caused a medical hall to be built for the eradication of epidemics and diseases.
He caused the impression made by himself to be bestowed upon the village of Bhoga,
as well as upon the village of Ārāmika, and he provided ornaments for the images.
He had medicinal halls constructed here and there throughout that city.
He caused food and clothing to be given to the monks who wear rag-robes.
He set free many animals that had been gathered into heaps,
and the army commander gave a great almsgiving to the poor.
Having prepared various kinds of curry, rice, gruel, and diverse hard foods,
and having fashioned the form of a pig, he caused sugar-candy to be given to the monks.
Having performed such meritorious deeds, the leader of the army—
With the rays of his moon-like feet, he illuminated all directions.
His kinsman, the leader named Rakkhasa,
built a most beautiful monastery in the village of Savāraka.
To the monks who were residents of the Mahāvihāra and followers of the essential practice,
he gave that which is excellent, setting aside only the supreme observance.
There was a great inscription named Sena on the Mahālekhaka mountain.
The king named Coḷa had the supreme dwelling place for the bhikkhus constructed at Mahāvihāra;
and the minister of that king built a pariveṇa,
which was well-established and never lost.
The king, having caused the construction of three types of monasteries—
charming with their architectural work— and having built variegated pavilions and victory towers,
performed offerings to the relics that captivated the hearts of the people.
Having gone according to his karma and remained there for seventeen years,
Kassapa was then born as the heir-apparent (yuvarāja) through the two consecrations;
he received the full royal consecration when the sovereignty of Laṅkā came into his sole possession.
Like one who has traveled the path with faith, like one possessed of wisdom and supernormal powers,
he is a speaker as if dying, generous like a giver of wealth.
He is learned, a preacher of the Dhamma, and confident in all skills.
Skilled in investigating what is appropriate and inappropriate, subtle and expert in method,
he stood firm in the teaching of the Sugata like the immovable Indra,
unshakable by any winds of opposing doctrines.
Free from deceit, hypocrisy, pride, and other such evils,
he was a mine of virtues and an ocean for all jewels.
That lord of men, the moon of the earth, [acted] toward his own lineage-born [son].
He bestowed the position of crown prince upon Dappula II.
Governing by means of the ten royal virtues and the four bases of sympathy,
he protected the world as if it were his own eye.
Thus, having upheld the entire teaching of the Teacher through formal acts of the Saṅgha (dhammakamma),
he took nine novice monks and completed the filling of the monastery site.
The Maricavaṭṭika [stūpa] was built by King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī.
Having had a ruined monastery restored and adorned with various dwellings,
he held a great festival and gave it to the monks born of the Elder lineage;
furthermore, he granted them five hundred villages of revenue.
There, in the delightful Tusita heaven, he beheld Maitreya,
the Lord of the World, honored by the assembly of gods, as he was teaching the supreme Dhamma—
appearing as if revealing it to the world from within a monastery fully prepared for his stay.
Seated in a delightful pavilion adorned with various jewels,
surrounded by all the kings and the monks,
the Lord of Laṅkā expounded the Abhidhamma with the playful grace of a Buddha.
Having then had the Abhidhamma Piṭaka inscribed upon golden plates,
and having fashioned a manuscript of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī adorned with various jewels,
he caused a magnificent golden pavilion to be erected in the center of the city.
Having established him there, he granted him an allowance.
Having given the office of General to his own son,
he appointed him to that position and directed him to look after the Dhamma-book there.
Every year, the king, having prepared his city like a city of the gods and surrounded by a decorated army,
shone like the King of the Gods, adorned with all manner of ornaments.
Seated upon the elephant-back, he proceeded through the city streets with great ceremony.
Having led him to that delightful Dhamma-saṅgaha monastery which he himself had built and fully prepared, [he entered].
There, having enshrined [the relics] upon a relic-stand within a delightful pavilion adorned with various jewels, he made offerings.
He constructed the Gaṇṭhākarapariveṇa in Mahāmeghavana.
He had the Vajjasālā built in the city and had it granted to them in their village.
Having constructed the Bhaṇḍika Pariveṇa and the Silāmegha mountain at Abhayagiri,
he had that village granted to them as well.
In the Jotivana Monastery, the King, the leader of Laṅkā,
granted a village for the distribution of alms-food, as he did likewise at Abhayagiri.
He also caused a monastery named Dakkhiṇagiri to be given.
Out of gratitude for what had been done for him, the most righteous King Sakkasenāpati,
having beautifully constructed a delightful pariveṇa together with its surrounding villages,
gave it to the therīs under their own name.
His wife Vajirā had them build for those very [monks] a pariveṇa named after her own village,
and she herself constructed a dwelling marked with her footprint.
She gave [the monastery] to the bhikkhunīs, who are honored everywhere in the lineage of the Elders (Theravamsa).
Sakkasenāpati’s mother built a dwelling for the forest-dwelling bhikkhus—
those who are lamps of the Elder lineage— and she named it after herself.
She herself, at the Maricavaṭṭi shrine, offered to the Teacher’s image a crest-jewel,
water for his feet, an umbrella, and a robe. The king,
right there in his royal palace, [established] a royal lineage bearing his own name.
The joyful Haraṇā built a palace named Pāḷika.
Another queen, named Rājinī, the consort of the king,
honored the Cetiya with an offering of a silk garment and a golden necklace.
His son was Siddhattha by name, established in sovereignty;
he was known as the King of Malaya, with a form like Makaraddhaja.
When that king had passed away, he built a *sāla* monastery for the supreme monks.
Having established the cycle of almsgiving, he then bestowed the merit thereof.
While the kingdom on the island of Laṅkā was thus being governed according to the Dhamma, King Paṇḍu,
having engaged in battle with the King of Coḷa, was defeated.
Having consulted with his ministers, that king, the lord Alaṃkissa, dispatched many gifts for the sake of military force;
having mobilized his army, he sent his own general, Sakka.
Making Bālāsa his leader, he approached the great camp.
Standing on the shore of the sea and proclaiming the victory of the former kings,
he inspired the troops with zeal and had them embark upon the ship.
Having assembled his army and then the general Sakkasena,
he crossed the ocean with ease and arrived at the region of Paṇḍu.
Upon seeing that army, King Paṇḍu was filled with joy.
"I shall establish a single umbrella over Jambudīpa," he declared.
Having gathered a two-fold force, that king,
born of the Coḷa lineage, being unable to conquer, abandoned the battle and departed.
To those who had gone forth with the thought, "I shall fight," the general Sakkha,
though seated and protected by a [magical] charm, died from that evil disease,
as did the wise Laṅkissara along with his army. By that same illness, many others perished.
Having heard this, out of compassion, he then commanded his army.
He then gave the position of commander-in-chief to that son;
having made his son the leader of the army, he caused him to prosper.
At that time, having had a protective charm (paritta) performed in the city by those residing in the three Nikāyas,
he destroyed the fear of disease and adverse weather for the people.
Having established peace for the Dispensation and for the world in many ways, [he passed away].
In his tenth year, that king departed happily for the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Having remained in the sovereignty of Laṅkā, he was a lamp of all sciences who had mastered the Three Piṭakas;
a poet who spoke with eloquence, pure in mindfulness and wisdom, he was both a teacher and a practitioner.

Or may this entire world also come to possess stainless virtues, like this Lord of Kings, Kassapa, who was devoted to the welfare of others and was a knower of the Vedas and the words of the world, endowed with faith, wisdom, and other such qualities. — In the *Mahāvaṃsa*,
composed for the purpose of inspiring confidence and spiritual urgency in virtuous people.
The Fiftieth Chapter, named "Dvirājaka.
The Fifty-first Chapter.
At that time, having been the crown prince named Pañcarājaka, King Dappuḷa appointed one bearing his own name to the position of viceroy.
Having given a village to the Maricavaṭṭi Monastery before that time,
and having protected this earth while maintaining the conduct of former kings,
he indeed did not enjoy [the land] for a long time due to his own past karma.
In the seventh month, that king entered the mouth of death.
The Upārāja and the Ahurājā, followed by Dappula,
bestowed the position of crown prince upon Udaya, the son of Ādipāda.
Then, out of fear of the Coḷas, King Paṇḍu abandoned his own kingdom,
boarded a ship, and arrived at Mahātittha.
Having given orders there, the king, seeing that [the place] was peaceful, became joyful in mind.
He gave him great wealth and formerly provided him with dwellings outside [the city].
Having fought with the King of Coḷa and captured two ports, he said,
"I give them to the King of Paṇḍu," while the King of Laṅkā was clad in armor.
On account of some business, the Kṣatriyas dwelling on the island engaged in a terrible conflict due to a wicked deed committed by Paṇḍu.
Thinking, "There is no work for me here because of my residence with King Paṇḍu," [he departed].
Setting aside his crown and other regalia, he went into the presence of Keraḷa.
When the dispute had been settled, the king then gave a village near the city to the Mahābodhi temple in the Mahāmegha forest.
The protector of that residence was named Senāpati;
near the Thūpārāma, he built a royal palace called Iḷaṅga.
That had been constructed by previous kings, and this king maintained it.
Having reached his twelfth year, he passed away according to his karma.
Udaya became the crown prince, the lord of those dwelling in Laṅkā;
he consecrated Sena and others as subordinate kings.
Terrified of the king, the ministers then entered the forest of asceticism;
but the king and his viceroy, having gone there, had their heads cut off.
Disgusted by that deed, the ascetics dwelling there [departed].
Having abandoned the king’s realm, they then went to Rohaṇa.
At that time, both the country folk and the city-dwellers, along with the armies,
were agitated by the fierce wind like the ocean tossed by a storm.
Having ascended the Jewel Palace in the Abhayuttara monastery,
and having terrified the king by showing him a terrifying vision,
[he went] to the Tapovana grove for a debate with the supporting ministers.
Then, having cut off their heads, they cast them down through the air.
Hearing that, the Crown Prince and his friend Ādipāda leaped over the wall and quickly went to Rohaṇa.
Because they were pursued by the army of Bālaka as far as the banks of the Kaṇha River,
and because they had no boats, they crossed over them and arrived there.
The princes, who had entered the forest seeking safety, came to that place.
Lying on their chests before those ascetics,
with their clothes still wet and their hair disheveled, they lamented in many ways;
having cried out and wept, they asked the practitioners of austerity for forgiveness.
Through the power of their forbearance and loving-kindness toward those Lords of the Teaching,
there arose for both of them— those Lords of the Island—
an emergence of merit. So too did the force of the crown prince and the members of the three Nikāyas [arise].
When those two great powers had become peaceful,
the two capable and wise princes, clad in rag-robes,
went to bring them back. Having requested [the items] from them and taken them, they returned to their own city.
The king came along the path in front of the bhikkhus and asked for their forgiveness;
taking them with him, he led them to the royal palace and departed.
From that time forth, he maintained the conduct of his predecessor.
In his third year, that king passed away according to his karma.
Having received the consecration of Laṅkā,
the wise Sena then made his friend Udaya the first prince and installed him as the heir apparent.
On the Uposatha day, that lord of men, having given a thousand kahāpaṇas to the destitute, remained an observer of the Uposatha for as long as he lived.
The lord of the earth also provided images, food, and clothing for the bhikkhus.
The wise one gave gifts to those who wielded power and to beggars and artisans.
Having had [dwellings] constructed for the artisans in various suitable places and in delightful palaces,
as well as in the village of Bhoga, he caused them to be provided with sustenance.
Having given either a thousand kahāpaṇas or five hundred,
he carried out new construction work on dilapidated dwellings in Laṅkā.
At the Abhayuttara Cetiya, forty thousand [kahāpaṇas were spent].
And the lord of the earth caused stone slabs to be laid down for paving.
In the great reservoirs of Laṅkā, he had the worn-out drains repaired,
carried out new construction work, and established embankments by means of stone and earth.
In the royal palace, he established a delightful and most costly flower-house;
having set it up, he again bestowed gifts and practiced generosity.
This was done by King Malaya, the chief minister Aggabodhi.
Having seen the Nāgasāla pariveṇa, he then rejoiced in the village.
